“哎呀，您停一停——别从我们这儿逃跑，”奇利太太说。“来同上校好好谈一谈，好孩子——可别莽撞。您*一定*要走，那就再见吧，”老太太说。他下楼去时，她满脸惊愕地坐着，望着马乔里班克斯小姐。“我是不是来得不是时候，露西拉？”奇利太太痛苦地说。“你回绝他了么，亲爱的？到底怎么回事？我怕死了我来得不是时候。”
“亲爱的奇利太太，”露西拉甜甜地说，“您从来不会来得不是时候；而且总的看，他没有——也好；我本来也没打算给他答复。恰恰相反，我确信这是天意，”马乔里班克斯小姐说；可是露西拉的心思这一回是否同她的话完全相符，却难说——虽然她那样和蔼，照奇利太太事后的说法。因为即使女人没把答复备好，她对求婚总存着几分好奇；何况这样一件精微的事被这样掐死在芽里，谁知它还会不会开花、还会不会畅吐衷肠？不能说马乔里班克斯小姐失望，可她无疑有点惋惜：不曾让他把话说完。至于奇利太太，等她明白了个中就里，懊丧得没法量，怎么也不能原谅自己扮演的那倒霉角色。
“你哪怕只说一声‘有客’呢，”老太太叫道，“或者‘不在家’——什么都行，露西拉！你知道，你同我从不须拘礼。难怪他那样子恨不得吃了我！可怜的人！我敢说他这会儿心里装得满满的走了，”奇利太太说，怀着最温柔的同情。这事她怎么也过不去，午饭吃不下，别的什么都不想。“可怜的宝贝孩子！犯不着同我这样一个老婆子这样不自在。他但凡给我一星暗示、甚至一个眼色，也该如何道我就会躲开的，”这位好心老太太说。“可他回来时，你要加倍待他好，露西拉。还有，亲爱的，我要是你，今天下午就守在家里。他准会回来，我不愿叫他悬着心。”

===Original===

“I don’t think he will come back,” Lucilla could not help saying; for she had a conviction that nothing more would come of it; but nevertheless she did stay in that afternoon, and received several visits, but saw nothing more of Mr. Cavendish. It was rather vexatious, to tell the truth; for to see a man so near the point and not even to have the satisfaction of refusing him, is naturally aggravating to a woman. But Miss Marjoribanks had far too much philosophy as well as good sense to be vexed on that account with Mrs. Chiley, who could not forgive herself, and to make up for the consequences of her unlucky visit, would have done anything in the world. The old lady herself returned in the afternoon to know the result, and was doubly vexed and distressed to hear he had not come back.

“I ought to be on the Archdeacon’s side, Lucilla,” she said, with tears in her eyes. “I know I ought, when it was I that brought him here: but I can’t help feeling for the other, my dear. He always was so nice﻿—a great deal nicer, to my way of thinking, than Mr. Beverley; not to say but that the Archdeacon is very agreeable,” Mrs. Chiley added, recollecting herself; for in matters of that description a woman of experience is aware that she cannot be too particular about what she says; and supposing that Mr. Cavendish did not come back, it would never do to prejudice Lucilla against the other candidate. “I never blamed Mr. Cavendish about that Lake girl,” the old lady continued. “It was not his fault, poor young man. I know he was always devoted to you in his heart; and to think he should come here the very first place as soon as he returned! I only wish I had had one of my headaches this morning, my dear, to keep me indoors for an old Malaprop. I do indeed, Lucilla. It would have served me right, and I should not have minded the pain.”

“But indeed I don’t wish anything of the sort,” said Miss Marjoribanks. “I would not have the best man in the world at the cost of one of those dreadful headaches of yours. It is so good of you to say so; but you know very well it is not that sort of thing I am thinking of. If I were to go off and marry just now, after all that has been done to the drawing-room and everything, I should feel as if I were swindling papa; and it is the object of my life to be a comfort to *him*.”

===Chinese===

“我想他不会回来了，”露西拉忍不住说；她确信这事不会再有下文；可她那天下午到底还是守在家里，接了几起客，却再没见卡文迪什先生的影儿。说老实话，这相当气人：眼看着一个男人逼到临门一脚，却连回绝他的那份快意都拿不到，女人自然觉得憋气。可马乔里班克斯小姐的哲学和常识都多得很，不至于为此怨奇利太太——老太太自己不能饶恕自己，为了弥补那次倒运来访的后果，叫她干什么都肯。老太太下午又亲自回来打听结果，听说他没再来，双倍地懊恼痛心。
“我本该站在会吏总一边，露西拉，”她眼里含着泪说。“我知道我该——是他我把带来的：可我总忍不住疼那一个，亲爱的。他一向那样好——照我的看法，比贝弗利先生好得多；这也不是说会吏总不可亲，”奇利太太又找补一句；因为在这一类事情上，有阅历的女人深知说话怎样仔细都不为过；倘若卡文迪什先生当真不回来了，叫露西拉对另一位候选人存了成见，那可了不得。“莱克那丫头的事，我从来没有怪过卡文迪什先生，”老太太接着说。“那不是他的错，可怜的年轻人。我知道他心里一向忠于你；你想想，他一回来，头一个就奔这儿来！我但愿今天早晨犯一场我的头疼，亲爱的，好把这样一个用错词的老太婆关在家里。真的，露西拉。那样才活该，那点疼我也不在乎。”
“可我实在不愿那样，”马乔里班克斯小姐说。“天下最好的男人，我也不要，若得拿您那可怕的头疼来换。您这样说太好了；可您非常清楚，我想的不是那种事。我若这就撒手嫁了人，客厅同一切都刚收拾停当，我岂不是像骗了爸爸；而我人生的目标，是做*他*的安慰。”

===Original===

“Yes, my dear,” said Mrs. Chiley, “but we must not neglect your own interest for all that. I think it is most likely he will come this evening. He has just come from the Continent, you know, where people do make calls in the evening. I meant to have asked you to come down to us, as we shall be all alone﻿—”

“All alone? Then where is the Archdeacon?” asked Lucilla.

“He has gone out to Sir John’s for a day or two, my dear,” said Mrs. Chiley, and she could not understand the little gleam of intelligence that shot into Lucilla’s eye. “He left word with me for you that he would be sure to be back before Thursday, but seeing Mr. Cavendish when I came in made me forget all about it. He would be quite distressed, poor man! if he thought I had forgotten to give you his message. I won’t ask you now to come down and cheer me up a little, Lucilla. I think poor Mr. Cavendish is sure to come this evening, and I will not stand in his way again. But, my dear, you must send me a little note after he has been. Now promise. I shall be quite in suspense all night.”

“Dear Mrs. Chiley, I don’t think he will come,” said Miss Marjoribanks. “For my part, I think it was providential your coming today﻿—for I am sure I don’t know what I should have said to him. And it is so odd the Archdeacon should be away just at this moment. I feel quite sure he will not come tonight.”

“There is nothing odd about the Archdeacon,” said Mrs. Chiley. “It was for today he was asked, you know; *that* is simple enough. If you are sure that you prefer the Archdeacon, my dear﻿—” the old lady added, with an anxious look. But Lucilla cut short the inquiry, which was becoming too serious, by bringing her kind visitor a cup of tea.

===Chinese===

“是，亲爱的，”奇利太太说，“可咱们也不能因此疏忽了你自身的利益。我看他今晚多半会来。他刚从欧洲大陆回来，你知道，那边的人兴晚间拜客。我本想请你下来陪陪我们，今晚我们冷冷清清——”
“冷冷清清？那会吏总呢？”露西拉问。
“他到约翰爵士家去了，住一两天，亲爱的，”奇利太太说；她看不愭露西拉眼里闪过的那一星机锋。“他留话给你，说礼拜四前一定回来；可我一进门看见卡文迪什先生，就全忘了。他若知道我忘了传话，准得难过，可怜的人！这会儿我就不清你下来给我解闷了，露西拉。我想可怜的卡文迪什先生今晚准来，我不再拦他的路了。可是，亲爱的，他来过之后，你得给我捎张小条来。现在就答应我。我要悬一整夜的心。”
“亲爱的奇利太太，我想他不会来，”马乔里班克斯小姐说。“拿我说，您今天来是天意——因为我实在不知道该对他说什么。会吏总偏偏这时候不在，也真怪。我确信他今晚不会来。”
“会吏总一点不怪，”奇利太太说。“人家请的就是今天，你知道；*这*再简单不过。你若断定你更中意会吏总，亲爱的——”老太太又说，一脸志忈。可露西拉端上一杯茶，截住了这句越来越认真的盘问。

===Original===

“I hope you don’t think I prefer any of them,” said the injured maiden. “If I had been thinking of that sort of thing, you know, I need never have come home. If they would only let one do one’s duty in peace and quiet,” said Lucilla, with a sigh; and to tell the truth, both the ladies had occasion on that trying afternoon for the consolation of their cup of tea. But while they were thus refreshing themselves, a conversation of a very different kind, yet affecting the same interests, was being carried on not very far off, under the shelter of a little flowery arbour in another of the embowered gardens of Grange Lane, where the subject was just then being discussed from the other side.

===Chinese===

“希望您别以为我更中意哪一个，”这位受了委屈的少女说。“我若想的是那种事，你知道，本来根本不必回家。他们若肯让人安安静静尽义务就好了，”露西拉叹一声说；而且说真的，在那个难堪的下午，两位太太都领受了茶杯的安慰。可就在她们这样滋润的当儿，一场性质全然不同、利害却是同一场的谈话，正在不远处进行——在格兰奇巷另一座花木掩映的园子里，一座小小的花棚下：同一个题目，正有人从另一面议论着。

## XX / 二十
===Original===

Mr. Woodburn’s house, everybody admitted, was one of the nicest in Carlingford; but that was not so visible out of doors as in. He was a great amateur of flowers and fruit, and had his garden lined on each side with greenhouses, which were no doubt very fine in their way, but somewhat spoiled the garden, which had not in the least the homely, luxuriant, old-fashioned look of the other gardens, where, for the most part, the flowers and shrubs grew as if they liked it and were at home﻿—whereas Mr. Woodburn’s flowerbeds were occupied only by tenants-at-will; but at one corner near the house there was a little arbour, so covered up and heaped over with clematis that even the Scotch gardener had not the heart to touch it. The mass was so perfect and yet so light that it was the most perfect hiding-place imaginable; and nobody who had not been in it could have suspected that there was a possibility of getting inside. Here Mrs. Woodburn and Mr. Cavendish were seated on this particular afternoon; she very eager, animated, and in earnest, he silent and leaning his head on his two hands in a sort of downcast, fallen way. Mrs. Woodburn had one of her lively eyes on the garden that nobody might enter unseen, and for this once was “taking off” no one, but was most emphatically and unquestionably herself.

“So you did not do it,” she said. “Why didn’t you do it? when you knew so much depended upon it! You know I did not wish for it myself, at first. But now since this man has come, and you have got into such a panic, and never will have the courage to face it out﻿—”

“How can I have the courage to face it out?” said Mr. Cavendish, with a groan. “It is all very easy for a woman to speak who has only to criticise other people. If you had to do it yourself﻿—”

“Ah, if I only had!” cried the sister. “You may be sure I would not make so much fuss. After all, what is there to do? Take your place in society, which you have worked for and won as honestly as anybody ever won it, and look another man in the face who is not half so clever nor so sensible as you are. Why, what can he say? If I only could do it, you may be sure I should not lose any time.”

“Yes,” said Mr. Cavendish, lifting his head. “To be sure, you’re a mimic﻿—you can assume any part you like; but I am not so clever. I tell you again, the only thing I can do is to go away﻿—”

===Chinese===

伍德伯恩先生的宅子，人人都承认，是卡灵福德最漂亮的人家之一；只是这漂亮在门外看不大出，要进了门才见。他是位花卉果品的大业余爱好者，花园两侧排满了暖房，暖房本身无疑各有其妙，却多少败坏了园子：别家的花园大都一派家常、繁茂、老式的光景，花木长得仿佛自己也乐意、也得其所；伍德伯恩先生的花坛里住的却只是一批随时可逐的佃户。不过近宅的一角有一座小凉亭，铁线莲层层覆压、堆得严严实实，连那位苏格兰园丁也下不去手。那团花簇既完足又轻盈，是天底下想得出的最好的藏身之所；不曾经身入内的人，断想不到这里面还钻得进去。这个特别的下午，伍德伯恩太太和卡文迪什先生便坐在这里：她热切、激昂、一本正经；他沉默着，两手托着额角，一副消沉潦倒的模样。伍德伯恩太太一只灵活的眼睛望着园子——谁也别想进来而不被看见——这一回她谁也不“学”，干干脆脆、明明白白是她本人。

“这么说你没有办，”她说。“你为什么不办？你知道这件事关系多大！你知道起先我自己也不愿意。可是如今这人来了，你又慌成这样，永远鼓不起胆量把它顶下去——”

“我怎么顶得下去？”卡文迪什先生呻吟着说。“女人家只消在旁边议论旁人，说起来自然容易。要是叫你自己去办——”

“啊，要是叫我去就好了！”做妹妹的喊道。“你放心，我决不这样大惊小怪。说到底，有什么可办的？照旧在你的社交位子上坐下去——那是你挣来的，挣得同谁一样清白——再同那个男人对脸看去，他还不及你一半聪明、一半明白。嘖，他能说什么？这事若交给我，你放心，我半点工夫也不耽搁。”

“是了，”卡文迪什先生抬起头来说。“你当然行——你是个模仿大家，什么角色都扮得来；我不行。我再说一遍，我唯一的出路是走——”

===Original===

“Run away, you mean,” said Mrs. Woodburn. “I should be foolish, indeed, if I were trusting to your cleverness to assume a part. My dear good brother, you would find it impossible to put yourself sufficiently in sympathy with another,” cried the mimic, in the Archdeacon’s very tone, with a laugh, and at the same time a little snarl of bitter contempt.

“Oh, for Heaven’s sake, Nelly, no foolery just now,” said Mr. Cavendish. “I don’t understand how you can be so heartless. To mimic a man who has my position, my reputation, my very existence in his hands!”

“Have you murdered anybody?” said Mrs. Woodburn, with intense scorn. “Have you robbed anybody? If you have, I can understand all this stuff. He is the very man to mimic, on the contrary. I’d like to let you see him as he was on that famous occasion when he delivered his opinions on art in Lucilla’s drawing-room. Look here,” said the mimic, putting one hand behind an imaginary coat tail, and with the other holding up a visionary drawing to the light; but this was more than her audience could bear.

“I think you must have vowed to drive me crazy,” cried the exasperated brother. “Put aside for once that confounded vanity of yours﻿—as if a man had always leisure to look at your playing the fool.” While he spoke in this unusual way, he got up, as was natural, and took one or two steps across the narrow space which was shut in by those luxuriant heaps of clematis; and Mrs. Woodburn, for her part, withdrew her chair out of his way in equal heat and indignation.

“You have always the leisure to play the fool yourselves, you men,” she said. “Vanity, indeed! as if it were not simply to show you that one can laugh at him without being stricken with thunder. But leave that if you like. You know quite well if you married Lucilla Marjoribanks that there would be no more about it. There *could* be no more about it. Why, all Grange Lane would be in a sort of way pledged to you. I don’t mean to say *I* am attached to Lucilla, but you used to be, or to give yourself out for being. You flirted with her dreadfully in the winter, I remember, when those terrible Woodburns were here,” she continued, with a shiver. “If you married Lucilla and got into Parliament, you might laugh at all the archdeacons in the world.”

“It is very easy for a woman to talk,” said the reluctant wooer again.

===Chinese===

“是逃跑，你的意思是，”伍德伯恩太太说。“我要是指望你的聪明来扮什么角色，那才是傻子。我亲爱的好哥哥，你要设身处地体察另一个人，那是万万不能的，”这位模仿家用会吏长本人的腔调喊道，笑了一声，同时夹着一点冷嘲的讥请。

“哦，看老天爷面上，内莉，这会儿别闹了，”卡文迪什先生说。“我不懂你怎么能这样没心肝。去学一个把我名位、名声、把我这条命都攒在手里的人！”

“你杀过人吗？”伍德伯恩太太带着极度的轻蔑说。“你抢过人吗？若是抢过，这一切名堂我就都懂了。恰恰相反，他正是顶好学的人。我倒要叫你看看他那回的光景——在露西拉客厅里大发艺术宏论的那一回。看这儿，”模仿家说着，一只手虚虚地别在想象中的燕尾后摆，另一只手把一张空中楼阁的画稿举向亮处；可这一下她的看客受不住了。

“你一定是立了誓要把我逼疯，”被激怒的哥哥喊道。“就把你那套该死的虚荣心搁下这一回吧——仿佛男人家永远有闲工夫看你出洋相似的。”他这样破例发作着，自然而然站起身来，在那铁线莲堆围出的一小方窄地里踱了一两步；伍德伯恩太太呢，也同样恼怒，把椅子挪开给他让路。

“你们男人家自己出洋相，倒永远有闲工夫，”她说。“还说虚荣！我无非叫你看看：笑他一笑，也天打不雷劈。这话搁下也随你。你清楚得很，你若娶了露西拉·马乔里班克斯，这事就再没有下文。*再不能有*下文。嘖，全格兰奇巷在某种意义上就都保了你的票。我不是说*我*同露西拉多亲，可你从前同她亲来着——至少放出那样的风声。那年冬天你同她调情调得吓人，我记得，正赶上那几个吓人的伍德伯恩家的亲戚在家，”她接着说，打了个寒嘣。“你要是娶了露西拉、再进了议会，天下的会吏长你尽可以一笑了之。”

“女人家说嘴总是容易，”这位勉强的求婚人又说。

===Original===

“I can tell you something it is not easy to do,” cried his sister. “It is frightfully hard for a woman to stand by and see a set of men making a mess of things, and not to dare to say a word till all is spoiled. What is this Archdeacon, I would like to know, or what could he say? If you only would have the least courage, and look him in the face, he would be disabled. As if no one had ever heard of mistaken identity before? And in the meantime go and see Lucilla, and get her consent. I can’t do that for you; but I could do a great deal of the rest, if you would only have a little pluck and not give in like this.”

“A *little* pluck, by George!” cried the unfortunate man, and he threw himself down again upon his chair. “I am not in love with Lucilla Marjoribanks, and I don’t want to marry her,” he added doggedly, and sat beating a tune with his fingers on the table, with but a poorly-assumed air of indifference. As for Mrs. Woodburn, she regarded him with a look of contempt.

“Perhaps you will tell me who you are in love with,” she said disdainfully; “but I did not ask to be taken into your confidence in such an interesting way. What I wish to know is, whether you want a wife who will keep your position for you. I am not in the least fond of her, but she is very clever. Whether you want the support of all the best people in Carlingford, and connections that would put *all that* to silence, and a real position of your own which nobody could interfere with﻿—that is what I want to know, Harry; as for the sentimental part, I am not so much interested about that,” said Mrs. Woodburn, with a contemptuous smile. She was young still, and she was handsome in her way (for people who liked that style), and it jarred a little on the natural feelings to hear a young wife express herself so disdainfully; but, to be sure, her brother was not unaccustomed to that.

“You said once that Woodburn was necessary to your happiness,” he said, with a mixture of scorn and appeal, “though I can’t say I saw it, for my part.”

===Chinese===

“我倒可以告诉你一件不容易的事，”他妹妹喊道。“眼睁睁看着一伙男人把事情搅成一团糟，不到全糟透不敢插一句嘴——这滋味，女人受来才叫可怕。我倒要问问，这个会吏长算什么，他能说什么？你只要有最小的一点胆量，同他对脸看去，他就残了。难道从前没人听说过认错了人？这其间你去看露西拉，把她的应允弄到手。这一件我替你办不了；可其余的，只要你有一点点胆气、不这样认输，我大半都替你办得来。”

“一点点胆气，好家伙！”那不幸的人喊道，又颓然倒回椅子上。“我并不爱露西拉·马乔里班克斯，我也不想娶她，”他执拗地补上一句，坐在那里用手指在桌上敲着一支曲子，装出一副淡漠的样子，只是装得不像。伍德伯恩太太则用轻蔑的眼色看着他。

“也许你要告诉我你爱的是谁，”她鄙夷地说；“我可没有求你用这样有趣的方式向我交心。我要知道的是：你到底要不要一位替你守住名位的太太。她半点不合我的喜欢，可她非常聪明。你到底要不要全卡灵福德最好人家的支持，要不要能把*这一切*压下去的姻亲，要不要一个谁也侵犯不动的、真正属于你自己的地位——我要知道的是这个，哈里；至于感情那一部分，我不大感兴趣，”伍德伯恩太太带着冷笑说。她还年轻，也有她那一路的姿色（对于喜欢那一款的人），一位年轻太太把话说得这样鄙夷，听在天然的感情里有点硌人；不过说真的，她哥哥对这种腔调原也听惯了。

“你从前说过，伍德伯恩是你幸福所必需的，”他说，一半讥请一半恳求，“虽然就我看，我并没有看出来。”

===Original===

“Did I?” she said, with a slight shrug of her shoulders; “I saw what was necessary on another score, as you don’t seem to do. When a man has nobody belonging to him, it is connections he ought to try for: and Lucilla has very good connections; and it would be as good as securing the support of Grange Lane. Do it for my sake, Harry, if you won’t do it for your own,” said Mrs. Woodburn, with a change of tone. “If you were to let things be said, and give people an advantage, think what would become of me. Woodburn would not mind so much if somebody else were involved; but oh, Harry! if he should find out *he* had been cheated, and he only﻿—”

“He was not cheated! You were always a great deal too good for him, Nelly,” said Mr. Cavendish, touched at last at an effectual point; “and as for *his* friends and family, and all that﻿—”

“Oh, please, don’t speak of them,” said Mrs. Woodburn, with a shudder; “but there are only two of us in the world; and, Harry, for my sake﻿—”

At this appeal Mr. Cavendish got up again, and began to pace the little arbour, two steps to the wall, and two steps back again. “I told you I had almost done it, when that confounded old woman came in,” he said: “that could not be called my fault?”

“And she said she was both your grandmothers,” said the mimic, with a slightly hysterical laugh, in Mrs. Chiley’s voice. “I know how she did it. She can’t be there still, you know﻿—go now and try.”

“Let alone a little; don’t hurry a fellow,” said her brother, somewhat sullenly; “a man can’t move himself up to the point of proposing twice in one day.”

“Then promise that you will do it tomorrow,” said Mrs. Woodburn. “I shall have to go in, for there is somebody coming. Harry, before I go, promise that you will do it tomorrow, for my sake.”

===Chinese===

“是吗？”她微微耸一耸肩说；“在另一层上什么必需，我可是看出来了——你好像还没看出来。一个男人举目无亲，就该往姻亲上用力：露西拉的姻亲很好；娶了她，等于把格兰奇巷的支持稳稳拿到手。为你自己你不肯办，那就为我办吧，哈里，”伍德伯恩太太换了口气说。“倘若你任凭人家说长道短、叫旁人占了先，想想我可怎么得了。若是牵连上别人，伍德伯恩倒不至于这样计较；可是啊，哈里！倘若他发现*他*一个人受了骗——”

“他没有受骗！你配他从来是太委屈了，内莉，”卡文迪什先生终于被戳中了一个痛处，“至于*他*那些朋友亲眷什么的——”

“哦，求你，别提他们，”伍德伯恩太太打了个寒嘣说；“这世上咱们只有两个人；哈里，看在我的份上——”

这一声恳求之下，卡文迪什先生又站起来，在那小凉亭里踱起步子：两步到墙，两步回来。“我告诉过你，我差一点就办了，偏偏那个可恶的老太太闯了进来，”他说，“总不能赖我吧？”

“她还说她一个顶你两位祖母呢，”模仿家用奇利太太的嗓音、带一点歇斯底里的笑说道。“我知道她是怎么搅的。她总不能还在那儿待着——这就去试试。”

“让人缓一缓；别逼人，”她哥哥有点闷闷地说；“一个人没法在同一天里把自己拔到求婚的高度两回。”

“那就答应我明天办，”伍德伯恩太太说。“我得进去了，有人要来。哈里，我走之前，答应我明天办，看在我的份上。”

===Original===

“Oh, bother!” said Mr. Cavendish; and it was all the answer he deigned to give before Mrs. Woodburn was called away, notwithstanding the adjuration she addressed to him. It was then getting late, too late, even had he been disposed for such an exertion, to try his fortunes again that day, and Lucilla’s allusion had given him a great longing to see Barbara once more before his sacrifice was accomplished. Not that it was such a great sacrifice, after all. For Mr. Cavendish was quite aware that Miss Marjoribanks was a far more suitable match for him than Barbara Lake, and he was not even disposed to offer himself and his name and fortune, such as they were, to the drawing-master’s daughter. But, to tell the truth, he was not a person of fixed and settled sentiments, as he ought to have been in order to triumph, as his sister desired, over the difficulties of his position. Perhaps Mrs. Woodburn herself would have done just the same, had it been she from whom action was demanded. But she was capable of much more spirited and determined conduct in theory, as was natural, and thought she could have done a great deal better, as so many women do.

===Chinese===

“哦，烦死了！”卡文迪什先生说；任凭伍德伯恩太太怎样叮嘱，他肯给的回答就这一句。随后她被唤了进去。这时天已晚，就算他还有意做这样的努力，当天也不便再去碰运气了；何况露西拉那一句话勾得他极想在牺牲成就之前，再见芭芭拉一面。说到底，这牺牲其实也没有那样大。卡文迪什先生很清楚，马乔里班克斯小姐做他的配偶，比芭芭拉·莱克合适得多；他甚至也不曾打算把他的名姓和家财——照实说也就那样——献给绘图教师的女儿。可是，说实话，他不是个情有定守的人；要照他妹妹期望的那样战胜处境的困难，他本该是个情有定守的人才对。倘若当初要行动的是伍德伯恩太太本人，说不定她也会照样办。只是在理论上她自然更波辣、更决断，心想自己会办得好得多——像天下许多女人一样。

===Original===

Mr. Cavendish lounged about the garden a little, with his hands in his pockets, and then strayed out quite accidentally, and in the same unpremeditating mood made his way to Grove Street. He meant nothing by it, and did not even inquire of himself where he was going, but only strolled out to take the air a little. And it was better to go up to the higher parts of the town than to linger here about Grange Lane, where all the people he knew might pass, and stop to talk and ask him where he had been, and worry his life out. And surely he had had enough of bother for one day. By this time it was getting dark, and it was very pleasant in Grove Street, where most of the good people had just watered their little gardens, and brought out the sweetness of the mignonette. Mr. Cavendish was not sentimental, but still the hour was not without its influence; and when he looked at the lights that began to appear in the parlour windows, and breathed in the odours from the little gardens, it is not to be denied that he asked himself for a moment what was the good of going through all this bother and vexation, and whether love in a cottage, with a little garden full of mignonette and a tolerable amount of comfort within, was not, after all, a great deal more reasonable than it looked at first sight? This, however, it must be allowed, was no conclusion arrived at on sufficient premises, and with the calmness that befitted such an important argument, but the mere suggestion, by the way, of an impatient, undecided mind, that did always what at the moment it found most agreeable to do, and reflected afterwards, when the moment of repentance, not of reflection, had arrived.

===Chinese===

卡文迪什先生两手插在口袋里，在园子里逛了一会儿，随后全然出于偶然地荡了出去，又怀着同样没主见的心绪，一路走到格罗夫街去了。他本来无所图，也不问自己要去哪里，不过是出来透透空气。往城的高处走走，总比在格兰奇巷一带流连强——这里熟人人人会撞见，会站住攀谈，问他去了哪里，烦死他。他这一天受的烦扰也尽够了。这时天黑下来，格罗夫街上很惬意：好人家多半刚给小花园浇过水，木樨草的甜香都引了出来。卡文迪什先生不多情善感，可这个时辰也不是全无影响；他望着一盏盏在客厅窗里亮起的灯，吸着小花园里飘来的香气，不能不承认他有一刻自问：受这一场烦恼折腾图个什么？小屋里的爱情，带一座满种木樨草的小花园、屋内有过得去的舒适，细想想，岂不是比乍看合理得多？不过得承认，这结论的前提并不充分，也没有这份重大论证所要求的镇定，不过是一个浮躁无断的心思顺路一闪——这心思向来是眼前什么最可意就做什么，事后悔恨的时刻到了——那原是悔恨、不是反省的时刻——才来想一想。

===Original===

He had paused by instinct under a lamp not yet lighted, which was almost opposite Mr. Lake’s house; and it was not his fault if he saw at the upper window a figure looking out, like Mariana, and sighing, “He cometh not.” Naturally the figure was concerned to find out who he was, and *he* was anxious to find out who was the figure. And, on the whole, it was in a very innocent manner that this entirely natural curiosity was satisfied. First the window was opened a little﻿—a very little, just enough to change the air﻿—and Mr. Cavendish down below heard the voice of Barbara singing softly up above, which settled the matter as to her identity. As to *his*, Barbara had never, from the first moment she perceived him, any doubt of that. Her heart leaped back, as she thought, to its right place when she first caught sight of that blessed apparition; and with her heart came the orange-flowers, and the wedding breakfast, and the veil of real Brussels for which Barbara had so much wept. She tried to sing something that would convey hope and assurance to her timid lover, according to romantic precedent; but her mind was far from being a prompt one, as has been said. Thus it was all in the most natural way that it came about. When Mr. Cavendish felt quite sure who it was, he took off his hat, which was only civil, and made a step or two forward; and then Barbara took the extreme step of going down to the door. No doubt it was an extreme step. Nothing but a great public aim, like that of Miss Marjoribanks, could have justified such a measure; but then Barbara, if she had not a great public, had at least a decided personal, purpose, and obeyed the impulse of that mingled inclination towards another and determination to have her own way, which in such a mind calls itself passion, and which sometimes, by sheer force of will, succeeds better than either genius or calculation. She went down to the door, all palpitating with renewed hope, and, at the same time, with the dread that he might escape her in the moment which was necessary for her passage downstairs. But when she opened the door and appeared with her cheeks glowing, and her eyes blazing, and her heart thumping in her breast, in the midst of that quiet twilight, the object of her hopes was still there.

===Chinese===

他凭着本能，在一盏尚未点亮的灯下站住了，那灯几乎正对着莱克先生的宅子；于是他望见楼上窗口有个身影朝外望着，像玛丽安娜，叹着“他还不来”。这自然怪不得他。那身影自然急着看清他是谁，*他*也急着看清那身影是谁。而总的说来，这份全然天然的好奇是循着极清白的方式满足的。先是窗户开了一条缝——很小的一条，刚够换换空气——楼下的卡文迪什先生听见楼上芭芭拉轻轻唱着的嗓音，她的身份就此定案。至于*他*的身份，芭芭拉从瞥见他的头一眼起就从未怀疑。她初见那可敬的身影，心便——如她所感——跳回了原位；随她的心一同回来的，还有橙花、喜宴，和那幅芭芭拉为之哭了多少场的真布鲁塞尔花边头纱。她想依着浪漫的成例，唱一支能给怯懦情人传去希望与担保的歌；可是如前所说，她的心思不灵敏。于是一切都以最自然的方式发生了。卡文迪什先生确知了那是谁，便脱下帽子——这不过是礼貌——又上前一两步；随后芭芭拉迈出了极端的一步：下楼到了门口。这无疑是极端的一步。除了马乔里班克斯小姐那样宏大的公众目标，没有什么能替这样一步辩护；可是芭芭拉纵然没有宏大的公众目标，至少有一个斩截的私人目标，顺服了那股又倾心又任性的冲动——在这样的心里，这冲动自称是激情，而且有时单凭意志的蛮力，比天才或算计都更成功。她下楼来到门口，满怀复燃的希望，同时生怕就在她下楼这一晌，他从她手里溜掉。可是当她打开门，红着脸、烈闪着眼、心口怦怦跳着，出现在那静谧的暮色里时，她的指望所寄还在那儿。

===Original===

He had even advanced a little, with an instinctive sense of her approach; and thus they met, the street being comparatively quiet just then, and the mignonette perfuming the air. To be sure, the poetry of the situation was of a homely order, for it was under a lamppost instead of a tree that the lover had placed himself; and it was not the dew, but the watering, that had brought out the odour of the mignonette; but then neither of the two were very poetical personages, and the accessories did perfectly well for them.

“Is it you, Mr. Cavendish? Goodness! I could not think who it was,” cried Barbara, out of breath.

“Yes, it is I. I thought, if I had an opportunity, I would ask how you were﻿—before I go away again,” said the imprudent man. He did not want to commit himself, but at the same time he was disposed to take the benefit of his position as a hero on the eve of departure. “I heard you had been ill.”

“Oh, no﻿—not ill,” said Barbara; and then she added, taking breath, “I am quite well now. Won’t you come in?”

===Chinese===

他甚至凭着感应她又来了、朝前挪了一点；他们就这样相遇了——街上那会儿正清静，木樨草香着空气。诚然，这局面里的诗意是家常一路的：情人站的是一根灯柱而不是一株树；引出木樨草香的不是露水，是浇花的水；可是他们两个都算不得多诗意的人物，这些点缀尽够他们受用了。

“是你吗，卡文迪什先生？天哪！我想不出是谁，”芭芭拉喘着气喊道。

“是，是我。我想着，若得机会，就问问你的近况——趁我再走以前，”这位冒失的人说。他不想把自己拴住，同时又乐得享一享临行英雄的地位。“听说你病了。”

“哦，不——不算病，”芭芭拉说；随后她喘定了又说，“我现在全好了。进来坐坐不好吗？”

===Original===

This was the perfectly simple and natural manner in which it occurred. There was nobody in, and Barbara did not see, any more than her lover did, why she should sacrifice any of her advantages. They were, on the whole, quite well matched, and stood in need of no special protection on either side. Though naturally Barbara, who felt by this time as if she could almost see the pattern of the real Brussels, had a much more serious object in view than Mr. Cavendish, who went in only because it was a pleasant thing to do at the moment, and offered him a little refuge from himself and his deliberations, and the decision which it was so necessary to come to. Thus it happened that when Mr. Lake and Rose came in from the evening walk they had been taking together, they found, to their great amazement, Barbara in the little parlour, singing to Mr. Cavendish, who had forgotten all about Grange Lane, and his dangers, and his hopes of better fortune, and was quite as much contented with the mellow contralto that delighted his ears, and the blazing scarlet bloom, and black level brows that pleased his eyes, as anybody could have desired. To be sure, he had not even yet given a thought to the wedding breakfast, which was all arranged already in the mind of the enchantress who thus held him in thrall; but perhaps that may be best accounted for by referring it to one of those indefinable peculiarities of difference that exist between the mind of woman and that of man.

===Chinese===

事情便是以这样再简单自然不过的方式发生的。家里没有人，芭芭拉同她的情人一样，看不出为什么该牺牲自己任何一点便宜。总的说来，他们俩倒是旗鼓相当，谁也不需特别的提防。虽然——此时几乎看得见那真布鲁塞尔花边花样的芭芭拉，眼里盯着的目标比卡文迪什先生严肃得多；他进去，只因为眼前这么做是件惬意事，能叫他暂避一避自己、避一避那些盘算和那个非下不可的决心。于是，莱克先生和罗斯傍晚散步回来——父女俩一路谈着威利、谈着艺术、互相指点着那些“效果”和“亮点”——却大为骇异地发现：小客厅里芭芭拉正给卡文迪什先生唱着歌，而这位早把格兰奇巷、把危险、把更好前程的指望忘了个干净，耳朵里灌着甜润的女低音、眼里看着烈红的面色和平直的黑眉，那份惬意，谁看了都满意。诚然，婚宴的事他至今连想也没想过，而那位把他迷住的巫女心里早都排布停当了；不过这也许最好归之于男女心思之间那种说不清的差异。

===Original===

When Mr. Lake and his daughter came in from their walk, and their talk about Willie, and about art, and about the “effects” and “bits” which Rose and her father mutually pointed out to each other, to find this unexpected conjunction in the parlour, their surprise, and indeed consternation, may be imagined. But it was only in the mind of Rose that the latter sentiment existed. As for Mr. Lake, he had long made up his mind how, as he said, “a man of superior position” ought to be received when he made his appearance in an artist’s house. Perhaps, to tell the truth, he forgot for the moment that his visitor was young, and his daughter very handsome, and that it was to visit Barbara and not himself that Mr. Cavendish had come. The little drawing-master would not suffer himself to be seduced by thoughts which were apart from the subject from carrying out his principles. When Mr. Cavendish rose up confused, with a look of being caught and found out, Mr. Lake held out his hand to him with perfect suavity﻿—“I have the pleasure of knowing you only by sight,” said the innocent father, “but I am very glad to make your acquaintance in my own house;” and as this was said with the conscious dignity of a man who knows that his house is not just an ordinary house, but one that naturally the patrician portion of the community, if they only knew it, would be glad to seek admittance to, the consequence was that Mr. Cavendish felt only the more and more confused.

“I happened to be passing,” he explained faintly, “and having heard that Miss Lake, whom I have had the pleasure of meeting﻿—”

===Chinese===

莱克先生同女儿散步回来——一路上谈着威利、谈着艺术、谈着父女俩互相指点的那些“效果”与“亮点”——撞见客厅里这意想不到的一对，他们的惊愕、乃至骇然，可以想见。不过骇然这份情绪只在罗斯心里。至于莱克先生，他早就拿定了主意：照他的说法，“一位身分优越的人”登艺术家的门，该怎样接待。也许，说句实话，他一时忘了来客年轻、女儿又生得十分好看，忘了卡文迪什先生是来看芭芭拉、不是来看他的。这位小小的绘图教师不肯让旁的心思诱他背离原则。卡文迪什先生慌慌张张站起来，一脸被拿住的狼狈，莱克先生却极温文地向他伸出手来——“我只是同您面熟，”这位天真的父亲说，“如今在我自己家里结识您，非常高兴”；这话是带着一种自觉的尊严说的——一个知道自家宅子不是寻常宅子、知道本城的贵种倘得知底细倒要巴望进来的人的尊严——结果是卡文迪什先生愈发慌了。

“我恰好路过，”他有气无力地解释道，“又听说莱克小姐——我有幸见过——”

===Original===

“I assure you,” said the drawing-master, “that I hail with satisfaction the appearance of a gentleman whose intelligence I have heard so much of. We artists are a little limited, to be sure; for life, you know, is short, and art is long, as the poet says; and our own occupation requires so much of our thoughts. But still we are sympathetic, Mr. Cavendish. We can understand other subjects of study, though we cannot share them. Yes, Barbara has been a little poorly﻿—but she does not look as if there was much the matter with her tonight. Ask for the lamp, Rose,” said Mr. Lake, with a little grandeur. There was no light in the room except the candles at the piano, which lighted that corner and left the rest of the apartment, small as it was, in comparative shade. There was something magnificent in the idea of adding the lamp to that illumination; but then it is true that, as Mr. Lake himself said, “every artist is a prodigal in his heart.”

Rose had been standing all this time with her hat on, looking at Mr. Cavendish like a little Gorgon. What did he want here? How had he been admitted? She scorned to go and interrogate the maid, which involved a kind of infidelity to her sister, but all the same she looked hard at Mr. Cavendish with a severity which had, on the whole, a reassuring effect upon him. For, to tell the truth, the benign reception which he was receiving from Mr. Lake, instead of setting the visitor at his ease, made him nervous; for he was not in the least aware of the heroic soul which existed in the drawing-master’s limited person. Mr. Cavendish thought nothing but that he was being “caught,” according to his own vulgar theory. He thought Barbara’s father was cringing to him, and playing the usual mean part of an interested parent who means to secure a good match for his daughter. But as for Rose, she evidently, either from jealousy or some other reason, was not in the plot. She stood apart and scowled, as well as she knew how, upon the intruder. “I suppose, papa,” said Rose, “Mr. Cavendish wished to hear Barbara sing, and she has been singing. She is always very good-natured in that way; but as we have none of us anything particular to do, I don’t see what need we have for a lamp.”

===Chinese===

“我向您担保，”绘图教师说，“一位才智如此闻名的绅士光临，我是欣然欢迎的。我们艺术家眼界不免窄些，这倒是真的；人生短，艺术长，诗人早说过了；本行的功课又占去我们这么多心思。但我们富于同情，卡文迪什先生。别的学问我们虽不能躬与，却能领会。是的，芭芭拉小意了一场——不过今晚看来并没有什么大碍。去把灯要点来，罗斯，”莱克先生带着一点雍容说。屋里除钢琴上的蜡烛，原没有别的光，照着那一角，把其余——屋子虽小——留在半暗里。再添一盏灯到这片照明里去，这想法里自有一种气象；而且，照莱克先生自己的说法，“每个艺术家骨子里都是挥霍的人”，这话也是真的。

罗斯一直站在那里，帽子也没摘，像一尊小小的戈耳工，瞪着卡文迪什先生。他来干什么？怎么放进来的？她不屑去盘问女仆——那是对姐姐的一种不忠——可她照样狠狠地盯着卡文迪什先生，那严厉倒总的说来叫他安了些心。因为，说实话，莱克先生这份厚待非但没叫来客自在，反倒叫他发慌；因为他全然不知绘图教师那具小小的身躯里住着一个英雄的灵魂。卡文迪什先生照他自己那套俗见，只当自己是被“拿住”了。他以为芭芭拉的父亲在向他巴结，扮演着那套庸俗的、存心给女儿攀高亲的家长角色。至于罗斯，她显然出于妒忌还是别的什么，不在局中。她站在一边，拿出全副本事对这闯入者怒目而视。“爸爸，我想，”罗斯说，“卡文迪什先生是想听芭芭拉唱歌，她也唱了。这方面她向来好说话；可我们谁都没有什么要紧事要干，我看不出有什么必要点灯。”

===Original===

At this trenchant speech Mr. Cavendish rose. He was quite grateful to the little Preraphaelite for her incivility. It made him feel less as if he had committed himself, and more as if he were an intruder, which was the more agreeable suggestion of the two under the present circumstances. “You remind me that I should thank Miss Lake for letting me come in and hear once more her lovely voice,” he said. “I am at present only a visitor in Carlingford, and indeed in England﻿—I may have to leave again in a day or two﻿—goodbye. If I am still here, I shall hope to meet you on Thursday.” And then he pressed Barbara’s hand, who, to tell the truth, was very reluctant to let him go away.

“If you must go﻿—” she said, so low that her father could not hear her, though the vigilant, suspicious little Rose caught the sound, and came a step nearer, like a little dragon, as Barbara was disposed to think she was.

“I *must* go,” murmured Mr. Cavendish; “but I shall see you﻿—we shall meet.” He dared not say another word, so alarming were the looks of the small Medusa, whose countenance he could see behind Barbara regarding the parting. As for Mr. Lake, he too regarded it with a momentary curiosity. He did not quite understand how it was that his daughter and his visitor could know each other well enough to communicate in this undertone.

“I am sorry to see so little of you,” said Mr. Lake. “I am afraid it is my little girl’s *brusque* way of speaking that hastens your going. I assure you we were quite unoccupied, and would have been very happy﻿—perhaps we may be more fortunate another time;” and with that the drawing-master gave a dignified dismissal to his surprising visitor. It was Rose herself who saw Mr. Cavendish to the door, which she opened for him with an utter disregard of his excuses and attempts to do that office for himself. She would not even shake hands, but made him the most majestic curtsey that was ever executed by a personage five feet high, under the influence of which Mr. Cavendish went away humbled, and, he could scarcely tell why, ashamed of himself. When Rose came back to the parlour, still with her hat on, she found that Barbara had gone to the window, and was looking out at the edge of the blind﻿—which was all that was wanted to put a climax to her sister’s exasperation.

===Chinese===

这一番锋利的话一出口，卡文迪什先生便起身了。他倒感激这位小小的拉斐尔前派的无礼。这叫他少觉几分自己已把话柄递了出去，多觉几分自己只是个闯入者——在眼前情形下，两样比起来，倒是后一样受用些。“承你提醒，我该谢谢莱克小姐许我进来，再听一次她可爱的歌喉，”他说。“我如今在卡灵福德不过是个客人，在英国也是——说不定一两天内又得走——再见了。倘若我还在，望礼拜四得见。”说完他握了握芭芭拉的手——说真的，芭芭拉很舍不得放他走。

“你既然非走——”她说，声音低得她父亲听不见，可是机警多疑的小罗斯捉住了这声音，朝前挪近一步，像一条小龙——照芭芭拉对她的看法。

“我*非走不可*，”卡文迪什先生低声说；“可我会再见你——我们会再见。”他不敢再多说一个字，那位小美杜莎的脸色太吓人了——他从芭芭拉肩后看得见她盯着这场话别。至于莱克先生，他也怀着一时好奇看着这场话别。他不大明白，他的女儿同这位来客怎么会熟到能用这样的低声耳语。

“同您聚得这样少，很遗憾，”莱克先生说。“怕是我小女*唐突*的口风催您走了。我向您担保我们实在闲着，本可以很高兴的——也许下次我们更有运气些；”说着，绘图教师体面地送走了他那惊人的客人。送卡文迪什先生到门口的正是罗斯本人，她替他开门，全然不理会他的推辞和想自己开门的尝试。她连手也不肯握，只朝他行了一个五英尺身量的人物所能行的最庄严的屈膝礼；卡文迪什先生在那礼下灰溜溜地走了，自己也说不清为什么，只觉得羞愧。罗斯回到客厅——帽子还戴着——发现芭芭拉已到了窗口，正从百叶帘边上朝外望——这一下恰好把她姐姐的怒火送上了顶点。

===Original===

“Papa,” said Rose, “I should like to know in your presence, or I should like you to ask Barbara herself, what is the meaning of all that has been going on tonight.”

Mr. Lake turned right round at this appeal with an expression of utter amaze and bewilderment, which at another moment would have struck Rose with the profoundest delight as a study; and as for Barbara, without any more ado she burst into a flood of passionate tears.

“Oh, you nasty, envious thing! oh, you jealous, disagreeable thing!” sobbed the elder sister; “to send him away and spoil everything with your airs! when he was as near﻿—just as near”﻿—but here Barbara’s voice lost itself in her tears.

“My dear, what does this mean?” said Mr. Lake.

“It means, papa, that she has encouraged him to come, and invited him in, and been singing to him,” cried Rose. “To think she should be one of us, and have no proper pride! If he was fond of her, he would tell her so, and ask your permission; but she is laying herself out to please *him*, and is content that they should all jeer at her in Lucilla’s parties, and say she is trying to catch him. I thought I could have died of shame when I saw him here tonight; and compromising you, as if that was why you were so civil. If it were for her good, do you think *I* would ever interfere?” cried Barbara’s guardian angel. At this point Rose herself would have liked excessively to cry, if the truth must be told; but Barbara had already appropriated that facile mode of expression, and the little artist scorned to copy. As for Mr. Lake, he turned from one to the other of his daughters with unmitigated consternation and dismay.

“It was all your coming in,” sobbed Barbara, “if you had only had the sense to see it. *That* was what he meant. If I was singing, it was just to pass the time; I know that was what he came for. And you to send him away with your airs!” cried the injured young woman. All this made up a scene entirely novel to the amazed father, who felt it his duty to put a stop to it, and yet could not tell what to say.

===Chinese===

“爸爸，”罗斯说，“我要当着你的面弄明白，或者请你问问芭芭拉本人：今晚这一切到底是怎么回事。”

这一声之下，莱克先生整个转过身来，满脸全然的错愕与迷惘——搁在别的时刻，这张脸在罗斯看来该是一幅多妙的研究；至于芭芭拉，二话不说，迸出一阵狂风暴雨般的眼泪。

“哦，你这个龌龊的、眼红的东西！哦，你这个嫉妒的、讨人嫌的东西！”做姐姐的抽噎着说；“把他赶走，拿你那套做派毁了一切！他差一点就——就差那么一点——”可芭芭拉的声音到这里就淹没在眼泪里了。

“亲爱的，这是怎么回事？”莱克先生说。

“是这样的，爸爸：她招他来，请他进屋，还唱歌给他听，”罗斯喊道。“想想她竟是我们家的人，却没有一点正当的自尊！他若真喜欢她，自会明说，来求你允许；可她一味地讨好*他*，人家在露西拉的聚会上拿她取笑、说她存心钓他，她也不在乎。今晚看见他在这儿，我羞得真想死；还连累你——仿佛你那份客气是为这个似的。倘若是为她好，你以为*我*肯来管这闲事？”芭芭拉的守护天使喊道。到这一步，说句实话，罗斯自己也极想哭一场；可是芭芭拉已经把这套现成的表达方式占了去，小小的艺术家不屑照抄。至于莱克先生，他从这张脸转到那张脸，惊骇惶恐得没了主张。

“都怪你们进来，”芭芭拉抽噎着说，“你要是有眼力，本来看得出。*那*才是他的意思。我唱歌，无非消磨时候；我知道他为这个来的。你倒拿你那套做派把他轰走了！”这位受了委屈的姑娘喊道。这一切在惊愕的父亲面前合成一个全然新奇的场面；他觉得有责任叫它停下，又不知说什么好。

===Original===

“Girls,” he began, with a trembling voice, “this is all perfectly new to me. I don’t understand. If Mr. Cavendish, or﻿—or anyone, wishes to pay his addresses to my daughter, it is, of course, his business to apply to me in the first place. Barbara, don’t cry. You know how I dislike to hear you cry,” said the poor man, gradually losing his head. “Don’t make a fuss, Rose; for Heaven’s sake, girls, can’t you say at once what you mean, and don’t worry me to death? Ah, if your poor mother had but been spared!” cried the unfortunate widower; and he had five daughters altogether, poor soul!﻿—and it was so easy to drive him out of his senses. At this point Rose intervened, and did what she could to calm matters down. Barbara, still sobbing, retired to her chamber; the boys came in from their cricket, and the little children had to be put to bed; and there was no one to attend to all these matters, in the absence of the eldest sister, except the little mistress of the School of Design, so that naturally all further explanation was postponed for this night.

===Chinese===

“孩子们，”他开口说，声音发颤，“这一切对我全然是新鲜的。我不明白。倘若卡文迪什先生，或者——随便哪一位，有意向我女儿求亲，那自然该先来找我。芭芭拉，别哭了。你们知道我最不爱听你哭，”可怜人说着，渐渐乱了方寸。“罗斯，也别闹了；孩子们，看老天爷面上，你们不能一口气把话说清么？别把我烦死了。唉，你们可怜的母亲要是还在！”这不幸的鳏夫喊道；他一共有五个女儿，可怜的人！——要把他逼疯原是极容易的。到这一步罗斯出来转圜，尽力把局面安抚下去。芭芭拉一路抽噎着回自己房里去了；男孩子们打完板球回来了，小的几个该上床了；大姐不在，这些事除了设计学校的小女主人再没有别人照管——于是进一步的解释自然顺延到了这一夜之外。

## XXI / 二十一
===Original===

It was thus that Mr. Cavendish, without particularly meaning it, impressed upon two interesting and amiable young women on the same day the conviction that he was about to propose, without in either case realising that expectation. After this last exploit he went home with his head more confused, and his will more undecided, than ever. For he had one of those perverse minds which cling to everything that is forbidden; and the idea that he ought not to have gone near Barbara Lake, and that he ought not to see her again, made him more anxious to seek her out and follow her than he had ever been before. If such a thing had been permissible in England as that a man might marry one wife for his liking and another for his interests, the matter might have been compromised by proposing to them both; and there cannot be a doubt that Lucilla, in such a case, would very soon have triumphed over her handsome, sullen, passionate rival. But then such a way of conciliating a man with himself does not exist in the British Islands, and consequently was not to be thought of. And to be sure, every time he came to think of it, Mr. Cavendish saw more and more clearly what a fool he would be to marry Barbara, who was evidently so ready to marry him. The same thing could not with any confidence be predicated of Miss Marjoribanks, though, if she were to accept him, and her father were to consent, nothing could be better for his interests. All this he felt, and yet an unconquerable reluctance kept him back. His history was not quite spotless, and there were chapters in it which he thought it would kill him to have brought before the public of Carlingford; but still he was far from being a bad fellow in his way. And down at the bottom of his heart, out of everybody’s sight, and unacknowledged even by himself, there was one little private nook full of gratitude to Lucilla. Though he scarcely knew what was passing at the moment, he knew, when he came to think of it, that she had saved him from the effects of his first panic at the unexpected appearance of Mr. Beverley. Perhaps it was partly this consciousness that made him so embarrassed in her presence; and he could not find it in his heart, with this sense of gratitude, to deceive her, and say he loved her, and ask her to marry him. To be sure, if Mr.

===Chinese===

卡文迪什先生便是这样，并非特别存心，却在同一天给两位有趣可爱的年轻女子各留下一个“他就要求婚”的确信，而又没在任何一个身上兑现那份指望。这最后一番功业之后，他回了家，脑袋比先前更乱，主意比先前更没个定。因为他是那路拗性子的头脑：凡是被禁的偏要抓牢；想到不该走近芭芭拉·莱克、不该再见她，他反而比先前任何时候更急于寻她、追她。倘若英格兰容得这样一种制度——一个男人可以娶一个合心意的太太、再娶一个合利益的太太——事情本可以两头一齐求了婚来折中；而且毫无疑问，真到那个地步，露西拉很快就可胜过她那位又美又阴又烈的情敌。可惜英伦三岛没有这样一套自我调和的办法，因而想也不用想。再说，确实，每回认真想起来，卡文迪什先生都越看越清：娶芭芭拉是傻瓜干的事——她显然巴不得嫁他。这话却不敢照样预许给马乔里班克斯小姐；虽然她若肯接受他、她父亲又肯点头，于他的利益再好不过。这一切他都感得到，然而一股征服不了的勉强把他拗在后头。他的历史并不全然清白，其中有几章，他想要是摊到卡灵福德的公众面前，非叫他死了不可；可他到底远不是那路坏人。而在他心底深处、人人看不见、连他自己也不认账的地方，有一个小小的私角，盛满了对露西拉的感激。当时虽浑然不觉，过后想起来，他知道：贝弗利先生意外现身、他头一阵惊惶时，是她救了他。也许正是这一半知觉，叫他在她面前那样窘；而且，怀着这份感激，他狠不下心欺骗她、说他爱她、求她嫁他。当然，卡文迪什

===Original===

Cavendish had been a very acute observer, he might have felt that Lucilla was quite able to take care of herself in such an emergency, and was at the least a match for him, however seductive he might appear to others; but then, few people are acute observers in a matter so entirely personal to themselves.

He felt furious with himself as he went home, and thought how foolish he had been ever to go near Barbara Lake in the present position of affairs; and yet he could not help feeling that it was more delightful to him to see the colour blaze into her cheeks, and the song rise like a bird from her full crimson lips, and that flush of excitement and triumph come from her eyes, than it could have been in any case to have been admitted to the same degree of intimacy with Lucilla, who was not in the least intoxicated by his presence. Thus the unfortunate man was torn asunder, not so much by love and duty, as by inclination and interest, though the inclination was not strong enough to have allowed of any great sacrifice, nor the interest sufficiently certain to have repaid the exertion. This only made it the more difficult to decide; and in his circumstances, and with the panic that pursued him, he did not feel it possible to adopt the only wise policy that remained to him, and wait.

===Chinese===

先生若是个极敏锐的观察者，本该觉出：这样的急难里露西拉完全照管得了自己，至少同他旗鼓相当——无论他在别人眼里怎样迷人；可是，在这种同自己切肤相关的事上，没有几个人是敏锐的观察者。
他一路回家，对自己窝火透了，想着事局这样，自己先前真是蠢，竟去招惹芭芭拉·莱克；可他又不能不觉得：看绯红烧上她的双颊、听歌像鸟儿一样从她饱满红润的唇间飞起、看兴奋和得胜从她眼睛里漫出来——这一切于他，比同露西拉亲密到同样地步更痛快——露西拉可一点不因他在场而陶然。这位不幸的人就这样被撕作两半：与其说是爱与责任，不如说是情性同利益；可情性又不够强，强到容得下什么大牺牲；利益又不够实，实到抵得过那番力气。这只会叫决断更难；以他的处境，加上追着他不放的惊惶，他只觉得唯一剩下的明智方针——等——他是采用不了了。

===Original===

As Mr. Cavendish was thus making his way home, horribly vexed and annoyed with himself, and avoiding Grange Lane as if the plague was in it, Miss Marjoribanks sat in her drawing-room alone, and thought the matter over. Certainly she had not expected him that evening, but still, when she heard ten o’clock strike, and felt that his coming now absolutely impossible, she was a little﻿—not exactly disappointed, but annoyed at herself for having felt a sort of expectation. Lucilla was not a person to hide her sentiments, or even to conceal a fact which was disagreeable to her amour propre. She had too thorough and well-founded a confidence in the natural interest of the world in all belonging to her to do that; so when ten o’clock had done striking, she opened her blotting-book and took one of her pretty sheets of paper, with Lucilla on it in delicate rose-tinted letters, the *L* very large, and the concluding letters very small, and dashed off her note to Mrs. Chiley. The Miss Blounts’ at Mount Pleasant had been one of the very first establishments to forsake the handwriting which was all corners, in favour of the bold running hand of the present female generation; and it was accordingly in a very free and strongly-characterised manuscript, black with much ink, that Miss Marjoribanks wrote:

**Dearest Mrs. Chiley**﻿—I never expected him to come, and he has not. I dare say he never meant it. I am so glad. It was Providence that sent you at that particular moment today.﻿—Always in haste, with fond love, your most truly affectionate

Lucilla.

===Chinese===

卡文迪什先生这样满腹自恼自恨地一路躲着格兰奇巷回家——仿佛巷里闹着瘟疫——马乔里班克斯小姐却独自坐在客厅里，把这事想了一遍。确实，她没指望他当晚来；可是，当十点钟敲响、他来是绝对不可能了的时候，她还是有点——说不准是失望，而是恼自己竟存过一种指望。露西拉不是藏感情的人，甚至不肯隐瞒一件有伤自尊的事实。她对全世界天然关注她的一切这点，信得太彻底、太有根据，不会那样做；于是十点钟敲完，她翻开吸墨纸夹，抽出一张她那漂亮信纸——纸上有露西拉的名字，淡淡的玫红字色，起首的*露*字顶大，收尾几个字母顶小——给奇利太太一挥而就。芒特普莱森特的布朗特小姐府上，是最早摡弃那种棱角满纸的手写体、改用当今女儿家这一手奔放行书的先驱宅第之一；于是马乔里班克斯小姐落笔的，是一笔十分自由、个性淋漓的墨迹，墨黑而饱满：

**最亲爱的奇利太太**——我从没指望他来，他果然没来。我敢说他从来没那个意思。我真高兴。今天在那个节骨眼上把您派来的，正是天意。——一如既往匆匆，怀着挚爱，您最亲爱忠实的

露西拉

===Original===

And when she had sent Thomas with this note, Miss Marjoribanks felt her mind relieved. Not that it had been much distressed before, but when she had put it in black and white, and concluded upon it, her satisfaction was more complete; and no such troublous thoughts as those which disturbed the hero of this day’s transactions﻿—no such wild tears as poured from the eyes of Barbara Lake﻿—interfered with the maidenly composure of Lucilla’s meditations. Notwithstanding all that people say to the contrary, there is a power in virtue which makes itself felt in such an emergency. Miss Marjoribanks could turn from Mr. Cavendish, who had thus failed to fulfil the demands of his position, to the serene idea of the Archdeacon, with that delightful consciousness of having nothing to reproach herself with, which is balm to a well-regulated mind. She had done her duty, whatever happened. She had not injudiciously discouraged nor encouraged the possible Member for Carlingford; and at the same time she was perfectly free to turn her attention to the possible Bishop; and neither in one case nor the other could anybody say that she had gone a step too far, or committed herself in any way whatsoever. While these consoling reflections were passing through Lucilla’s mind, Dr. Marjoribanks came upstairs, as had grown to be his custom lately. Sometimes he took a cup of tea, though it was against his principles, and sometimes he only sat by while his daughter had hers, and amused himself with her chat before he went to bed. He was later than usual tonight, and naturally the tea-tray had disappeared some time before. As for Lucilla, she did not for a moment permit her own preoccupation to interfere with the discharge of her immediate duty, which was unquestionably to be amusing and agreeable, and a comfort to her dear papa.

“So you had Cavendish here today?” said the Doctor. “What brought him here? What has he been doing? Since you and he are on such good terms, I hope he gave you an account of where he has been.”

===Chinese===

打发托马斯送出这张条子，马乔里班克斯小姐心头的事便落了地。倒不是先前有多少烦难；可是白纸黑字写下、作了结论，她的满意才更圆满；今日这桩公案中扰着男主角的那些纷乱的念头——从芭芭拉·莱克眼里涌出的那些狂泪——都不曾搅扰露西拉闺阁静思的端庄。尽管世人反着说的话很多，德性自有一种力量，在这样的关口自会显出来。马乔里班克斯小姐可以从这位辜负了其位置之要求的卡文迪什先生，转向会吏总那个安详的意念，怀着那种“无可自责”的甜蜜自觉——对一个有条不紊的头脑，那是香膏。她尽了她的本分，无论出什么事。她不曾失策地打击、也不曾失策地鼓动那位卡灵福德的可能议员；同时又全然自由地可以把注意力转向那位可能的主教；而无论这一头还是那一头，谁也不能说她走过了一步，或于名节有丝毫牵涉。这些自慰的念头正从露西拉心头流过，马乔里班克斯医生上楼来了——这已是他晚近的习惯。有时他喝一杯茶，虽然违他的原则；有时只在女儿用茶时坐在旁边，同她说笑一阵再就寝。今晚他比平常晚，茶盘自然早撤下去多时了。至于露西拉，她一刻也不容自己的心事妨碍眼前义务的履行——那义务无可置疑，就是有趣、可亲、做亲爱的爸爸的安慰。
“这么说，卡文迪什今天来过了？”医生说。“他来干什么？他这一向在做什么？你同他交情这样好，我希望他把去向对你交代了一番。”

===Original===

“He has been nursing a sick friend on﻿—the Continent,” said Lucilla, with that largeness of geographical expression which is natural to the insular mind. “Who are Mr. Cavendish’s friends, papa?” added Miss Marjoribanks, with confiding simplicity; and it was beautiful to see how the daughter looked up into her father’s face, with that angelic confidence in his knowledge on all subjects which is so rarely to be met with in the present generation. But it was not a question to which the Doctor found it easy to respond.

“Who are his friends?” said Dr. Marjoribanks. “He’s one of the Cavendishes, they say. We have all heard that. I never knew he had any friends; which is, after all, next best to having very good ones,” said the philosophical old Scotchman; and there, as it appeared, he was quite content to let the matter drop.

“I like to know who people belong to, for my part,” said Lucilla. “The Archdeacon, for example, one knows all about his friends. It’s a great deal nicer, you know, papa. Not that it matters in the least about the Cavendishes﻿—”

“Well, I should have thought not, after the way you made an end of him,” said the Doctor. “I hope he doesn’t mean to begin that nonsense over again, Lucilla. He is a good fellow enough, and I don’t mind asking him to my house; but it is quite a different thing to give him my daughter. He spends too much money, and I can’t see what real bottom he has. It may all flare up and come to nothing any day. Nobody can have any certainty with an expensive fellow like that,” said Dr. Marjoribanks. “There is no telling where he draws his income from; it isn’t from the land, and it isn’t from business; and if it’s money in the Funds﻿—”

“Dear papa,” said Lucilla, “if he had the Bank of England, it would not make any difference to me. I am not going to swindle you, after you have had the drawing-room done up, and everything. I said ten years, and I mean to keep to it﻿—if nothing very particular happens,” Miss Marjoribanks added prudently. “Most likely I shall begin to go off a little in ten years. And all I think of just now is to do my duty, and be a little comfort to you.”

===Chinese===

“他在欧洲大陆上照看一位害病的朋友，”露西拉说，用的是岛民头脑天生的那种地理上的宽泛。“卡文迪什先生的朋友们都是谁呢，爸爸？”马乔里班克斯小姐又说，一脸信托的天真；女儿仰望着父亲的脸，对他无所不知的知识怀着天使般的信心——这一代里已少见的景象，繁是好看。可这个问题，医生发现并不好答。
“他的朋友是谁？”马乔里班克斯医生说。“人家说他是卡文迪什家的一位。这话咱们都听过。我从不知道他有什么朋友；这嘛，终究仅次于有一班极好的朋友，”这位哲人般的苏格兰老头说；而且看起来，他满愿意就让这事到此为止。
“拿我说，我喜欢知道人是从哪儿出来的，”露西拉说。“比如会吏总，他的朋友咱们一清二楚。那就好得多，您知道，爸爸。倒不是说卡文迪什家有什么要紧——”
“是啊，照你把他了结的那副干净利落，我原也以为不要紧了，”医生说。“我希望他不打算把那套胡闹再从头来一遍，露西拉。他人不坏，请到家里来我不在乎；可把女儿给他，完全是另一回事。他花钱太洒，我看不出他有什么真实的底子。说不定哪天火光一闪，就什么都不是了。同这样一个挥霍的家伙，谁也拿不到准头，”马乔里班克斯医生说。“他的进项从哪儿来，没人说得清；不从地里来，不从生意上来；若是放在公债里的钱——”
“亲爱的爸爸，”露西拉说，“就算他坐拥英格兰银行，于我也毫无分别。客厅和一切都刚收拾好，我不打算骗了您。我说过十年，就打算守它十年——倘若不出什么特别的事，”马乔里班克斯小姐又谨慎地补一句。“多半到十年头上，我也该开始走下坡了。眼下我想的，只是尽我的本分，给您一点安慰。”

===Original===

Dr. Marjoribanks indulged in a faint “humph!” under his breath, as he lighted his candle; for, as has been already said, he was not a man to feel so keenly as some men might have felt the enthusiasm of filial devotion which beautified Lucilla’s life. But at the same time he had that respect for his daughter’s genius, which only experience could have impressed upon him; and he did not venture, or rather he did not think it necessary, to enter into any further explanations. Dr. Marjoribanks did not in the least degree share the nervousness of Mr. Cavendish, who was afraid of deceiving Lucilla. As for her father, he felt a consoling conviction that she was quite able to conduct her own affairs, and would do him no discredit in any engagements she might form. And at the same time he was amused by the idea that he might be swindled in respect to the drawing-room, if she married at this early moment. He took it for wit, when it was the most solid and sensible reality; but then, fortunately, the points in which he misapprehended her redounded as much to Lucilla’s credit, as those in which he seized her meaning clearest, so that on every side there was something to be gained.

===Chinese===

马乔里班克斯医生点蜡烛时，从鼻子里淡淡哼了一声；因为如前所说，女儿这份点缀了露西拉生平的孺慕热忱，他不比有些男人那样感受得深。但同时他对女儿的天才怀有那份敬意——唯有阅历才压得上身的敬意；他不敢——或者不如说，他觉得不必要——再作什么申说。马乔里班克斯医生丝毫没有卡文迪什先生那种紧张；后者怕的是欺骗露西拉。至于做父亲的，他怀着一种足以自慰的确信：她全然照管得了自己的事，无论订下什么名分，都不会叫他丢脸。同时，想到她若趁这个早岁嫁人，他就要在“客厅”这件事上受骗，他又觉好笑。他把这话当俏皮话听，殊不知那是最扎实不过的正经话；不过所幸，他误解她的那些地方，同他最懂她的那些地方一样，都给露西拉增光；于是面面都有赚头。

===Original===

And when Miss Marjoribanks too retired to her maidenly chamber, a sentiment of general content and satisfaction filled her mind. It is true that for the moment she had experienced a natural womanly vexation to see a proposal nipped in the bud. It annoyed her not so much on personal as on general principles; for Lucilla was aware that nothing could be more pernicious to a man than when thus brought to the very point to be thrown back again, and never permitted to produce that delicate bloom of his affections. It was like preventing a rose from putting forth its flowers, a cruelty equally prejudicial to the plant and to the world. But when this pang of wounded philanthropy was over, Miss Marjoribanks felt in her heart that it was Providence that had sent Mrs. Chiley at that special moment. There was no telling what embarrassments, what complications she might not have got into, had Mr. Cavendish succeeded in unbosoming himself. No doubt Lucilla had a confidence that, whatever difficulties there might have been, she would have extricated herself from them with satisfaction and even éclat, but still it was better to avoid the necessity. Thus it was with a serene conviction that “whatever is, is best,” that Miss Marjoribanks betook herself to her peaceful slumbers. There are so many people in the world who hold, or are tempted to hold, an entirely different opinion, that it is pleasant to linger over the spectacle of a mind so perfectly well regulated. Very different were the sentiments of Mr. Cavendish, who could not sleep for the ghosts that kept tugging at him on every side; and those of Barbara Lake, who felt that for her too the flower of her hero’s love had been nipped in the bud. But, to be sure, it is only natural that goodness and self-control should have the best of it sometimes even in this uncertain world.

===Chinese===

等马乔里班克斯小姐也退回她的闺房，一种总的满足与惬意充溢了她的心。不错，眼看一桩求婚掐死在芽里，她此刻是领受了一阵女人天性自然的懊恼。那懊恼，与其说是私人的，不如说是原则性的；因为露西拉深知：一个男人被这样逼到临门一脚又被摡回去、永不准他拿出他那份感情的娇嫩花朵，再没有比这更有害于他的了。这好比不许玫瑰开花，对植株、对世界，是同等的残害。可等这阵博爱受伤的刺痛过去，马乔里班克斯小姐心里认定：在那个千钧一发的时刻把奇利太太派来的，正是天意。倘若卡文迪什先生当真畅吐了衷肠，她会陷入什么样的窘境、什么样的纠葛，谁也说不准。无疑露西拉自信：无论困难多大，她都能脱身出来，脱得体面、甚至轰烈；可免掉这个必要总归更好。于是马乔里班克斯小姐带着“凡是存在的都是最好的”那一份宁静的确信，就了她安宁的睡眠。世上抱有、或受着诱惑要抱完全相反意见的人那样多，在一副调停得这样完美的心思上多流连一会儿，是件快事。卡文迪什先生的心情可大不相同——四面的鬼扯着他，叫他睡不着；芭芭拉·莱克的心情也不同——她觉得她那位英雄的爱情之花，也被掐死在芽里，于她自己。可是，确实，善与自制即便在这个无常的世界上也该有时占上风，这本是自然。

## XXII / 二十二
===Original===

The Archdeacon returned to Carlingford before Thursday, as he had anticipated; but in the interval Mr. Cavendish had not recovered his courage so far as to renew his visit to Miss Marjoribanks, or to face the man who had alarmed him so much. Everybody in Grange Lane remarked at the time how worried poor Mrs. Woodburn looked. Her eyes lost their brightness, which some people thought was the only beauty she had, and her nerves and her temper both failed her, no one could tell why. The personal sketches she made at this moment were truculent and bitter to an unheard-of degree. She took off Mr. Beverley with a savage force which electrified her audience, and put words into his mouth which everybody admitted were exactly like him, if he could ever be imagined to have fallen into the extraordinary circumstances in which the mimic placed him. In short, Mrs. Woodburn made a little drama out of the Archdeacon. Mr. Beverley, of course, knew nothing about this, and showed some surprise now and then at the restrained laughter which he heard in the corners; but when anybody spoke of Mrs. Woodburn, he showed an instinctive want of confidence. “I have not studied her sufficiently to give an opinion of her,” he said, which was certainly the very reverse of her deliverance upon him. To tell the truth, she had rather studied him too much, and gave too keen an edge to his characteristic qualities, as is natural to all literary portraiture, and even went so far that, in the end, people began to ask whether she had any personal spite against him.

===Chinese===

会吏长赶在礼拜四之前回到了卡灵福德，正如他预期的；可是这中间，卡文迪什先生始终没能把胆气养回到再访马乔里班克斯小姐、或同那个叫他那样惊惶的人对面的地步。格兰奇巷人人当时都议论：可怜的伍德伯恩太太一脸愁容。她那双眼睛失了光彩——有人认为那是她仅有的一点美——她的神经和脾气一齐失灵，谁也说不出缘故。她这个时期的私人速写，凶狠刻毒到前所未闻的地步。她学贝弗利先生，学得那么凶悍，叫她的看客触电，还往他嘴里安话——人人都承认，倘若真能想象他落进模仿家给他安的那等奇境，那些话就活脱是他。简而言之，伍德伯恩太太拿会吏长编了一出小戏。贝弗利先生自然毫不知情，只不时对他听见角落里憋着的笑声表示一点诧异；可是一有人提起伍德伯恩太太，他便露出一阵本能的不信任。“我对她的研究还不够，提不出意见，”他说——这同她对他的定评恰恰相反。说真的，她对他的研究毋宁说过了头，把他的特质磨得太锋利——这是一切文学肖像的通病——甚至到后来，人们开始问她是不是同他有什么私怨。

===Original===

“She don’t know him,” Mr. Woodburn said, when he heard some faint echo of this suggestion. “She’s clever, and it carries her away, you know. She enters into it so, she don’t know how far she is going; but I can answer for it she never saw the Archdeacon before; and Hal isn’t here to give her the keynote, as she says. *He* has met everybody, I believe, one place or another,” the simple man said, with a little natural pride; for in his heart he was vain of his fashionable brother-in-law. As for Mr. Cavendish himself, it began to be understood that he was with a friend who was sick, on the Continent; and soon﻿—for news had a wonderful tendency to increase and grow bigger as it spread in Grange Lane﻿—that his friend was dying, and that a probable large increase of fortune to the popular favourite would be the result, which was an idea that did credit to the imagination of Carlingford. He had disappeared completely once more after the eventful day which we have described, carrying out in the fullest way Lucilla’s prediction, but striking Barbara Lake with bitter disappointment. Miss Marjoribanks had a great many things to occupy her, but Barbara had nothing except the humble duty of looking after her little brothers and sisters, and attending to her father’s comfort, which had never been occupations particularly to her mind. And then Barbara was aware that, if she neglected her duties, Rose, on her return from the School of Design, would do them, though with a fierce little outbreak of indignation, which the elder sister felt she could bear; and accordingly, she did little else but brood over his sudden disappearance, and spend her time at the window looking for his return.

===Chinese===

“她不认识他，”伍德伯恩先生听见这话的一点风声尾巴，便说。“她聪明，一聪明就收不住，你知道。她入戏太深，自己也不知道走到多远了；可是我可以担保，她从来没有见过会吏长；哈尔又不在家，没法给她定调门，照她的说法。*他*倒是哪儿的人都见过，我相信，东一处西一处，”这老实人说，还带着一点天然的自豪；因为他心里原是以他那位时髦的内兄为荣的。至于卡文迪什先生本人，渐渐传开的是：他正在大陆上陪一位生病的朋友；不久——消息在格兰奇巷传着传着就有越长越大的神奇倾向——又传成那朋友快死了，结果这位大众宠儿多半要添一大笔家财，这想法倒给卡灵福德的想象力添了光彩。在我们描述过的那个多事之日以后，他又一次消失得无影无踪，把露西拉的预言应验了个十足，却叫芭芭拉·莱克失望得心口发苦。马乔里班克斯小姐有的是事情占心，芭芭拉却什么也没有，只有照料幼弟幼妹、照管父亲起居这份低微的本分——这些从来算不得她特别爱做的事。再说芭芭拉知道，她若掠了这些本分，罗斯从设计学校回来也会做，只是要带一场凶小的发作——做姐姐的自觉这还受得住；于是她终日无所事事，只是闷想着他的突然失踪，把时间都耗在窗口，盼他回来。

===Original===

Lucilla conducted herself, as might have been expected, in a much more rational and dignified manner. She made herself very agreeable to the Archdeacon, who unbended very much, and grew very nice, as Mrs. Chiley herself allowed. “But, my dear, I am uneasy about his opinions,” the old lady said. He certainly had a very free way of talking, and was ready to discuss *anything*, and was not approved of by Mr. Bury. But still he had very good connections and a nice position, and had always a chance of being Bishop of Carlingford; and in marriage it is well known that one never can have everything one wants. So that, on the whole, even Mrs. Chiley did not see what difference his opinions made, so far as Lucilla was concerned. When Miss Marjoribanks went down to Colonel Chiley’s in the evening and made tea for the old people, like a daughter of the house, Mr. Beverley was always disposed to go over to the enemy, as the old Colonel said. No doubt he had enough of Colonel Chiley, who had not received a new idea into his mind since the battle of Waterloo, and did not see what people had to do with such nonsense. And then the Archdeacon would very often walk home with the young visitor. During this time, as was natural, Mr. Beverley heard Mr. Cavendish’s name a hundred times, and regretted, like all the world, that so eminent a member of the Carlingford commonwealth should be absent during his visit; but, at the same time, Lucilla took great care to avoid all personalities, and kept a discreet silence even about the gifts and accomplishments of her almost-lover. Mrs. Chiley sighed, poor soul, when she saw how her young friend avoided this subject, and thought sometimes that he was forgotten, sometimes that the poor dear was breaking her heart for him; but it is needless to say that neither of these suppositions was in the least true.

===Chinese===

露西拉的行止，不出所料，理性而有尊严得多。她对会吏长极其和婉可亲，会吏长也大大松弛下来，变得很可爱——连奇利太太自己也承认。“可是，亲爱的，我不放心他的见解，”老太太说。他谈吐确实很随便，什么都肯讨论，伯里先生便不以为然。可是他姻亲很好、地位很好，说不定哪天就当上卡灵福德的主教；而婚姻大事，谁都知道，从不能样样如意。所以总的说来，就连奇利太太也看不出：就露西拉而论，他的见解能碍着什么。马乔里班克斯小姐晚上到奇利上校家去、像个自家女儿似的给两位老人斟茶的时候，贝弗利先生总倾向于倒向敌方——照老上校的说法。他无疑受够了奇利上校——这位老先生自滑铁卢一战之后再没往脑子里进过一个新见解，也看不出人们同那些胡扯有什么相干。而会吏长又常常陪这位年轻访客走路回家。这段日子里，贝弗利先生自然把卡文迪什先生的名字听了百十来遍，也同世人一样惋惜：卡灵福德邦国如此显赫的一员，竟在他访问期间缺席；但同时，露西拉小心地避开一切私人话题，连她那位“准情人”的天赋才艺也绝口不提。奇利太太看见年轻朋友避开这个话题，可怜的人，叹气；有时想他是被忘了，有时想这可怜的宝贝正为他心碎；可不用说，这两个设想没有一个是真的。

===Original===

And then it began to be considered rather odd in Carlingford that the Archdeacon should pay such a long visit. Mrs. Chiley no doubt was very kind and hospitable, and exceedingly glad to receive such a distinguished clergyman; but when a man has been six weeks in anyone’s house, and shows no inclination of going, it is natural that people should feel a little surprised. His visitation was over, and he had dined with everybody, and studied the place and its characteristics, and entered into everything that was going on. The only thing, indeed, that he did not seem to think of, was going away. If it had been Mr. Cavendish, the chances are that he would have made himself so much one of the family, that his departure would have been felt as a domestic calamity; but the Archdeacon was very different from Mr. Cavendish. So long as he was in the house it was impossible to forget either his position or his ways of thinking, or the absence of any real connection between himself and his hosts. He did not combat or contradict anybody, but he would give a faint smile when the Colonel uttered his old-fashioned sentiments, which drove the old soldier frantic. “As if I was not able to form an opinion, by Jove!” Colonel Chiley said; while, on the other hand, the Archdeacon was quite ready to enter into the young people’s absurd theories, and discuss the very Bible itself, as if that were a book to be discussed. As for the Rector, he turned his head away when he passed Colonel Chiley’s door, and Miss Bury made visits of condolence and sympathy. “You must feel it a great responsibility having Mr. Beverley with you,” the Rector’s sister would say, though naturally without any distinct explanation of her meaning; and then she would look at Mrs. Chiley and sigh.

“Oh, I am sure it is a great pleasure,” Mrs. Chiley answered, not willing to let down the prestige of her guest. “He is very nice, and takes a great deal of interest in everything; and then, you know, he is a connection of ours. The Colonel’s niece, Mary Chiley﻿—”

“Yes, I know,” said Miss Bury. “Poor thing! she looked suffering the last time I saw her. I hope she has found the true consolation to support her, now she has entered into the troubles of life.”

===Chinese===

跟着，卡灵福德渐渐觉得奇怪了：会吏长怎么作起这样长的客来。奇利太太自然又好心又好客，得了这样一位知名教士做客，欢喜不尽；可是一个人在谁家住了六个星期、又毫无去意，人们自然要有点惊异。他的巡访职务早完了，家家都请他吃过饭，地方和风物他研究够了，进行中的一切他都参与了。唯一像是想不到的事，就是走。倘若来的是卡文迪什先生，多半早把自己融成这家的一分子，他一走便要算一场家庭的不幸；会吏长却同卡文迪什先生大不相同。他只要在宅里，人便忘不掉他的地位、他的思路、以及他同主人家之间那份并无真正烟亲的干系。他不驳谁、不顶谁，可是上校一发他那老派的议论，他便淡淡一笑，笑得老兵发狂。“仿佛我就不配有个见解似的，天晓得！”奇利上校说；另一面，会吏长又极肯附和年轻人的荒唐理论，连《圣经》本身也拿来讨论，仿佛那是本供讨论的书。至于教区长，他路过奇利上校家门口就把头扭开，伯里小姐则一趟一趟来吊慰。“家里住着贝弗利先生，您一定觉得责任重大，”教区长的姐姐总这样说，自然从不说清她的意思；说罢便望着奇利太太叹气。

“哦，我相信这是极大的乐事，”奇利太太答道，不愿折了客人的威望。“他很好，样样都有兴致；再说您知道，他是我们的亲戚。上校的侄女，玛丽·奇利——”

“是，我知道，”伯里小姐说。“可怜的人！我上回见她，一脸病容。但愿她既已入了人生的忧患，已寻得真正的安慰扶持她。”

===Original===

“Well, yes, I hope so,” said Mrs. Chiley, a little doubtfully; “but you know one does not feel the troubles of life very severely at her age; and I don’t think I should have called a baby a trouble when I was like her. I never had any, you know, and I used to fret over it a great deal; but the Colonel never liked the noise of children, and I suppose it is all for the best.”

“One may always be sure of that,” said Miss Bury, in her instructive way. “I suppose the Archdeacon is going soon,” she added; “he has been here a long time now. I almost wonder he likes to be so long absent from his parish. Two months, is it not?”

“Oh, no﻿—not quite six weeks,” said Mrs. Chiley briskly. “I hope he may be persuaded to stay some time longer. I look upon it as quite a compliment to Carlingford; for, to be sure, he would not stay if he had not some attraction,” said the imprudent old woman. And this was precisely what Miss Bury wanted, as anyone of acute perceptions might have seen from the first.

===Chinese===

“呃，但愿如此，”奇利太太说，带点迟疑；“可你知道，她那样年纪的人受人生的忧患也受得不重；换了我像她那时，我可不会把一个娃娃叫忧患。您知道，我一个也没有生过，从前为这个难过了好一阵；可是上校嫌孩子闹，我想这样也自有它的好处。”

“那是一定的，”伯里小姐以她那教诲的口气说。“会吏长快要走了吧，”她又添一句；“他来得很久了。他离了教区这样久还住得惯，我几乎奇怪。两个月了吧？”

“哦，不——不到六个星期，”奇利太太爽快地说。“我巴不得劝他再多住些时。我看这是对卡灵福德的一番抬举；因为他要是没有什么吸引，自然不会住的，”这位不谨慎的老太太说。而这恰恰是伯里小姐所要的——凡眼力稍尖的人，本来一开始就看得出。

===Original===

“It must be a great responsibility for you,” said the Rector’s sister, with a sigh, pressing Mrs. Chiley’s hand. “If it should turn out badly, you know﻿—Of course, my brother and I don’t agree with Mr. Beverley on all points﻿—though I am sure I hope he is quite conscientious; but I do feel for you with such a responsibility,” said Miss Bury, with a look that made the old lady nervous in spite of herself. Thus, notwithstanding all her sense of the duties of hospitality, and her anxiety about Lucilla’s interests, she could not but feel that it would be rather a relief to get so formidable a guest fairly out of the house. It is uncomfortable, it must be allowed, to entertain in your house anybody, particularly a clergyman of whom your Rector does not approve; and there could be no doubt that the Archdeacon was not like the clergymen that Mrs. Chiley had been accustomed to. “And he could come back another time,” she said to herself, by way of conciliating her own weariness with her visitor’s advantage and the interests of Lucilla. But notwithstanding these reflections on Mrs. Chiley’s part and notwithstanding the Colonel’s less amiable growl, uttered every morning﻿—“Does that parson of yours never mean to go away?”﻿—the Archdeacon showed no intention of budging. It was poor Mrs. Chiley who had all the brunt to bear, to exhaust herself in civilities and to be upbraided with “that parson of yours”﻿—whereas he was not in the least her parson, nor even the kind of man she approved of as a clergyman. All this, however, the brave old woman bore with fortitude for Lucilla’s sake: certainly it must be Lucilla who kept him in Carlingford﻿—if it were not something else.

===Chinese===

“这对您一定是一副重担，”教区长的姐姐说着叹了口气，握住奇利太太的手。“倘若到头来坏了事，您知道——当然，家兄同我并不处处赞同贝弗利先生——虽然我诚心希望他全然出于良知；可您担着这样一副担子，我真替您难受，”伯里小姐说，那眼色叫老太太不由自主地发慌。于是，纵然她满心好客的本分、又挂虑露西拉的利益，也不能不觉得：把这样一位可畏的客人妥妥送出门，倒是松一口气。在自己家里款待一个自家教区长不以为然的人——尤其是一位教士——那滋味，得承认，是不好受的；而会吏长也确实不像奇利太太向来交往惯的那一类教士。“他下回还可以再来嘛，”她对自己说，拿这个来调停自家的厌倦同客人的利益以及露西拉的利益。可是，尽管奇利太太有这样一番想头，尽管上校每天早晨都发一遍不那么客气的哠哠——“你那位牧师到底走不走了？”——会吏长却毫无挪窝的意思。苦的是奇利太太：殷勤要她一个人撑，“你那位牧师”的数落要她一个人受——可他又根本不是她的牧师，连她中意的那一类教士都不是。这一切，这位勇敢的老太太都为露西拉的缘故坚忍地受了：把他留在卡灵福德的一定是露西拉——若不是另有缘故的话。

===Original===

Things were in this condition, Mr. Cavendish having again disappeared into utter darkness, and Carlingford beginning to enter warmly into the question whether or not Mr. Beverley was paying attention to Lucilla, when it happened to Miss Marjoribanks one morning to meet the Archdeacon in a little lane running between Grove Street and Grange Lane. Opening from this lane was a little door in the wall, which admitted to a little garden very bright with flowers of the simplest old-fashioned kinds, with a little house planted at its extremity, which had pretensions to be an old-fashioned and quasi-rural cottage, on the score of being very rickety, uncomfortable, and badly arranged. But it must be a very impracticable erection indeed which does not look tolerable under the bright sunshine on a summer noon, at the end of a pretty garden where children are playing and birds singing, and a woman or two about. Lucilla was standing at the door of this little closed-up hermitage, almost filling up the opening with her crisp summer draperies, and affording only a very partial and tempting glimpse of its flowers and shrubs and whitewashed walls inside; and when Mr. Beverley came up to Miss Marjoribanks he felt his curiosity excited. “Is it Armida’s garden, or the Elysian fields﻿—” said the Archdeacon; and he made a dead stop before the door, not knowing any more than any other blind mortal what he was going to find inside.

“I don’t know anything about Armida,” said Miss Marjoribanks; “unfortunately they were all Cambridge in their ways of thinking at Mount Pleasant, and our classics got dreadfully neglected. But you may come in if you like﻿—at least I think you may come in, if you will promise not to frighten the children. I am sure they never saw an Archdeacon in their lives.”

“Are there children?” said Mr. Beverley, with a doubtful air; for, to tell the truth, he had come to the age at which men think it best to avoid children, unless, indeed, they happen to have a personal interest in them; and he stretched his neck a little to see in over Miss Marjoribanks’s head.

===Chinese===

事势便是如此：卡文迪什先生又消失得无影无踪，卡灵福德正起劲地争论贝弗利先生究竟是不是在向露西拉献殷勤；就在这时，一天早晨，马乔里班克斯小姐恰巧在格罗夫街与格兰奇巷之间一条小巷里迎面遇上了会吏长。这条小巷的墙上开着一扇小门，进去是一座小花园，满种着最朴素老式的花，明艳照眼；园子尽头贴着一所小屋，凭着自己摇摇欲坠、住着别扭、格局糟糕，自命为一座老式半村舍。可是，夏日的正午，明亮的阳光下，在一座漂亮花园的尽头——孩子们在玩耍，鸟在叫，一两个女人在旁边——再不像样的建筑也看着过得去了。露西拉正站在这座封闭小隐庐的门洞里，一身窸窣作响的夏裙几乎堵满了门口，只叫人窥见里面一角撩人的花木和粉墙；贝弗利先生走到马乔里班克斯小姐跟前，好奇心被勾起来了。“这是阿尔米达的花园呢，还是极乐的原野——”会吏长说；他在门前死死站住，同任何瞎眼的凡人一样，不知道自己将在这门里撞见什么。

“阿尔米达我一无所知，”马乔里班克斯小姐说；“不巧，芒特普莱森特（Mount Pleasant）的先生们思想上一律是剑桥一路，我们的古典学荒疏得厉害。可你愿意就进来——至少我想你可以进来，只要你答应不吓着孩子们。我担保他们生平没见过会吏长。”

“还有孩子们？”贝弗利先生带着迟疑的神气说；因为，说实话，他已到了男人们认为最好躲开孩子的年纪——除非恰好同孩子有切身利害；他从马乔里班克斯小姐的头顶上略略伸长脖子往里张。

===Original===

“There are a whole lot of children, and a pretty governess,” said Lucilla. “It is a school, and I am so much interested in it. I may call it my school, for that matter. I came to know her in the funniest way; but I will tell you that another time. And it was just my luck, as usual. She is so nice, and quite a lady. If you will not say you are an Archdeacon, to frighten the children, I will let you come in.”

“You shall call me whatever you like,” said Mr. Beverley; “when I am with the lady-patroness, what does it matter what I call myself? Let me see how you manage your educational department. I have already bowed before your genius in the other branches of government; but this ought to be more in my own way.”

“I don’t think you care for visiting schools,” said Lucilla. “I know you think it is a bore; but she is so nice, and so nice-looking; I am sure you will be pleased with her. I am quite sure she is a lady, and has seen better days.”

“Oh, those dreadful women that have seen better days!” said the Archdeacon; “I think Mrs. Chiley has a regiment of them. It is hard to know how to get one’s self into sympathy with those faded existences. They fill me with an infinite pity; but then what can one do? If one tries to recall them to the past, it sounds like mockery﻿—and if one speaks of the present, it wounds their feelings. It is a great social difficulty,” said Mr. Beverley; and he fixed his eyes on the ground and entered meditatively, without looking where he was going, in his Broad-Church way.

“Dear Mrs. Chiley is so kind,” said Lucilla, who was a little puzzled for the moment, and did not know what to say.

===Chinese===

“有一大群孩子，还有一位漂亮的女教师，”露西拉说。“是一所学校，我对它关心极了。也不妨说是我的学校。我认识她的经过有趣极了；那个改天告诉你。又是我素来的运气。她人那么好，十足的大家风范。只要你不说自己是会吏长、吓着孩子们，我就放你进来。”

“你叫我什么都行，”贝弗利先生说；“跟着女保护人，我自称什么又有什么要紧？让我看看你怎样办你的教育部。你治理其他各部的天才我已拜服过了；可这一项总该更合我本行些。”

“我看你不爱参观学校，”露西拉说。“我知道你觉得腻烦；可她人那么好，人又那么好看；我担保你会喜欢她。我拿得准她是位大家闺秀，见过好日子。”

“哦，那些见过好日的可怕的女人们！”会吏长说；“我看奇利太太就养着一整团这样的人。要把自己调到同那些褪了色的存在合拍，真难。她们叫我满心无限的怜悯；可又有什么办法呢？同她们提从前，听着像讥唱——谈眼前，又伤她们的心。这是一大社交难题，”贝弗利先生说；他两眼望着地上，一路沉思着走进去，也不看走向哪里，一副广教会派做派。

“亲爱的奇利太太人真好，”露西拉说，一时有点茫然，不知说什么好。

===Original===

“Mrs. Chiley is a good, pure, gentle woman,” said the Archdeacon. He spoke in a tone which settled the question, and from which there was no appeal; and no doubt what he said was perfectly true, though it was not a very distinct characterisation. Thus they went in together into the bright little garden, thinking of nothing in particular, and loitering as people do who do not know what is coming. There was something that morning in Mr. Beverley’s tone and manner which struck Lucilla as something more than usual. She was not a young woman to attach undue importance to looks and tones; but the Archdeacon’s manner was so softened and mellowed, and his eyes had so much expression in them, and he looked at Lucilla with such marked regard, that it was impossible for her not to recognise that a crisis might be approaching. To be sure, it was not by any means so near as that crisis manqué which had so lately passed over her head in respect to Mr. Cavendish. But still Miss Marjoribanks could not but remark the signs of a slowly approaching and most likely more important climax; and as she remarked it, Lucilla naturally by anticipation prepared herself for the coming event that thus threw a shadow upon her. She did not make up her mind to accept Mr. Beverley any more than she had made up her mind to accept Mr. Cavendish; but she thought it only her duty to him and to herself, and to society in general, to take his claims into full consideration. And no doubt, if these claims had seemed to her sufficiently strong to merit such a reward, Miss Marjoribanks had it in her to marry the Archdeacon, and make him an admirable wife, though she was not at the present moment, so far as she was aware, absolutely what foolish people call in love with him. At the same time, she made herself all the more agreeable to Mr. Beverley from her sense of the dawn of tenderness with which he regarded her. And in this way they went up the broad central path which traversed the little garden, neither looking to the left nor the right, but presenting all that appearance of being occupied with each other, which, especially to a female observer, is so easy of interpretation. For, to be sure, the Archdeacon had not the remotest idea into whose house he was going, nor who it was whom he was about to see.

===Chinese===

“奇利太太是个善良、纯净、温柔的女人，”会吏长说。他这口吻把问题一锤定音，再无上诉；他说的无疑全然是真话，虽然算不得多有特色的定评。他们就这样一同走进那座明亮的小花园，心里并无一定的想头，像不知将要发生什么的人们那样信步走着。那天早晨，贝弗利先生的声口和举止里有点什么，给了露西拉超出寻常的印象。她不是那种把眼色声口看得过重的年轻女子；可是会吏长的态度那样温柔熨帖，他眼里那样有话，望着露西拉的那份关切那样分明，她不能不承认：一场关口也许正在逼近。诚然，这关口远不及方才从她头顶上过去的、关于卡文迪什先生的那场未遂的关口来得切近。可是马乔里班克斯小姐不能不注意到那缓慢逼近的、多半也更重大的顶点的种种征兆；她一注意到，露西拉自然预先为这桩向她投下阴影的事件做了准备。她同不曾打定主意接受卡文迪什先生一样，也不曾打定主意接受贝弗利先生；可是她认为，为他、为她自己、也为全社会计，把他的权利全盘掂量一番，正是她的本分。而且毫无疑问，倘若这些权利在她看来强大到配得上那样的报偿，马乔里班克斯小姐完全嫁得成会吏长，也做得出他出色的太太——尽管就此刻她的自知而言，她并不是蠢人们所谓的在爱着他。同时，觉出他看她的眼光里那点初萌的柔情，她便愈发待他可亲。他们就这样走上横贯小花园的宽宽的中路，眼不旁视，只顾现出彼此全神贯注的那副样子——尤其在一个女看客眼里，这副样子是再好解释不过的。因为，说真的，会吏长万万想不到他进的是谁的家，也万万想不到他即将见到的这个人是谁。

===Original===

But as it happened, Lucilla’s protégée, who had seen better days, had just finished one of her lessons, and sent her little pupils out into the garden. She was preparing for the next little class, when, raising her eyes accidentally, she saw Miss Marjoribanks coming through the garden with the Archdeacon by her side. She was the same person whom Mr. Bury had brought to Lucilla with the idea of recommending her to Dr. Marjoribanks as a companion and chaperone for his daughter; but since then Mrs. Mortimer’s appearance had considerably changed. She had grown younger by ten years during the period of comparative comfort and tranquillity which Lucilla’s active help and championship had procured for her. Her house, and her garden, and her little scholars, and the bloom on her cheeks, and the filling-up of her worn frame, were all Miss Marjoribanks’s doing. In the intervals of her legislative cares Lucilla had run about all over Carlingford searching for pupils, and at the same moment had cut and stitched and arranged, and papered walls, and planted flowerbeds, for the feeble creature thus thrown upon her. This was a side of Lucilla’s character which certainly she did nothing to hide from the public, but which, at the same time, she never made any fuss about; and it was an endless pleasure to her to find a protégée so perfectly content to be “done for,” and do as she was told to do. It was thus that the poor faded widow, who was sensitive and had feelings, and forgot herself so far as to faint, or nearly to faint, just at the most unlucky moment possible, when the Rector’s character and dignity demanded superior self-control on her part, had found her youth again and her good looks under Lucilla’s shadow. When she looked up and saw the two approaching, Mrs. Mortimer’s first impulse was to smile at the conjunction; but the next moment she had dropped the books out of her hands, and was standing gazing out like a woman in a dream, with the colour all gone out of her cheeks, and even out of her lips, in the surprise of the moment. It was only surprise and a kind of dismay; it was not terror, like that which Mr. Cavendish had exhibited at the same apparition. She dropped into her chair without knowing it, and probably would have fainted this time also, if something more urgent than mere “feelings” had not roused her up.

===Chinese===

可是恰巧，露西拉这位见过好日的被保护人刚上完一堂课，把小学生们打发进了园子。她正备着下一小班的功课，无意间一抬眼，望见马乔里班克斯小姐穿过花园走来，身边伴着会吏长。她就是当初伯里先生领来见露西拉、想把她荐给马乔里班克斯医生做女儿伴护的那个人；可自那以后，莫蒂默太太的模样大变了。靠着露西拉奔走的援手与撑腰替她挣来的那段比较安逸清静的日子，她年轻了十岁。她的房子、她的花园、她的小学生、她脸颊上的红润、她瘦损身架的丰盈，全是马乔里班克斯小姐的功劳。露西拉在立法诸务的间隙跑遍卡灵福德替她寻学生，同时又裁又缝又布置，糊墙、砌花坛，伺候这个被抛到她手里的孱弱人。这是露西拉性格的一面——她固然毫不向公众隐瞒，却也从不声张；而发现一个被保护人这样百分之百甘心“受人安排”、叫怎就怎，对她真是无穷的乐事。这位可怜的褪色的寡妇——她敏感、有心气，竟至于在最不巧的关口晕倒、或几乎晕倒，害教区长的威严差点经受不住——便这样在露西拉的荫庇底下找回了她的青春和她的容色。她抬头望见两人走来，莫蒂默太太的第一个冲动是朝这对搭配一笑；可下一刻，书已从她手里掉了下去，她站在那里像梦游人一样直勾勾望着，脸颊上、连嘴唇上的血色都褪尽了——那是那一惊的缘故。那只是惊讶、是一种惶乱，并不是恐怖，不像卡文迪什先生在那同一个现身面前表现的那样。她不知不觉跌坐回椅子里，这一回多半真要晕过去，倘若不是有比单纯的“心绪”更要紧的事把她惊起来。

===Original===

As it was, it happened very happily for her that she had thus a little preparation.
