“说真的，露西拉，你这位朋友给你增光，”马乔里班克斯医生说。“像你这样把她拾起来、把她调理成一个女人的——还是个好看的女人——真是一手才情，”他不知轻重地补上一句；仿佛他那把年纪，同“好看”还有什么相干似的。

===Original===

“I am so glad you think so, papa,” said Lucilla, in her dutiful way. “I don’t think myself that she has gone off at all to speak of. In some lights she might pass for being no older than I am﻿—if she was very well dressed, you know; and it really does not matter what age a woman is if she keeps her looks. I should be very glad to see her nicely married, for my part; she is one of the people who ought to be married,” Miss Marjoribanks continued, with an inflection of compassionate tolerance in her voice. As for the Doctor, he mistook her as usual, and took her tone of pity and kindly patronising disdain for another instance of his daughter’s policy and high art; whereas the truth was she was quite in earnest, and meant every word she said. And then Dr. Marjoribanks’s sense of humour was keener than that of Lucilla. After this the conversation flagged slightly, for Miss Marjoribanks had undeniably received a shock. In the midst of her benevolent preoccupation and care for other people, it had suddenly dawned upon her that her own stronghold might be attacked, and the tables turned upon her in the twinkling of an eye. There are days of discouragement in the most triumphant career and this was one of those uncomfortable moments. Her faith in herself did not fail her for an instant; but the faith of her natural born subjects﻿—the creatures of her bounty﻿—had visibly failed her. Neither Rose Lake nor Mrs. Mortimer had shown that confidence in Lucilla’s genius which experience and loyalty both called upon them to show. When Dr. Marjoribanks had gone downstairs to resume the case which he was writing out for the *Lancet*, Lucilla passed through one of those moments of sublime despondency which now and then try the spirits of the benefactors of their race. A few tears came to her eyes as she reflected upon this great problem. Without such trials genius would not fully know itself nor be justly aware of its own strength. For no temptation to give up her disinterested exertions had any effect upon the mind of Miss Marjoribanks; and even her sense of pain at the unbelief of her followers was mingled with that pity for their weakness which involves pardon. Even when they wounded her she was sorry for them. It was nature that was in fault, and not the fallible human creatures who had it not in them to believe in the simple force of genius.

===Chinese===

“您这样想，我真高兴，爸爸，”露西拉以她孝顺的口气说。“就我自己看，她谈不上见老。有些光线下，她冒充同我一般年纪也过得去——穿得很像样的话，你知道；一个女人只要守住容貌，年纪实在无关紧要。我很愿意看她好好地嫁出去；她就是那种该嫁的人，”马乔里班克斯小姐接着说，嗓音里带着怜悯宽容的顿挫。至于医生，他照例把她领会错了，把她这份怜悯与慈祥的屈尊，又当作女儿权术与高艺的一例；其实她全然是真心，一字一句都当真。何况马乔里班克斯医生的幽默感原比露西拉敏锐。这以后谈话就有点冷了，因为马乔里班克斯小姐无可否认地受了一惊。在她一心为旁人操持、慈心占满的当口，她馨然醒悟：她自家的堡垒也可能挨攻，局面一转眼就可能倒转过来。最凯旋的事业也有沮丧的日子，而这正是那种不自在的时刻之一。她对自身的信心一刻也不曾动摇；可是她天生的子民——她所济度的众生——的信心，却眼见得动摇了。罗斯·莱克也罢，莫蒂默太太也罢，都没有拿出经验和忠诚都要求她们拿出的、对露西拉天才的那份信。马乔里班克斯医生下楼继续写他那篇给《柳叶刀》（Lancet）的病案之后，露西拉经历了一阵庄严的沮丧——那是要不时考验人类恩主们心神的时刻之一。她想着这个大问题，眼里涌上几滴泪。没有这样的试炼，天才便不能充分认识自己、不能公道地掂出自己的力量。因为，任什么诱惑都不能叫马乔里班克斯小姐放下她无私的努力；连门徒不信带给她的痛感里，也掺着对他们软弱的那份怜悯——有怜悯便有宽赦。他们即便伤了她，她也替他们难过。错的是天性，不是那些生来便信不了天才之单纯力量的、易谬的凡人。

===Original===

When Lucilla had shed these few tears over her subjects’ weakness and want of faith, she rose up again in new strength from the momentary downfall. It was, as we have said, a sublime moment. The idea of giving them up, and leaving their affairs to their own guidance, never for an instant penetrated into her heroic mind; but she was human, and naturally she felt the prick of ingratitude. When the crisis was over she rose up calmly and lighted her candle, and went to her room with a smile upon her magnanimous lips. As she performed that simple action, Lucilla had lifted up the feeble widow, and taken the family of Lakes, and Mr. Cavendish, and even the burly Archdeacon himself, upon her shoulders. They might be ungrateful, or even unaware of all she was doing for them; but they had the supreme claim of Need upon Strength; and Miss Marjoribanks, notwithstanding the wound they had given her, was loyal to that appeal, and to her own consciousness of superior Power.

At the same time, it would not be just to omit all mention of a consolatory recollection which occurred to Lucilla in this moment of her weakness. At such a crisis the mind of genius may be supported by a matter very trifling in itself. Even at the instant when the moisture sprang to her eyes, Miss Marjoribanks said to herself, “Poor Tom!” and felt that the bitterness, to a certain extent, had evaporated out of her tears. He was a long way off, and Lucilla would have thought it madness indeed to connect herself in any way with the fortunes of her unlucky cousin; yet it gave her a certain support to think that, amid all the want of faith she was encountering, Tom believed in her, heart and soul. It was an insignificant matter, so far as any practical result was concerned, if, indeed, anything can be called insignificant which gives strength to a great mind in a moment of discouragement. She said “Poor Tom!” and felt as if for the moment she had something to lean on, and was comforted. We mention this fact rather as a contribution to the history of those phenomena of the human mind, which have as yet escaped the metaphysician, than as an actual circumstance in the life of Miss Marjoribanks. She was a woman of genius, and he only a very simple, unlucky fellow; and yet a sensation of comfort came to Lucilla’s heart when she said “Poor Tom!”

===Chinese===

露西拉为自己的子民之软弱、之无信洒过这几滴泪，便从一时的颓唐里重新振作起来。如前所说，这是庄严的一刻。丢开他们、任他们的诸事自流，这样的念头一刻也不曾渗进她那英雄的头脑；可她到底是人，自然觉出忘恩的刺。关口一过，她平静地站起身，点上蜡烛，唇边带着宽宏的微笑进了自己的房间。就在这简单的动作里，露西拉把那孱弱的寡妇、把莱克一家、把卡文迪什先生、连那位魁伟的会吏长本人，都一举扛上了肩。他们可以忘恩，甚至可以全不知她为他们做的一切；但“需要”对“力量”握有至高的债权；马乔里班克斯小姐——尽管他们伤了她——忠于那声呼吁，也忠于她对自身优越力量的自觉。

同时，若只字不提露西拉在这软弱的时刻得着的一桩安慰，也有失公道。这样的关头，天才的心神可以靠一件本身极小的事撑住。甚至就在泪水涌上眼眶的那一瞬，马乔里班克斯小姐也对自己说了一声“可怜的汤姆！”，觉得泪里的苦味，凭空蒸发掉了一截。他远在天边，露西拉若把自己同这倒霉表哥的运数牵上半分，必以为是发了疯；然而这样一想仍给她一点撑持：在她遭遇的遍地无信之中，汤姆信她，全心全意地信。就实际结果而论，这是小事一桩——倘若凡能给伟大的心智在沮丧之刻以力量的东西都可以唤作小事的话。她说“可怜的汤姆！”便觉得此刻有了倚靠，得了安慰。我们记下这一笔，与其说它是马乔里班克斯小姐生平的一件实事，不如说是给人类心智诸现象的历史添一份材料——那些现象，形而上学家至今还没能解释。她是天才的女人，他不过是个再简单不过的倒霉人；然而一声“可怜的汤姆！”出口，露西拉心头就涌起一阵安慰。

## XXVIII / 二十八
===Original===

Lucilla prepared her toilette the next evening, to take tea with the Lakes, with greater care than she would have spent upon a party of much greater pretensions. She was, to be sure, dressed as usual in the white dress, *high*, which she had brought into fashion in Carlingford; but then that simple evening toilette required many adjuncts which were not necessary on other occasions, seeing that this time she was going to walk to her destination, and had in her mind the four distinct aims of pleasing Rose, of dazzling Barbara, of imposing upon Mr. Cavendish, and, finally, of being, as always, in harmony with *herself*. She was as punctual to the hour and minute of her engagement as if she had been a queen; and, indeed, it was with a demeanour as gracious that she entered the little house in Grove Street, where, naturally, there had been also sundry preparations made for her visit. Mr. Lake himself, who had postponed his usual walk, and was taking his tea an hour later than usual, received his young visitor with all the suavity natural to him; and as for Barbara, she did the honours with a certain suppressed exultation and air of triumph, which proved to Lucilla that her plan was indeed an inspiration of genius. As for Rose, it would be impossible to describe what were her sensations. Her faith still failed her at that momentous hour. She was sceptical of Lucilla, and naturally of all the world, and regarded everybody with jealous scrutiny and expectation and distrust, as was natural to a young conspirator. She was profoundly excited and curious to know what Miss Marjoribanks meant to do; and at the same time she did not believe in Miss Marjoribanks, and was almost disposed to betray and interfere with her, if such treachery had been possible. It was Rose Lucilla specially came to visit, and yet Rose was the only one who was cool to her, and did not seem fully to appreciate her condescension; but then, happily, Miss Marjoribanks was magnanimous, and at the same time had a purpose to support her, which was much more comprehensive and of larger application than anything that had entered into the mind of Rose Lake.

===Chinese===

第二天傍晚，露西拉为到莱克家吃茶打扮仪容，用的心思比一场排场大得多的宴会还多。她照例穿那条白裙，高腰的——她带进卡灵福德风气的那条；可这趟简单的晚妆需要许多别的场合用不着的附加：一来她这回要步行去；二来她心里揣着四个判然的目标：取悦罗丝，震住芭芭拉，慑服卡文迪什先生，最后，一如既往，同*她自己*相和谐。她赴约守时守到时与分，俨然一位女王；而她走进格罗夫街那所小宅时，气派也果真雍容；宅子里自然也为她的光临做了种种准备。莱克先生本人，把惯常的散步推后了，吃茶比平常晚了一个钟头，以他天生的和蔼接待年轻的来客；至于芭芭拉，她尽着地主之谊，带着一股压住的得意与得胜的神气——这向露西拉证明了：她的计划确是天才的灵光。至于罗丝，她的感受无法描摹。到了这要紧的时辰，她的信心还是不济。她疑露西拉，自然也疑全世界，用嫉妒的审视、期待与不信任看每一个人——年轻的同谋者天然如此。她深深激动着，极想知道马乔里班克斯小姐要干什么；可同时又信不过马乔里班克斯小姐，倘若那背叛办得到，她几乎打算出卖她、阻挠她。露西拉特意来访的是罗丝，可对她冷淡的偏偏也只有罗丝，仿佛全不领她这份屈尊的情；所幸马乔里班克斯小姐宽宏大量，况且还有一桩宗旨撑着她——那宗旨比进过罗丝·莱克心头的一切，都更宽泛、更恢阔。

===Original===

“I am proud to see you in my house, Miss Marjoribanks,” said Mr. Lake. “I have always considered your excellent father one of my best friends. I am not able to give my children the same advantages, but I have always brought them up not to have any false pride. We have no wealth; but we have some things which cannot be purchased by wealth,” said the drawing-master, with mild grandeur; and he looked round upon the walls of his parlour, which were hung with his own drawings, and where one of Willie’s held the place of honour. In all Carlingford there was no other house that enjoyed a similar distinction; and, consequently, it was with a delicious sense of chivalrous deference yet equality that the exceptional man of Grove Street received the young sovereign of Grange Lane.

“I am so glad to come, Mr. Lake,” said Lucilla. “It is so nice to be among such old friends; and, besides that, you know there never was any voice that suited mine like Barbara’s; and that dear old Rose was always my pet at Mount Pleasant. I should have come long ago if anybody had ever asked me,” said Miss Marjoribanks. And as for Mr. Lake, he was so overpowered by this implied reproach upon his hospitality that he scarcely knew how to reply.

“My dear Miss Marjoribanks, if you have not been asked it has been from no want of﻿—of goodwill,” said Mr. Lake anxiously. “I do not know what the girls can have been thinking of. You see Rose’s genius takes another line; and Barbara, naturally, has a great many things to think of; but in the future, I hope﻿—”

“马乔里班克斯小姐光临舍间，我不胜荣辜，”莱克先生说。“我一向把您那位令尊看作我最好的朋友之一。我无力给儿女们同等的优遇，可我一向教养他们，不叫他们存半点虚骄。我们没有财富；可我们有些东西，是财富买不来的，”图画先生说，带着温和的庄严；他环顾客厅四壁——挂的都是他自己的画，其中一幅威利的，占着荣位。全卡灵福德再没有第二家享有同样的荣典；于是，格罗夫街这位异数的人物，怀着一种骑士风的敬而不卑之感，接待格兰奇巷这位年轻的女王。

===Original===

“Oh, yes; I shall come without being asked,” said Lucilla. And when the tea came it was all she could do to keep herself quiet, and remember that she was a visitor, and not take it out of the incapable hands of Barbara, who never gave her father the right amount of sugar in his tea. To tell the truth, Barbara’s thoughts were occupied by a very different subject; and even Rose had but little attention to spare for her papa’s comforts at that special moment. But Lucilla’s larger mind embraced everything. She sat with her very fingers itching to cut the bread-and-butter for him, and give him a cup of tea as he liked it; and asked herself, with indignation, what was the use of that great creature, with her level eyebrows and her crimson bloom, who could not take the trouble to remember that three lumps was what Mr. Lake liked. Miss Marjoribanks had never taken tea with him before; but his second cup, had she dispensed it, would have been exactly to his taste﻿—which was a thing Barbara had not learned to make it in all these years. No wonder that a certain sense of contemptuous indignation arose for one moment, even in the calm and impartial bosom of genius. Perhaps Rose would not have done much better; but then Rose was good for something else, which was always a set-off on the other side. Thus it will be seen that Lucilla had a respect for use, even of a kind which in her own person she did not much appreciate, as became a person of a truly enlightened mind; but a creature who was of no earthly good irritated her well-regulated spirit; for, to be sure, the possession of a fine contralto (which is, at the same time, not fine enough to be made use of professionally) is not a matter of sufficient moment in this world to excuse a young woman for not knowing how to give her father a comfortable cup of tea.

===Chinese===

“哦，是；不请我也来，”露西拉说。茶端上来时，她好容易才管住自己，记得自己是客，没把它从芭芭拉那双无能的手里接过来——芭芭拉给她父亲茶里放的糖，从来数目不对。说老实话，芭芭拉的心思被另一个全然不同的题目占着；连罗丝，在那个特别的时刻，也匀不出多少心照管爸爸的舒适。可露西拉那副大头脑什么都揽。她坐在那里，指头痒着，想替他切黄油面包、照他爱的样子给他斟一杯茶；又愤愤自问：那个大个子有什么用——平眉毛、红喷喷的一张脸——竟不肯费心记一记：莱克先生要的是三块糖。马乔里班克斯小姐从前没同他吃过茶；可她若来斟，那第二杯会正中他的口味——这是芭芭拉这些年一直没学会的。难怪连天才那平静公正的胸中，也有一刻升起了轻蔑的义惯。罗丝也许高明不了多少；可罗丝别有所长，天平那头总有个抵数。由此可见，露西拉尊重“有用”，连她自己并不怎么赏鉴的那一种也尊重——这合于一个真正开明的头脑；可一样全然无用的造物，要激恼她那井然的性灵；因为，说到底，占着一条好女低音（同时还没好到可以职业登台的地步），在这个世界上并非重到足以开脱一个年轻女子的事——她竟不会给父亲斟一杯舒服的茶。

===Original===

It was nearly nine o’clock before Mr. Lake went out for his walk, and by that time it was almost dark, and the lamp outside was lighted, which was not far from the door. Lucilla had taken a seat near the window, with the view of witnessing everything; and it cannot be denied that she felt a little excited when Barbara went out of the room after her father, leaving Rose alone with her guest. Miss Marjoribanks’s heart gave a beat or two the more in the first minute, though before the next had passed it had fallen into its usual measure. There were no candles as yet in the parlour, and Grove Street﻿—or at least the bit of it which lay before the window, lighted by the lamp outside, and relieved against a little square of bluish-green sky which intervened between Miss Hemmings’s house and that of old Mr. Wrangle on the opposite side﻿—was very clear to the interested spectator. There was nobody visible but an organ-man, who was grinding a popular melody very dolorously out of his box, in what Rose would have called the middle distance; and beyond, Miss Jane Hemmings looking out of the long staircase window, and three little boys in different attitudes below﻿—that is, if one did not count a tall figure which, perhaps with the view of listening to the music of the organ, was coming and going in a limited circuit round the light of the lamp.

“How convenient it is to have the lamp so near,” said Lucilla. “Oh, don’t light any candles, please; it is so nice to sit in the dark. Where is Barbara, I wonder? Let us have some music, and put down that dreadful organ. I hope she has not gone out. And where are you, you sulky little Rose?”

“She has gone upstairs,” said Rose, who began to feel all the enormity of her conduct in thus betraying her sister. “I hate sitting in the dark. I hate being a spy; come in from the window, Lucilla, now you are here﻿—”

“My dear Rose,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “I think you forget a little. For my part I do not understand what being a spy means. Barbara knows very well I am here. I should scorn to take an advantage of anybody, for my part. If she does not bring him past the very window, and under my eyes﻿—Ah, yes, that is just what I thought,” said Lucilla, with gentle satisfaction. But by this time poor little Rose had roused herself into an innocent fury.

===Chinese===

将近九点，莱克先生才出门散步；那时天已擦黑，门外不远的街灯亮了。露西拉拣了窗边一个座，为的是目击一切；不能否认，芭芭拉随父亲出去、把罗丝单独撂给客人时，她觉得有点心跳。头一分钟，马乔里班克斯小姐的心多跳了一两拍；下一分钟没过，已落回它惯常的节律。客厅里还没点蜡烛；格罗夫街——至少窗前那一段，被门外的街灯照着，衬在海明斯小姐府上与对面兰格尔老先生府上之间那一小块蓝绿色天空里——在看客眼中历历分明。街上望得见的只有一名摇琴师，在他的箱匣里凄凄惨惨地摇一支流行调子，在罗丝所谓的中间景深处；再远些，简·海明斯小姐从长楼梯窗口望出来，底下三个小男孩姿势各异——倘若不算那个高挑的身影：那一位，也许是为了听琴，正绕着灯光一圈来一圈去。
“灯安得这样近，多方便，”露西拉说。“哦，请别点蜡烛；坐在暗处多好。芭芭拉上哪儿去了，我想？来点音乐吧，把那要命的琴声压下去。但愿她没出门。你藏到哪儿去了，你这不痛快的小罗丝？”
“她上楼了，”罗丝说，她开始觉得出自己这番出卖姐姐的行径的分量。“我恨坐在黑地里。我恨做奸细；从窗口回来，露西拉，既来了就——”
“亲爱的罗丝，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“我看你有点忘形了。拿我说，我不懂做奸细是什么意思。芭芭拉很知道我在这里。我这个人，耻于占任何人的便宜。她若不把他领到窗口跟前、领到我眼皮底下——啊，是，正同我想的一样，”露西拉说，带着温和的满意。可这时可怜的小罗丝已经把自己激成了一场天真的狂怒。

===Original===

“What is just as you thought?” said Rose, laying an impatient grasp on Miss Marjoribanks’s arm. “Come in from the window, Lucilla, this moment﻿—this moment! Oh, me, to think it should be my doing! Oh, Lucilla, don’t be so mean and shabby and wretched. I tell you to come in﻿—come in directly! If you do not shut the window, and come and sit here in the corner, I will never, never speak to you again!”

Miss Marjoribanks, as was natural, took no notice of this childish fury. She was sitting just where she had been sitting all the evening, within sight of the street lamp and the organ-grinder, and Miss Jane Hemmings at the staircase window;﻿—just where Barbara had placed her, and where that young woman calculated on finding her, when she made a promenade of triumph up the partially lighted street by the side of her clandestine suitor. Perhaps Barbara had seen Miss Jane as well, and knew that public opinion was thus watching over her; but at all events she was not at all ashamed of herself, or indignant at being spied upon. On the contrary, it was a kind of apotheosis for Barbara, only second to the grand and crowning triumph which would be accomplished in Carlingford Church under the shadow of that veil of real Brussels, which grew more and more real every day. Thus neither the actors in the drama, nor the principal spectator, were in the smallest degree disturbed by horror or shame or sense of guilt, excepting always the fanciful little Rose, who suffered for everybody; who could have wished that the earth would open and swallow up Barbara and her lover; who could have slaughtered Lucilla on the spot, and given herself over to any kind of torture for her treachery. Naturally nobody paid any sort of attention to Rose. Barbara, for her part, took her admirer’s arm in the twilight with a swelling of exultation, which the gaining of the very highest prize in the department of ornamental art could scarcely have conveyed to the bosom of the little artist; and Lucilla put back her small assailant softly with her hand, and smoothed down her ruffled plumes.

“My dear, it is Miss Hemmings that is spying,” said Lucilla; “and poor Barbara would be so disappointed if I were to go away from the window. Have patience just a little longer﻿—there’s a dear. It is all exactly as I thought.”

===Chinese===

“什么正同你想的一样？”罗丝说，一把急切抓住马乔里班克斯小姐的胳膊。“从窗口回来，露西拉，这就回来——这就回来！哦，天哪，想想竟是我干出来的！哦，露西拉，别这样卑劣、这样下作、这样不堪。我叫你回来——马上回来！你若不关上窗、过来坐在这个角落里，我永远、永远不再同你说话！”
马乔里班克斯小姐自然全不理会这场孩子气的狂怒。她坐的正是她一晚坐惯的地方：看得见街灯、摇琴师和楼梯窗口的简·海明斯小姐的地方；正是芭芭拉安置她的地方，也是那位年轻女子算定会在原地找到她的地方——等她挽着她那位地下的求婚人，沿着半明半暗的街道、得胜阅兵似地走过来。芭芭拉兴许也望见了简·海明斯，知道舆论正这样监护着她；可她无论如何毫不羞慚，也不因被窥伺而愤慨。恰恰相反，这于芭芭拉是一种封神；仅次于那顶大的、加冕的胜利——那胜利将在卡灵福德教堂、在那条真布鲁塞尔面纱的荫下完成；面纱一天比一天真。于是这出戏的演员、连同主看客，都毫无半点恐怖、羞慙或罪感之扰——只有那个多想的小罗丝永远除外：她替人人受罪；她恨不得大地裂开，把芭芭拉和她的情人一并吞了；她恨不得当场宰了露西拉，再把自己交给任何酷刑，赎她的背信。自然，谁也不理会罗丝。芭芭拉呢，在暮色里挽住她崇拜者的胳膊，得意得心口发涨——那种涨法，装饰艺术界最高的奖落到小艺术家胸中，也未必给得了；露西拉则用手轻轻推开她那小小的攻击者，抚平她炸起的翎毛。
“亲爱的，窥伺的是海明斯小姐，”露西拉说；“我若从窗口走开，可怜的芭芭拉要多失望就有多失望。再忍一小会儿——好宝贝。一切都同我想的一毫不差。”

===Original===

And then there followed a pause, which was a terrible pause for Rose. The organ-grinder stopped his doleful ditty, and there was scarcely any sound to be heard in the street except the footsteps approaching and retiring, the measured tread of two people occupied with each other, going now more slowly, now more quickly, as the humour seized them, or as their conversation grew in interest; even the sound of their voices came by times to the auditors﻿—Barbara’s with an occasional laugh or tone of triumph, and the other deeper, with which Rose had but little acquaintance, but which was perfectly known to Lucilla. All this time, while her companion sat panting in the dark corner, Miss Marjoribanks was looking to the joints of her harness, and feeling the edge of her weapons. For, after all, it was no small enterprise upon which she was going forth. She was going to denounce the faithless knight to his face, and take him out of the hands of the enchantress; but then she herself meant to take him in hand, and show him his true dangers, and vindicate his honour. A more disinterested enterprise was never undertaken by any knight-errant. Yet, at the same time, Lucilla could not help entertaining a certain involuntary contempt for the man who had deserted her own standard to put himself under that of Barbara Lake, and who was being paraded up and down here without knowing it, to gratify the vanity of his new sovereign, and make an exhibition of his weakness. Lucilla would have been more than mortal if she had not felt the difference between her own rule, which would have been all to his good, and the purely egotistical sway of Barbara; and even in her magnanimous mind, it was impossible that pity itself should not be mingled with a certain disdain.

===Chinese===

随后是一阵静默，于罗丝是一阵可怕的静默。摇琴师停了他那支悲凉的调子，街上几乎听不见别的声息，只有那渐近渐远的脚步——两个人彼此占有着、有节律的步子，忽而慢、忽而快，随他们的兴致、随他们谈兴的增长；连他们说话的声音也不时送到听者耳中——芭芭拉的，带着一阵阵笑或得胜的调子；另一个深沉些，罗丝不大熟，露西拉却熟透了。这一路，同伴在黑角落里发着喘，马乔里班克斯小姐却在检视她挽具的关节、试她兵刃的锋。因为她此去毕竟不是小事：她要当面告发那位负心的骑士，把他从魔女的掌心里取出来；然后她亲自接管他，指给他看他真正的险处，替他挽回名誉。任何游侠骑士所曾承担的事业，都没有比这更无私的。然而同时，露西拉对这个人不能不怀着一份不由自主的轻蔑：他撇下她的旗，投到芭芭拉·莱克的旗下，此刻正被牵着在这里来回展览而不自知——为的是餍足他新君主的虚荣，展览他自己的弱点。露西拉若不觉出这两副统治的分别——她自己的统治，事事为他好；芭芭拉的，纯粹利己的拨弄——那她就不是人了；连她那宽宏的心里，怜悯也免不了掺着一分讥请。

===Original===

She sat quite still for so long that Barbara grew intoxicated with her triumph. “It is perhaps the last time,” Lucilla said to herself, with a movement of compassion; and the breadth of her human sympathy was such that she waited till the very latest moment, and let the deluded young woman have the full enjoyment of her imaginary victory. Then Miss Marjoribanks rose with a certain solemnity, and put on her hat, and gave an unappreciated kiss to Rose, who kept in her corner. “Good night; I am going,” said Lucilla. The words were simple enough, but yet they rang in Rose’s ears like the signal of a conspiracy. When the calm leader of the expedition went forth, sensible of the importance of her mission, but tranquil as great minds always are in a moment of danger, Rose got up too and followed, trembling in every limb. She was capable of having thrown herself upon the spears in her own person in a sudden élan of indignation and passion; but she was not capable of waiting till the right moment, and meeting her antagonists in reasonable combat. Miss Marjoribanks went out deliberately, without any unnecessary haste, sweeping into the dusky twilight with her virginal white draperies. It was a very ordinary scene, and yet, even in the midst of her excitement, Rose could not help observing involuntarily its pictorial qualities﻿—if only any painter could have transferred to his canvas the subdued musical hum of surrounding life, the fragrance of the mignonette, and the peaceful stillness of the summer night. The sky shone out green-blue, lambent and wistful, from the vacant space between Miss Hemmings’s and Mr. Wrangle’s, and there were the dusky twilight shadows below, and the yellow gleam of the lamp, and Barbara’s exulting, triumphant figure, and the white robes of the avenging angel. Rose could not have observed all this if she had not been stilled into a kind of breathless awe by the solemn character of the situation, which struck her as being somehow like one of Millais’s pictures. As for the lovers, they had just turned at the moment that Miss Marjoribanks came out, and consequently met her straight in the face, as she stood suave and smiling at the little garden door.

“It *is* Mr. Cavendish,” said Lucilla; “I am so glad; I have been hoping and trying to see you for ever so long; and as soon as ever I heard you talking I felt sure it was your voice.”

===Chinese===

她一动不动坐了这样久，芭芭拉陶醉在她的胜利里。“这兴许是最后一回了，”露西拉自语，带着一阵怜惘；她那人类同情的胸怀这样宽，直等到最后一刻，让那受骗的年轻女子把她想象的胜利享受了个足。然后马乔里班克斯小姐带着几分庄严起身，戴上帽子，赏了罗丝一个不被领情的吻——罗丝缩在她的角落里。“晚安；我走了，”露西拉说。话再简单不过，可落在罗丝耳中，却像密谋的号令。远征的平静首领出发了，自觉使命之重，却同伟大的头脑临危时一样安详；罗丝也起身跟上，四肢发着抖。她能在义惯与激情的一阵突发里，以身扑向枪尖；可她没有本事等到恰当的时机、同对手作讲理的交锋。马乔里班克斯小姐从容而出，不带一点多余的仓促，一身雪白的衣裾扫入昏冥的暮色。这是顶寻常的一幕；然而连激动中的罗丝，也不由自主地看出了它的画境——但凡有一位画家，能把四围生活那低抑的音乐似的嗡鸣、木樨草的芬芳、夏夜的宁静移到画布上。天宇在海明斯小姐府与兰格尔先生府之间的空隙里，闪出蓝绿的光，幽微而缱绻；底下是昏冥的暗影，街灯的黄光，芭芭拉得胜扬扬的身影，还有那复仇天使的白袍。罗丝若不是被局面的庄严镇得屏息生畏——她觉得这局面不知怎么像米莱的一幅画——原也观察不到这一切。至于那对情人，马乔里班克斯小姐出来的当口他们恰好转身，于是同她打了照面：她含着温和的微笑，立在小园门口。
“真是卡文迪什先生，”露西拉说；“多高兴；我一直盼着见你、想法子见你，盼了好久；一听见你们说话，我就断定是你的嗓音。”

===Original===

This was the greeting she addressed to Barbara Lake’s lover. For his part he stood before her, growing red and growing pale, struck dumb by the unlooked-for meeting, and with such a sense of being ashamed of himself as never before had entered his mind, though, no doubt, he had done worse actions in his day. Even Barbara had not calculated upon this open encounter; and instead of giving him any assistance, as was a woman’s duty in such a case, she only tossed her head, and giggled with an embarrassment which was more pride than shame. As for Mr. Cavendish, he would have liked to disappear under the pavement, if it had been possible. For once he and Rose were agreed. If a gulf had opened before him, he would have jumped into it without ever pausing to ask himself why. And yet all the time Miss Marjoribanks was looking as placid as if she had been in her own drawing-room, and expecting his reply to her friendly observations. When he realised that he ought to say something, Mr. Cavendish felt that he had as much need to wipe his forehead as ever the Archdeacon had. He turned hot and cold, and felt his mind and his tongue frozen, and could not find a word to say. With a sudden horror he woke up, like one of Comus’s revellers, and found himself changed into the likeness of the creature he consorted with. If he had found an ass’s head on his shoulders, he could not have felt more startled and horrified than when he heard himself, in the imbecility of the moment, giggle like Barbara, and answer to Lucilla’s remark, “Oh! yes, it was my voice.”

===Chinese===

这就是她对芭芭拉·莱克的情人所道的寒暄。他呢，站在她面前，红了又白，白又红，被这场意外撞得哑口无言，心里那股自慙，是生平从来不曾有过——虽说无疑他从前干过更坏的事。连芭芭拉也没算到这场公开遭遇；她非但不帮他一把——这种场合本是一个女人的本分——只把头一扬，带着傻笑窘在那里，那窘里骄傲多于羞恥。至于卡文迪什先生，倘若做得到，他情愿钻到街面底下去。这一回，他同罗丝意见一致了。倘若面前裂开一道深渊，他会一跃而入，全不停下来问自己为什么。而这一路，马乔里班克斯小姐安详得仿佛坐在自家客厅里，只等他对她友好的话作答。等他明白自己该说点什么时，卡文迪什先生觉得，他擦脑门的需要，不减当年那位会吏总。他一阵热一阵冷，觉得舌头和心思都冻住了，一个字也找不出。他带着一阵突来的恐怖醒了——像科玛斯宴客中的一个——发现自己变成了他所交往的那个东西的模样。倘若他肩上摸到一颗驴头，其惊骇也未必更甚于听见自己——在那痴呆的一刻——像芭芭拉一样傻笑着，答露西拉的话：“哦！是，是我的嗓音。”

===Original===

“I am very sorry to separate you from Barbara,” said Miss Marjoribanks; “but she is at home, you know, and I want so much to talk to you. Barbara, good night; I want Mr. Cavendish to walk home with me. Rose, don’t stand in the garden and catch cold; thank you, dear, for such a pleasant evening,” said Lucilla, pressing another kiss upon her little friend’s unwilling cheek. When she had done this, she put out her hand to Barbara, and passed her, sweeping her white garments through the narrow gateway. She took Mr. Cavendish’s arm as if he had been a young brother come to fetch her. “Let us go round by the chapel,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “I have so much to say to you. Be sure to practise for Thursday, Barbara, and bid your papa good night for me.” This was how she carried off Mr. Cavendish finally out of Barbara’s very fingers, and under her very eyes.

===Chinese===

“很抱歉把你从芭芭拉身边拆开，”马乔里班克斯小姐说；“可她在家里，你知道；而我有这么多话要同你讲。芭芭拉，晚安；我要卡文迪什先生陪我走回家。罗丝，别站在园子里着凉；谢谢你，亲爱的，这样一个愉快的晚上，”露西拉说着，又在她小朋友那不情愿的脸颊上印了一个吻。然后她向芭芭拉伸出手，从她身边过，一身白裙扫过窄窄的门道。她挽住卡文迪什先生的胳膊，仿佛他是来接她的一个小弟弟。“咱们绕礼拜堂那边走吧，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“我有这么多话同你说。芭芭拉，礼拜四务必练唱；替我向你爸爸道晚安。”她便是这样，从芭芭拉的手指缝里、眼皮底下，把卡文迪什先生彻底掳走了。

===Original===

When the two sisters were left standing together at the door, they could do nothing but stare at each other in the extremity of their amazement. Rose, for her part, remained but a moment, and then, feeling by far the guiltiest and most miserable of the whole party, ran upstairs to her own room and cried as if her heart would break. Barbara, on the contrary, who was past crying, stood still at the door, and watched Lucilla’s white dress disappearing on the way to Grange Lane with indescribable emotions. A young woman cannot call the police, or appeal to the crier, when it is her lover whom she has lost: but to see him carried off by the strong hand﻿—to watch him gradually going away and disappearing from her eyes﻿—to hear his steps withdrawing into the distance﻿—was such a trial as few are called upon to bear. She stood and looked after him, and could not believe her eyes. And then it was all so sudden﻿—an affair of a moment. Barbara could not realise how the world had turned round, and this revolution had been effected;﻿—one minute she had been leaning on his arm triumphant, making a show and exhibition of him in the pride of her heart, though he did not know it; and the next was not she standing here watching him with a blank countenance and a despairing heart, while Lucilla had pounced upon him and carried him off in her cruel grasp? The blow was so sudden, that Barbara stood speechless and motionless till the two departing figures had vanished in the darkness. Would he come back again tomorrow, or was he gone forever and ever? Such were the thoughts of the forsaken maiden, as she stood paralysed under this sudden change of fortune, at her father’s door. If some cruel spectator had thrown into the fire that Brussels veil with which her imagination had so long played, and Barbara had stood heart-struck, watching the filmy tissue dissolve into ashes before her eyes, her sense of sudden anguish could not have been more acute. Yet, after all, Barbara’s pangs were nothing to those of Mr. Cavendish, as he felt Miss Marjoribanks’s light touch on his arm, and felt his doomed feet turn in spite of himself in the most dangerous direction, and became conscious that he was being led beyond all possibility of resistance, back to Grange Lane and to his fate.

===Chinese===

姐妹两个被撂在门口，面面相覷，惊到极处。罗丝只站了一刻，随即——自觉是全场罪最重、最苦的一个——跑上楼回自己房里，哭得心都要碎了。芭芭拉则相反，哭已经哭过了，呆立在门口，望着露西拉的白裙在往格兰奇巷去的路上消逝，百感交集，难以言表。一个年轻女子丢了情人，不能叫警察，也不能求传令官；可是眼看他被人仗力掳走——眼看他渐渐远去、从她眼前消失——听着他的脚步退进远处——这样的刑罚，被传到的人寥寥。她站着望他的背影，不能信自己的眼睛。而且这一切这样快——一瞬问的事。芭芭拉想不通世界怎么转了向、这场革命怎么完成的；——一分钟前，她还胜利地倚着他的胳膊，拿他展览夸示，心里的得意——他自己倒不知道；下一分钟，不就是她站在这里，一张空白的脸、一颗绝望的心望看他，而露西拉已扑上去、用她残忍的一把攫住他掳走了么？打击这样突然，芭芭拉无言无动地立着，直到那两个远去的身影没入黑暗。他明天会回来，还是一去永不再来？被弃的少女立在父亲门口、瘫痪在这场命运的突变里，心里想的就是这些。倘若哪个残忍的看客，把她想象里摆弄了这样久的布鲁塞尔面纱扔进火里，芭芭拉心碎地看着那薄纱的织质在她眼前化为灰烬，她的骤痛也未必更尖锐。然而，芭芭拉的苦楚，比起卡文迪什先生的，到底不算什么：他觉出马乔里班克斯小姐轻轻搭上手臂的一触，觉出自己那双注定的脚不由自主拐向最凶险的方向，并意识到自己正被引着，越过一切反抗的可能，回到格兰奇巷、回到他的命运里去。

===Original===

To be sure it was dark, which was one consolation; but it was not dark enough to conceal Lucilla’s white dress, nor the well-known form and lineaments of the young monarch of Grange Lane, in whose company nobody could pass unobserved. Mr. Cavendish could have faced danger by sea and land with the average amount of courage; but the danger of the walk down the little street, which afterwards led to St. Roque’s, and up the embowered stillness of Grange Lane, was more than he was equal to. He could not be sure of making a single step by these garden-walls without meeting somebody who knew him﻿—somebody whose curiosity might ruin him in Carlingford; or even without the risk of encountering in the face of that arch-enemy, who would not go away, and whose presence had banished him from the place. It may be supposed that, under these terrible circumstances, Mr. Cavendish’s thoughts of Barbara, who had got him into this scrape, were far from lover-like. He was a man universally popular among ladies, and who owed a great deal of the social consideration which he prized so highly to this fact; and yet the most gentle sentiment in his mind at that moment, was a “Confound these women!” which he breathed to himself, all low and deep, as he went slowly along by Lucilla’s side. As for Miss Marjoribanks, her thoughts were of a very much more serious description than anything her unlucky escort was thinking of, and a minute or two passed in silence before she could make up her mind to speak.

“I have been thinking a great deal about you lately, and wishing very much to see you,” said Lucilla. “Did not Mrs. Woodburn tell you?﻿—I think I should have written to you had I known your address.”

“And I am sure you would have made me the happiest of men,” said the victim, with rueful politeness. “What had I done to deserve such a privilege? But my sister did not tell me; she left me to hear it from your own﻿—”

“Yes,” said Miss Marjoribanks, with a certain solemnity, interrupting him; “I have been thinking a great deal﻿—and *hearing* a great deal about you, Mr. Cavendish.” When she had said this Lucilla sighed, and her sigh found a terrible echo in her hearer’s bosom. She knew that he turned green in the darkness as he gave an anxious look at her. But he was too much alarmed to give her an opportunity of studying his face.

===Chinese===

天黑，这算一点安慰；可黑得还不足以遮住露西拉的白裙，遮不住格兰奇巷那位年轻君主无人不晓的身形与眉目——同她作伴，谁也休想悄然过街。海陆的危险，卡文迪什先生凭寻常的勇气本可以面对；可这条小街的凶险——它后来通向圣罗克堂——再上格兰奇巷花木掩映的静道，超出了他的本领。他不敢保沿着这些花园墙走一步而不撞见认得他的人——那人的好奇可能叫他毁在卡灵福德；甚至不敢保不迎面撞上那位宿敌——那位不肯走、他的在场把他逐出此地的人。可以想见，在这骇人的情形下，卡文迪什先生对芭芭拉——把他拖进这泥潭的人——的念头，与情人大相径庭。他是个深得太太们欢心的男人，他那样珍视的社交体面，欠这笔账的极多；可他此刻心里最温和的一句情，是一声“这些女人该死！”——他低低地、深深地呼吸着，傍着露西拉慢慢走时，自言自语的。至于马乔里班克斯小姐，她所想的比她那位倒运的护卫所想的严肃得多；过了一两分钟沉默，她才拿定主意开口。
“这一向我常常想起你，非常想见你，”露西拉说。“伍德伯恩太太没告诉你么？——我想，我若知道你的地址，早就写信给你了。”
“那你一定把我做成了天下最幸福的男人，”这位牺牲品苦笑着说。“我何德何能，当得起这样的殊荣？可我妹妹没告诉我；她留给我，让我亲耳从你——”
“是，”马乔里班克斯小姐带着几分庄严打断他；“我想了很多——也*听了*很多关于你的事，卡文迪什先生。”说完这句，露西拉叹了一口气；那一声叹，在听者胸中激起了可怕的回响。她知道，黑暗里他焦灼地看了她一眼，脸都绿了。可他吓得太厉害，没给她端详他面目的机会。

===Original===

“*Hearing* of me,” he said, and tried to laugh; “what have my kind friends been saying?” and for one moment the sufferer tried to delude himself that it was some innocent gossip about Barbara which might be circulating in Grange Lane.

“Hush,” said Lucilla, “don’t laugh, please; for I want to have a very serious talk. I have been hearing about you from some very, very old friends, Mr. Cavendish﻿—not anything about *this*, you know,” Miss Marjoribanks added, waving her hand in the direction of Grove Street. And then Barbara Lake and everything connected with her vanished like a shadow from the unfortunate man’s mind. It was horribly ungrateful on his part, but it was, as Miss Marjoribanks would have said, just what might have been expected, and how They always behave. He had no longer any time or patience for the object which had been giving occupation and interest to his solitude. He woke up in a moment, and gave a passing curse to his folly, and faced the real danger as he best could.

“You must be making a mistake, Miss Marjoribanks,” he said, with some bitterness; “it should have been, very, very old enemy. I know who it is. It is that Archdeacon you ladies make such a fuss about. It is he who has been telling lies about me,” said Mr. Cavendish. He breathed a deep hard breath as he spoke, and the blood came back to his face. Perhaps for the first moment he felt satisfied, and breathed freer after it was over; but at the same time it was very dreadful to him to feel that he was found out, and that henceforth Grange Lane would shut its doors and avert its countenance. “If you take his word for it, I may give in at once,” he continued, bitterly. “A parson will say anything; they are as bad as﻿—as women.” This the poor man said in his despair, because he did not know what he was saying; for in reality he knew that women had been his best friends, and that he had still a chance, if the judgment was to rest with them.

===Chinese===

“*听了*我的事，”他说，强笑了一声；“我的好朋友们都说了些什么呀？”一时，受难者哄着自己：兴许只是格兰奇巷流传的关于芭芭拉的无伤大雅的闲话。
“别响，”露西拉说，“请别笑；我要同你谈一件顶正经的事。我从几位顶老顶老的朋友那里听说了你的事，卡文迪什先生——同*这个*毫不相干，你知道，”马乔里班克斯小姐说着，朝格罗夫街的方向摆了摆手。于是芭芭拉·莱克、连同与她有关的一切，像影子一样从这不幸的人心里消失了。他这忘恩负义得可怕；可是——照马乔里班克斯小姐会说的那样——这正是可以预料的，*他们*向来如此行。对那个曾给他孤独岁月添过营生与兴味的对象，他再没有半点闲情耐心。他一霎醒转，对自己那段糊涂暗咒一声，尽力直面真正的危险。
“你一定是弄错了，马乔里班克斯小姐，”他带几分苦涩地说；“那应该说，顶老顶老的仇人。我知道是谁。就是你们太太们大惊小怪的那位会吏总。是他一直在造我的谣，”卡文迪什先生说。他说话时深深吐出一口硬气，血回到脸上。也许头一刻他竟觉得畅快，说完了呼吸也松了些；可同时，想到自己已经败露、此后格兰奇巷将对他闭门敛容，又叫他不寒而栗。“你若信他的话，我不如立刻投降，”他苦湿地接着说。“牧师什么都说得出；他们跟——跟女人一样坏。”可怜人绝望之下说这话，因为不知自己嘴里说的什么；其实他心里明白，女人一向是他最好的朋友，倘若审判归她们，他还有一线生机。

===Original===

“You are very ungrateful to say so,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “but it is only because you are excited, I suppose. No, Mr. Cavendish, it was not the Archdeacon; on the contrary, it was a lady, and she said nothing but good of you,” said Lucilla; and then there was a pause. As for Mr. Cavendish, it would be altogether impossible to describe the state of his mind. He was like a man suddenly reprieved, but giddy with the shock, and feeling the halter still round his neck, and knowing that he had himself undermined the ground on which he was standing. It was Lucilla who supported him in the shock of the moment, for all his self-command could not keep him from a momentary shiver and stagger when he found that things were not so bad as he thought.

“A lady, and she said nothing but good!” he muttered, under his breath; and then he made an effort to recover himself. “Pardon me, I cannot guess who my unknown friend may be. It is very soothing to one’s feelings to be spoken well of by a lady,” said Mr. Cavendish, and he laughed again in a discordant unsteady way. Lucilla regarded him through all these fluctuations with natural pity, and at the same time with the calmness of a knowledge which was aware of all and had nothing more to discover; and at the end Mr. Cavendish perceived her calm, and the absence of wonder and curiosity in her face, and began to perceive that he had something very serious to deal with﻿—more serious even than he had at first supposed.

“I am going to tell you all about it,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “but in the meantime wait a minute and let me speak to you. I have something very serious to say.”

===Chinese===

“你这样说太忘恩负义了，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“不过我想那只是因为你激动了。不，卡文迪什先生，不是会吏总；恰恰相反，是一位太太，而且说的净是你的好话，”露西拉说；随后是一阵静默。至于卡文迪什先生，他那时的心境全然无法描摹。他像一个突获缓刑的囚徒，惊得发晕，还觉着套索仍套在颈上，还知道自己脚下的地面正是自己控空的。撑住他熬过这一震的是露西拉；因为事情既不像他想的那样糟，他纵有全副自持，也止不住一霎的战栗与踉跄。
“一位太太，而且净说好话！”他低声念叨；随即努力恢复自己。“恕我冒昧，我猜不出我这位无名的恩人是谁。叫一位太太说好话，于人的感情真是莫大安慰，”卡文迪什先生说，又用一种走调的、不稳的声气笑了。露西拉看着他这一路起落，怀着天然的怜惘，同时又怀着一种全知的平静——一切已知、再无可发现的平静；到末了，卡文迪什先生觉出她的平静，觉出她脸上没有惊讶、没有好奇，开始明白自己面对的非常严重——比他起初想的还严重。
“我这就把一切告诉你，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“可眼下先等一等，让我同你说句话。我有非常正经的话要说。”

===Original===

It was for this they stopped short at the foot of Grange Lane just where the land was already parcelled out for St. Roque’s. What Lucilla was going to say was too important to be spoken while walking, and she withdrew her hand from Mr. Cavendish’s arm. They were both so much absorbed that they did not see anybody coming, nor indeed had any attention to spare for external affairs. The blood had deserted Mr. Cavendish’s face, and he was once more green with anxiety and inquietude. He stood facing her, feeling that the crisis of his fate had come, and not knowing whether it was absolute despair or a faint dawning of hope that possessed him. If he had been the most passionate of lovers, and if she had held in her hands the dreadful alternative between rapture and misery, there could not have been a more rapt and absorbing attention in Mr. Cavendish’s face.

“I want to tell you, first of all, that you must have confidence in me,” said Lucilla; “you﻿—must﻿—have confidence in me. We can do nothing without that. I know everything, Mr. Cavendish,” Miss Marjoribanks added compassionately﻿—“*everything*; but nobody else knows it. I hope I can arrange everything if it is left in my hands. This is what I wanted to tell you first of all. Before everything, you must have confidence in me.”

What Mr. Cavendish might have answered to this solemn appeal it would be vain to imagine; for the truth was, he was stopped before he could utter a word. He was stopped and seized by the hand, and greeted with a frankness which was, perhaps, all the more loud and cordial from what appeared to the newcomer the comic character of the situation. “It *is* Cavendish, by Jove!” the intruder exclaimed, waving his hand to some people who were coming on behind him. “I beg a thousand pardons for disturbing you, my dear fellow; but they all talk about you so, that I was determined to make sure it was you. Good heavens, Miss Marjoribanks!” General Travers added, taking off his hat. It was Mr. and Mrs. Centum who were coming down behind him﻿—she with a light shawl thrown over her head, tempted out by the beauty of the evening; and Lucilla saw in a moment the consequences of this encounter, and how it would be over all Carlingford before tomorrow morning that she and Mr. Cavendish were betrothed at the very least. Miss Marjoribanks had all her wits about her, as ever, fortunately for both.

===Chinese===

他们便为此停在格兰奇巷巷口——圣罗克堂的地皮已在那里划片分块。露西拉要说的话太重，不能边走边说；她把手从卡文迪什先生的臂弯里抽出来。两人都这样专注，来人竟谁也没看见，也实在匀不出半点注意力给外物。血已从卡文迪什先生脸上退尽，他又因焦灼与不安泛了绿。他面对她立着，自觉命运的危机到了，又不知攫住自己的，是绝望到底，还是一线希望的微明。哪怕他是天下最炽烈的情人、她手里握着大喜大悲的生死裁决，卡文迪什先生脸上也未必能有比这更攫人的专注了。
“我首先要告诉你：你必须信任我，”露西拉说；“你——必须——信任我。没有这一样，我们什么也做不成。我什么都知道，卡文迪什先生，”马乔里班克斯小姐怜惘地补一句——“*什么都知道*；可再没有别人知道。只要交到我手里，我想我能样样安排妥当。这是我要最先告诉你的。先于一切，你必须信任我。”
卡文迪什先生对这庄严的呼吁会怎样作答，想也无益；因为实情是，他一个字还没出口就被拦住了。他被人拦住、捉住手，被人那样坦率地招呼——那股热閙劲，兴许正因为新来者眼里这局面滑稽，反倒加倍响亮亲热。“真是卡文迪什，老天作证！”闯入者喊道，向后头来的人挥着手。“搅扰了你们，老兄，千万抱歉；可人人这样念叨你，我非弄确实了不可。天哪，马乔里班克斯小姐！”特拉弗斯将军又加一句，脱帽致意。后面下来的是森特姆先生同太太——她头上搭一条薄披巾，是被这傍晚的美引出来的；露西拉一眼看到了这场遭遇的后果：明天早晨以前，她同卡文迪什先生至少已订婚的消息，将传遍卡灵福德。所幸两人而言，马乔里班克斯小姐一如既往地心眼齐全。

===Original===

“Yes, it is me,” she said calmly; “I have been taking tea with the Lakes, and I made Mr. Cavendish give me his arm home. He did not like being found out, to be sure, but he could not help himself; and we all know about that,” Lucilla added, with a smile, taking once more the unfortunate man’s arm. “Oh, yes, we all know,” said Mrs. Centum, with a laugh; but yet, notwithstanding, everybody felt sure that it was all Lucilla’s cleverness, and that Barbara Lake was a myth and fiction. And it was thus, with Miss Marjoribanks leaning on his arm, and General Travers, in all the warmth of renewed friendship, guarding him on the other side, that Mr. Cavendish, whose head was in a whirl of excitement, and who did not know what he was doing, was led back in triumph past Colonel Chiley’s very door, where the Archdeacon was lying in wait to crunch his bones, back from all his aberrations into the very heart of Grange Lane.

===Chinese===

“是，是我，”她平静地说；“我在莱克家吃茶，叫卡文迪什先生送我回家。给人撞破了，他自然不乐意；可由不得他；这一层咱们心里都有数，”露西拉笑着补一句，重新挽住那不幸的人。“哦，是，咱们都有数，”森特姆太太笑着说；可是尽管如此，人人还是认定：这全是露西拉的手段，芭芭拉·莱克不过是讹传。于是，马乔里班克斯小姐挽着他的手臂，特拉弗斯将军怀着旧谊复热的全部温暖，在另一侧护送——卡文迪什先生，脑袋转得发晕、不知自己在做什么——就这样凯旋地被人领着，走过奇利上校家的大门口——会吏总正埋伏在那里要嚼他的骨头——从他的一切迷途，回到格兰奇巷的正中心来。

## XXIX / 二十九
===Original===

Mr. Cavendish was led back to his own house that evening by General Travers, whose claim of acquaintance was too decided to be rejected. He never knew very well what passed between the moment when Miss Marjoribanks began to expound to him the urgent necessity that he should confide in her, and the moment in which he found himself in his own house, admitted eagerly by the surprised and anxious servants, and conducted by the energetic soldier. That he had taken leave of Lucilla at her own door, that he had watched her white dress sweep away into the dark garden with a faint sense that it was his only remaining protector who thus left him, and that after that he had smoked a horrible cigar with Mr. Centum, and been accompanied home by the old acquaintance, who had turned up at so unlucky a moment﻿—was all that the poor man was aware of. And yet it is to be supposed that on the whole he behaved himself very much like other people, since General Travers had no distinct idea that his company was undesirable, or that his cordial recognition was anything but welcome. The General, indeed, took it as quite natural, under the circumstances, that Cavendish should be a little confused. A man who is no longer a very young man, and has a character to support, does not care to be found mooning with the object of his affections on a summer evening, like a boy of twenty; and General Travers was perfectly aware that he had thus a very good joke against Cavendish. “It is worth a man’s while to set up a bachelor establishment in the country,” the General said. “By Jove! I wish I could do it. It makes a fellow feel Arcadian, and ready for anything;” and for his own part he was very ready to seize upon his former acquaintance, a man who belonged to his club, and had a chance to know what he was talking about. “As for Charlie Centum,” the soldier said, “what between business and matrimony, he has grown the greatest guy imaginable; and I can’t go off directly, you know; and then there’s always this business about the depot. It’s immense luck to find you here, Cavendish,” General Travers added, with flattering cordiality; and if poor Mr. Cavendish was not grateful, it certainly was not his friend’s fault. He led the way into his house with a glum countenance and a sinking heart, though fortunately the latter was not visible.

===Chinese===

那天晚上，卡文迪什先生被特拉弗斯将军领回了自己的宅子——将军那认交情的架势太斩截，推拒不得。从马乔里班克斯小姐开始向他晓陈“把事情托给她”的紧急必要，到发现自己进了自家的门——惊惶的仆人们热切迎入、由那位精力充沛的军人一路押送——这中间究竟经过了什么，他自己也不大了然。他只记得：他在自家门口向露西拉道了别，望着她一身白裙扫进黑沉沉的花园，隐隐觉得那走开的是他仅存的保护人；随后他同森特姆先生抽了一支可怕的雪茄，又由这位偏在那样不巧的时刻冒出来的旧相识一路送回了家——这可怜人所知道的，就这些。可是想必总的说来他的举止同旁人也差不多，因为特拉弗斯将军丝毫没有觉出自己不受欢迎，也不觉得他那热络的相认有半点不讨好。将军确实觉得，处在这种情形下，卡文迪什有点神魂颠倒，再自然不过：一个不再年轻、又有人设要撑的男人，可不愿意叫人撞见他在夏夜对着心上人出神，像个二十岁的毛头小子；特拉弗斯将军清清楚楚地知道，他这一下攒住了卡文迪什一个绝好的把柄。“在乡下置一副单身汉的家业，值，”将军说。“老天！我倒想置呢。这叫人觉得自己进了世外桃源，什么都干得出来；”就他自己而论，他巴不得抓住这位旧相识——他俱乐部里的人、有机会懂行的人。“至于查理·森特姆，”军人说，“叫生意和婚事两头一夹，长成了天底下头一号的活宝；您知道，我又不能说走就走；驻地那摊子事总缠着。在这儿撞见你，真是运气大发了，卡文迪什，”特拉弗斯将军添上一句，那份亲热简直叫人受宠若惊；可怜的卡文迪什先生若不知感激，实在怪不得他这位朋友。他黑着脸、心往下沉，引路进了自己的宅子——所幸后一样从外面看不见。

===Original===

It was a very nice house, fitted up with all that luxury of comfort which a man who has, as Mrs. Centum said, “only himself to look to,” can afford to collect around him. Mr. Cavendish had only himself, and he had made his habitation perfect, though, on the whole, he did not pass a very great deal of his time at home. He had some nice pictures and a good library, though he was not particularly given to the arts; and he had an admirable cellar, as all the gentlemen owned in Carlingford, though, for his own part, he was very moderate in that point, and did not give himself any airs on the subject. Mr. Centum, on the contrary, was one of the men who talk about vintages, and raise expectations never to be carried out. And General Travers could not but feel the force of the contrast as he sat deep into the night, and “talked over everything,” with the man who by that time he felt convinced was one of his best friends.

===Chinese===

这是一所非常好的宅子，陈设着一个“只需要照管自己”的男人——照森特姆太太的说法——所置办得起的一切舒适的奢华。卡文迪什先生只需要照管自己，他把自己的居处弄得十全十美，虽然总的说来他在家的时候并不很多。他有几幅好画、一个像样的书房，虽然他于艺术并不怎样上心；他有一座人人称道的酒窖——卡灵福德的绅士们个个承认——虽然他自己于这一层十分节制，也绝不拿它摆谱。森特姆先生恰相反，是那一类谈年份、抬人指望、永不全兑现的男人。特拉弗斯将军同这位——他这时已认定的——至交之一，坐到夜深，“把什么都谈了个遍”，两相对照之下，不能不感到这反差的力量。

===Original===

As for Mr. Cavendish, it would be very difficult to describe his feelings. He had been knocking about in all sorts of poor places, making clandestine visits to his sister, and hovering round the more than suburban simplicity of Grove Street, and the sense of being once more enveloped and surrounded by all that was pleasant to the eye and comfortable to the outer man was wonderfully consolatory and agreeable. But his mind was in a dreadfully harassed condition all the same. He was preoccupied to the last degree, wondering what Miss Marjoribanks really knew, and how far he had betrayed himself, and to what extent it would be safe, as she herself said, to confide in Lucilla; and at the same time he was obliged to listen to and show a certain interest in the General’s stories, and to make now and then a painful effort of mind to recall some of the mutual friends referred to, whose names and persons had in the meantime slipped out of his memory. All the babble of the club, which General Travers felt must be so refreshing to the ears of a rusticated member, fell as flat upon Mr. Cavendish, whose mind was full of other matters, as if it had been the merest old woman’s gossip, which, to be sure, it slightly resembled in some points. The gallant General made himself so agreeable that he nearly drove the unfortunate man out of his senses, and, when he had exhausted all other means of aggravation, returned with fresh zest to the sentimental circumstances in which, as he supposed, he had found his companion out.

“Very sensible I call it,” said General Travers. “To be candid, I don’t call her strictly handsome, you know; she’s too big for that﻿—and I don’t suppose she’s of any family to speak of; though perhaps you don’t mind that trifling circumstance; but a woman that will dress well and light up well, and knows how to give a man a capital dinner, by Jove! and no doubt has a pretty little bit of money into the bargain﻿—I respect your taste, Cavendish,” said the friendly critic, with effusion; and somehow this applause irritated its recipient more than all that had gone before.

===Chinese===

至于卡文迪什先生，他的心绪很难描摹。他这些日子在种种寒酸地方东躲西藏，偷偷摸摸去探望姐姐，绕着格罗夫街那比郊区还朴素的简陋打转；此刻重新被一切悦目适体的东西包裹环绕，那份慰帖实在受用。可他的心同时又被折磨得苦不堪言。他的心事重到了顶点：揣摩马乔里班克斯小姐究竟知道多少，自己露馅露到了哪一步，照她本人的说法，把信托给露西拉究竟稳到什么程度；同时他还不得不听将军的故事、装出几分兴致，还得时时痛苦地动用记性，把人家提起的那些共同朋友想回来——那些姓名和面孔早从他记忆里溜出去了。俱乐部的那一套闲话——特拉弗斯将军认定对一个放逐乡居的人的耳朵必定如清泉——落在心装他事的卡文迪什先生身上，同最无聊的老太婆的家长里短一样平塌——说真的，某些方面也确实相像。这位英勇的将军把自己表现得那样可亲，几乎把那不幸的人逼疯了；等一切磨人的招数使尽，他又抖擞精神，回到他自以为拿住同伴的那柱风流局面上来。

“我看这事办得很有见地，”特拉弗斯将军说。“说句老实话，她算不得严格意义的美人，你知道——她块头太大——我想她家门第也谈不上；不过那一点小事您也许不放在心上；可一个女人，会穿、灯下亮，还懂得给男人一顿像样的晚饭，老天！又无疑还带着一小笔钱——佩服您的眼光，卡文迪什，”这位友好的评论家热络地说；不知怎么，这一番喝彩比先前一切更叫它的受主冒火。

===Original===

“I am sure I am much obliged to you,” said Mr. Cavendish, “though, unfortunately, I don’t merit your approbation. Miss Marjoribanks is a great friend of mine, but she wouldn’t have me, and I don’t mean to ask her. At the same time, she has very good connections; and that is not the way to talk of a girl of twenty. She is worth a dozen of your fast young ladies,” said the sufferer, with some heat. He was not in the least in love with Lucilla, and indeed had a certain dread of her at this present moment; but he could not forget that she had once stood by him in his need﻿—and, besides, he was glad of any subject on which he could contradict his visitor. “I dare say her family is better than either yours or mine. Scotch, you know,” said Mr. Cavendish, trying to laugh. As for the General, he leaned back on his chair with an indulgent air, and stroked his mustache.

“Beg your pardon﻿—meant no offence,” he said. “For my part, I don’t see that it matters, if a woman is good-looking and has something, you know. For instance, there was a pretty little thing﻿—a charming little thing﻿—Lake, or something like that﻿—”

“Ah!” said Mr. Cavendish. It was a frightful want of self-control; but he had been a long time at full strain, and he could not help it. It did not occur to him, for the moment, that nobody in his senses would have applied the term “little thing” to Barbara; and, after all the slow aggravation that he had been submitting to, the idea of this insolent soldier interfering in Grove Street was beyond his power of endurance. As for the General, the tone of this exclamation was such that he too turned round on his chair, and said, “Yes?” with equally unmistakable meaning, startled, but ready for the emergency, whatever it might be.

===Chinese===

“我相信我很领您的情，”卡文迪什先生说，“可惜，我当不起您的赞许。马乔里班克斯小姐是我的至交，可她不肯要我，我也不打算再求。同时，她的姻亲极好；对一位二十岁的小姐，可不能那样议论。她抵得上一打您那些放荡的时髦小姐，”受难的人带着火气说。他一点也不爱露西拉，此刻甚至有点怕她；可他忘不了她曾在他的患难里站在他一边——再说，随便哪个题目，只要能驳他的客人，他都高兴。“我料想她的家世比您我两家的都强。苏格兰人，你知道，”卡文迪什先生说着，勉强笑了一笑。将军呢，带着宽容的神气往椅背上一靠，捻着髭须。

“恕罪——没有得罪的意思，”他说。“就我看，一个女人只要好看、有点家当，别的都不打紧，你知道。比如说，前几天在您那位——您那位朋友府上，见着一个小可人儿——迷人的小东西——姓莱克，还是什么的——”

“啊！”卡文迪什先生说。这一声实在失于自持；可他绷了太久，忍不住了。他一时没想到，凡神志清明的人谁也不会把“小东西”三个字安在芭芭拉头上；再说，捱了半宿的闷气之后，一想到这个无礼的军人要插手格罗夫街，便超出了他忍耐的限度。将军听这一声的腔调，也在椅子上转过身来，应了一声“唔？”——同样意味深长：吃了一惊，却不论来的是什么，都预备好了应付。

===Original===

Thus the two looked at each other for a second, friends in the ordinary acceptation of the word, and yet, perhaps, on the eve of becoming enemies. Mr. Cavendish had, up to that moment, pretty nearly forgotten Barbara Lake. It was a piquant sort of occupation when he had nothing else to do, and when the world, according to his morbid fancy, was on the eve of turning its back upon him﻿—but from the moment when he had said between his teeth “Confound these women!” and had felt the excitement of the approaching crisis, Barbara, and her crimson cheeks, and her level eyebrows, and her contralto, had gone altogether out of his mind. At the same time, it is quite true that a man may feel himself at liberty to forget a woman when other matters of more immediate interest are absorbing his attention, and yet be driven furious by the idea suddenly presented to him that somebody else, who has nothing earthly to do with it, is about to interfere. Mr. Cavendish, however, recovered himself while the General sat staring at him, and began to see how ridiculous his defiance was.

“Well?﻿—go on. I did not say anything,” he said, and lighted another cigar. Yet he did not face his companion as a friendly listener should, but began to beat measure to an irritating imaginary air on the table, with a certain savage energy by moments, as if he were beating time on the General’s head.

“Then why do you stop a fellow short like that?” said General Travers; “I was going to tell you of someone I saw the other day in the house of your﻿—your friend, you know. She was under Miss Marjoribanks’s wing, that was how I saw her﻿—and I hope you are not playing the gay deceiver, my friend;﻿—a little thing, round-faced, hazel-eyed﻿—a little soft rosebud sort of creature,” said the General, growing eloquent. “By Jove! Cavendish, I hope you don’t mean to make yourself disagreeable. These sort of looks, you know﻿—”

===Chinese===

于是两人对望了一秒：按这词的寻常意义，是朋友；而下一刻，也许就是仇人。直到那一刻，卡文迪什先生几乎把芭芭拉·莱克忘了。那是他闲来无事时的一碟俏皮的消遣——尤其当他病态地幻想着社交界就要背过身去的时候；可是自他咬着牙说“这帮女人真该死”、感到那逼近的关口以来，芭芭拉，连同她的红脸膛、平直的眉、她的女低音，整个从他心里出去了。同时，这倒也是实情：一个男人尽可以在更要紧的事情吸住他注意力的时候心安理得忘掉一个女人，却又被突然摆到面前的一个念头逼得暴跳——另有一个同这事毫不相干的人，要来插一手。可是趁将军瞪着他的当口，卡文迪什先生缓过来了，开始觉出自己这副寻衅的样子多么可笑。

“怎么？——接着说呀。我又没说什么，”他说，又点上一支雪茄。只是他不以友好听客的架势面对同伴，却开始在桌上按一支恼人的想象中的曲子打拍子，时时带着一股凶劲，仿佛敲的是将军的脑袋。

“那你干嘛叫人半截里刹住？”特拉弗斯将军说；“我正要告诉你，前几天我在你那位——你那位朋友家里见着的一个人。她在马乔里班克斯小姐的翅膀底下，我这才见着——我望你没有在做那个甜嘴蜜舌的骗子，我的朋友；——一个小东西，圆脸，榛子眼晴——小玫瑰骨朵似的一个软软的人儿，”将军说得兴起。“老天！卡文迪什，我望你不打算叫人不痛快。这一路的神气，你知道——”

===Original===

“It was Rose, I suppose,” said Mr. Cavendish, relieved in a moment; and, to tell the truth, he could not help laughing. The more eloquent and angry the General grew, the more amused and contemptuous grew his entertainer. He was so tickled by the position of affairs, that he actually forgot his anxieties for the moment. “No doubt it was Rose,” he repeated, and laughed; Rose! what anybody could see in that little dragon! And then the contrast between the soldier, who prided himself on his knowledge of the world, and liked to talk of his family and position, to the annoyance of those who had none, and the amusement of those who happen to possess these valuable qualifications﻿—and the mistress of the Female School of Design, filled Mr. Cavendish with amusement: perhaps all the more because he himself was in a similar scrape. As for General Travers, he was as much disposed to be angry as, a moment before, Mr. Cavendish had been.

===Chinese===

“那想必是罗斯，”卡文迪什先生说，登时松了口气；而且，说实话，他忍不住笑了。将军越是激昂动气，他的东道越发觉得好笑、觉得轻蔑。这局面把他痒得这样厉害，一时竟把焦虑都忘了。“没疑问，是罗斯，”他又说一遍，笑了；罗斯！那条小龙身上到底有什么可看的！再者，将军其人——自负通晓世故，爱谈自家的门第地位，叫没有的人着恼、碰巧有的人开心——同女子设计学校的校长这一对照，把卡文迪什先生填满了快意：也许更因为他自己正陷在同样的窘局里。至于特拉弗斯将军，他此刻动怒的火气，同方才卡文迪什先生的一般无二。

===Original===

“It might be Rose,” he said, “or Lily either, for anything I can tell; but there is nothing laughable in it that I can see. You seem to be perfectly au courant, at all events﻿—which I hope is quite satisfactory to Miss Marjoribanks,” said the soldier; and then he resumed, after a disagreeable little pause, “they tell me that everybody meets at the Doctor’s on Thursdays. I suppose I shall see you there. Thursday, ain’t it? tomorrow?” He looked as he spoke, with what seemed to his victim an insulting consciousness, in poor Cavendish’s face. But, in reality, the General did not mean to be insulting, and knew nothing whatever of the horrible internal pang which rent his companion when it was thus recalled to him that it *was* tomorrow﻿—a fact which, up to this moment, had not occurred to the unfortunate. Tomorrow; and not even tomorrow﻿—today﻿—for by this time it was two o’clock in the morning, and the unwelcome intruder was wasting the little time he had for deciding what he should do. Once more his own personal anxieties, which he had put aside for a moment at the sudden dictate of jealousy, surged over everything, and swallowed up all lesser sensations. Tomorrow!﻿—and by this time everybody knew that he was in Carlingford, and he could not stay away from the weekly assembly without attracting general attention to himself, and throwing open the floodgates of suspicion. What was he to do? should he turn his back on the enemy once for all, and run away and break off his connection with Carlingford? or should he dare everything and face the Archdeacon, and put his trust in Lucilla, as that high-minded young woman had invited him to do? With these thoughts in his mind, it may be supposed that Mr. Cavendish gave but a very mingled attention to the babble of his visitor, who found the wine and the cigars so good, and perhaps had begun to be a little moved out of his ordinary lucidity by their effect.

===Chinese===

“也许是罗斯，”他说，“也许是莉莉，天晓得；可我看这里面没有什么可笑的。您倒是样样都门儿清——我望这对马乔里班克斯小姐十分可心，”军人说；接着不痛快地顿了一顿，又续上，“他们告诉我，礼拜四医生家里人人到齐。我料想会在那儿见到您。礼拜四，是不是？就是明天？”他说话时带着一种——在他的受害者看来——侮辱性的自觉，直望着可怜的卡文迪什的脸。可实际上将军并无侮辱之意，也全然不知他这一提，叫同伴五内俱焚地想起：果然*就是*明天——这个事实，到此刻为止那不幸的人竟一直没有想起。明天！而且不止是明天——是今天——因为这时已是凌晨两点，这位不速之客正耗着他用来决定何去何从的本已无多的时间。他自己那番焦虑——方才被醋劲的一声突令暂时推开——重新漫过一切，吞掉了所有较小的感觉。明天！如今人人都知道他回了卡灵福德；每周的聚会他若缺席，必致万众瞩目、疑窦大开，那可怎么好？他该怎么办？就此同敌人一刀两断、一走了之、同卡灵福德断绝干系？还是孤注一掷，直面会吏长，把信托给露西拉——正如那位高风的年轻女子所邀请的？怀着这些念头，可以想见，卡文迪什先生对客人的闲谈只给了三分混着的注意；那客人呢，只觉得酒好雪茄好，也许已被它们熏得稍稍出了他素常的清明。

===Original===

“You’ve got a nice little house, Cavendish,” said the General, “but it’s too small for a married man, my boy. These women are the very deuce for turning a man out of his comfortable quarters. You’ll have to go in for boudoirs and those sort of things; and, by George! you’ll be an ass if you do, with a snug little box like this to retire into,” said the philosophical warrior; and poor Cavendish smiled a ghastly smile, with the strongest inclination all the time to take him by the collar and turn him out of doors. But then he *was* a warrior and a general officer, and a member of the same club, and six feet high﻿—all which particulars, not to speak of the sacred rights of hospitality, made it somewhat difficult to carry this idea out.

===Chinese===

“你这小宅子真好，卡文迪什，”将军说，“可对娶了亲的人就太小了，我的孩子。这班女人，最擅长的就是把男人从舒服的窝里撵出去。你就得置办闺阁那一套了；老天！你要真置，就是一头蠢驴——放着这样一个舒舒服服的小窝好退守，”这位哲学家式的武人说；可怜的卡文迪什挂着一脸死白的笑，心里却有一股最强烈的冲动，想揪住他的领子把他轰出门去。可是，*他*到底是员武将、一位将官、同一俱乐部的会员，还身高六英尺——这一切，更不必说待客的神圣权利，叫这个念头执行起来颇有难度。

===Original===

“Don’t you think Centum will be sitting up for you?” he said mildly; “it’s past two o’clock; and it’s Thursday morning,” the victim added, with a sigh. The last words were an involuntary utterance of his own despair, but fortunately they struck General Travers’s vein of humour, which happened to be lively at the moment, and worked the desired but unexpected result. The General laughed loud and long, and declared that he respected a man who was aboveboard, and meant to look respectable for Miss Marjoribanks’s sake; and then he poured a mighty libation to Lucilla, and took an affectionate leave of her supposed lover. The General made a great commotion in the decorous quiet of Grange Lane when he knocked at Mr. Centum’s door. Though it was nearly three o’clock in the morning, nothing but his inherent dread of a woman would have prevented him from knocking up the banker to share his hilarity; but Mrs. Centum, in her nightcap, peaceably asleep as she was at the moment, daunted the soul of the gallant soldier; and naturally his recollection was not very perfect next day. “I had something very funny to tell you; but, by Jove! I forget what it was!” General Travers said next morning when he met his host at breakfast; and thus one bad joke at least was spared. But Mr. Cavendish shut his door upon his departing guest, without any sense, poor fellow, of having done or said anything in the least funny. He said, “Thank Heaven!” with a kind of groan of relief when his troublesome visitor was gone. And then he went back again into his library, where they had been sitting. Perhaps he had never fully appreciated before the comfort of everything, the handsome house which he had enjoyed so long without thinking anything of it, and all the pleasant luxurious accessories of life. He had been doing without them for a week or two, and he had not liked it; and yet at that moment it seemed to Mr. Cavendish that he could rather be content to lose them all at a stroke, to make it known in Carlingford that he was ruined and had lost his fortune, than that Carlingford should find out that he was not, after all, one of the Cavendishes, nor the person it took him for. But, alas! all his fortune could not bring reality to these pretensions, nor hinder the exposure to which he looked forward with such horror.

===Chinese===

“您不觉得森特姆在等您回去吗？”他婉转地说；“过两点了；这可是礼拜四的早晨了，”受难者叹一口气补了一句。末了一句原是他绝望的无心之失，幸而正撞上特拉弗斯将军此刻正活跃的幽默脉，收到了期望之外、却是求之不得的效果。将军放声大笑，笑了个够，宣称他敬重一个光明磊落、肯为马乔里班克斯小姐装点体面的人；随后他为露西拉满斟一杯、一饮而尽，同她那位准情人依依而别。将军敲响森特姆先生家门时，在格兰奇巷端庄的静夜里闹出好大一阵动静。虽已将近凌晨三点，若不是他天生的怕女人，他真要敲起来把银行家从床上提起来分享他的高兴；可是森特姆太太戴着睡帽、此际正安安稳稳睡着，就把这位英武军人的魂吓住了；于是第二天他的记忆自然不很完整。“我本来有件顶好笑的事要告诉你；可是，老天！我忘了是什么了！”特拉弗斯将军第二天早晨在早餐桌上遇见他的东道时说；于是至少有一个糟糕的笑话免于出笼。可是卡文迪什先生送走这位难缠的客人、关上门时，可怜的人，半点不觉得自己做了或说了什么好笑的事。“谢天谢地！”客人一走，他呻吟似地松了一口气。随后他回到方才对坐的书房。这一切的舒适，这所他享用了这么久、从未多想过的漂亮宅子，以及生活里一切惬意的奢华点缀——也许他从未充分领略过。他离了它们一两个星期，过得不惯；而此刻在卡文迪什先生看来，他宁肯叫它们一下子全失去、叫卡灵福德知道他破了产、失了家财，也不肯叫卡灵福德发现他到底不是卡文迪什家的人、不是大家认定的那个人。可是，唉！他全部的家财，也换不来那名头的真、挡不住他望之魂飞的拆穿。

===Original===

It is true that he was an adventurer, but he was not a base one; nor had he done anything dishonourable either to gain his fortune or to captivate the good opinion of society, which had become so important to him. But there are actual crimes that would be sooner forgiven to a man than the folly of having permitted himself to be considered one of the Cavendishes, and having set his heart on making a figure in that mild provincial world. Mr. Cavendish knew enough of human nature to know that a duchess or a lord-chamberlain would forgive more readily than Mr. and Mrs. Centum any such imposition upon them, and intrusion into their exclusive circle. And then his sister, who could not run away! For her sake it seemed to him that he had better rush off at once, and sell his house and furniture and horses, and give up Carlingford. As he thought of that, all the advantages of Carlingford came upon him stronger than ever. Perhaps a man who has always been used to be recognised as one of the members of a local aristocracy, would not have seen anything half so precious as Mr. Cavendish saw in the fact of being everywhere known and acknowledged as a constituent part of Grange Lane;﻿—recognised by the county people, and by the poor people, and pointed out as he passed by one and another to any stranger who might happen to be so ignorant as not to know Mr. Cavendish. To people who are not used to it, there is a charm in this universal acknowledgment. And then he had more need of it than most men have; and, when Carlingford signed his patent of gentility, and acknowledged and prized him, it did an infinite deal more than it had any intention of doing. To keep its regard and recognition he would have done anything, given up the half or three parts, or even, on emergency, all he had. Perhaps he had an undue confidence in the magnanimity of society, and was too sure that in such a case it would behave with a grandeur worthy of the occasion; but still he was quite right in thinking that it could forgive the loss of his fortune sooner than his real offence. And now it was Thursday morning, the day upon which he must either fight or flee. He too had laughed at Miss Marjoribanks’s evenings in his time, and thought of Thursday lightly as Lucilla’s day; but there was nothing in the least amusing in the prospect of that assembly now.

===Chinese===

诚然，他是个冒险家，可不是个卑劣的冒险家；他之得财、他之赢得社交界——如今这于他这样要紧——的好评，都不曾用过什么不名誉的手段。可是世上有这样的罪，人倒肯更快地赦免，胜过赦免他这一柱糊涂：容人把自己认作卡文迪什家的一员，又一门心思要在这一方温和的外省天地里崭露头角。卡文迪什先生于人情懂得足够：一位公爵夫人或一位宫务大臣，都要比森特姆夫妇更快赦免这样的蒙混、这样闯进他们小圈子的偺越。还有他姐姐——她是跑不掉的！为她计，他觉得自己不如立刻逃走，卖掉宅子、家具和马，弃了卡灵福德。一想到这里，卡灵福德的好处又空前有力地涌上他心头。一个一向惯于被认作地方贵族一员的人，怕是看不见卡文迪什先生在“处处被认作格兰奇巷的组成部分”这件事里所看见的一半珍贵——郡里人认得他，穷人们认得他，他走过时人人把他指给那些无知得不识卡文迪什先生的生客看。对于不惯这个的人，这种普遍的承认自有一种魔力。何况他比多数人更需要它；卡灵福德签发他绅士身分的特许状、承认他、器重他时，办的远超它自己的本意。为保住这份敬重与承认，他什么都肯做：让出一半、让出四分之三，急难里甚至倾其所有。也许他对社交界的宽宏信得过头了，太拿准它届时自会有配得上场面的恢弘；可是他认定它宁肯饶他破财、不肯饶他真正的罪，这一点倒是全然不错的。而此刻已是礼拜四的早晨，他非战即逃的日子。从前他也笑话过马乔里班克斯小姐的晚会，把礼拜四轻飘飘看作露西拉的日子；可如今那场聚会在望，没有半点可笑之处了。

===Original===

When a man has thoughts like these to entertain him, nothing can be more useless than to go to bed, although in ordinary circumstances, at three o’clock in the morning, that is about the only thing one can do. Poor Mr. Cavendish, however, was not quite free to act as he thought proper. He had been a long time away from home, and he did not feel himself in a position to shock his servants’ feelings with impunity. He went to his room, accordingly, like a martyr, carrying all his difficulties with him, and these unpleasant companions naturally made a night of it when they had him all to themselves. When sheer fatigue and exhaustion procured him a moment’s sleep, it was only getting deeper and deeper into trouble: for then it was the Archdeacon who had planted a heavy foot on his neck, or General Travers, who, with still more fatal force, had found out the way to Grove Street. When Mr. Cavendish awoke, he said to himself, “Confound these women!” with more fervour than ever; but, at the same time, he swore a mighty oath to himself that he would horsewhip the fellow who ventured to come in his way. Barbara Lake might be no great things, but at least it was to him, and no one else, that she belonged. Such was the complication that afforded him a little outlet for his temper in the midst of the dreadful difficulties of his position, and the question which was constantly renewing itself in his thoughts, as to whether he should go or stay. The idea of presenting himself in the centre of society in Miss Marjoribanks’s drawing-room, and being met by the Archdeacon, and held up to public contempt there and then, with all the world looking on, and even Travers, who would carry the narrative out of Carlingford, was something too horrible to be contemplated; and yet how was he to escape? He was still in this state of mind, driven backwards and forwards by every new wind, when the morning came, and when Miss Marjoribanks’s note was put into his hand.

===Chinese===

一个男人怀里抱着这样的念头，上床便全然无用了——虽然按寻常情形，凌晨三点，人也就只剩这一件事可做。可是可怜的卡文迪什先生不能全由着自己的性子来。他离家日久，自觉没有资格无所忌惮地惊扰仆人们的感情。于是他像个殉道者一样进了自己的房间，把全部难题随身带了上去；这些不快的伴侣一旦独自占有了他，自然闹了个通宵。等到纯粹的疲惫把他按入片刻的睡眠，那也只是越陷越深：梦里，要么是会吏长一只重脚踏上他的脖颈，要么是特拉弗斯将军——以更致命的威力——寻到了去格罗夫街的路。卡文迪什先生一觉醒来，比任何时候更热切地对自己说：“这帮女人真该死！”但同时，他也对自己发下重誓：谁敢来横插一手，他就抽谁一顿马鞭。芭芭拉·莱克算不得什么了不得的人物，可她到底归他、不归别人。在他处境的重重困难里、在那盘据不去的“走还是留”的问题里，这团乱麻倒给他的一点火气留了个出口。想到自己站到社交界中央——马乔里班克斯小姐的客厅里——迎面撞上会吏长、当场被高高吊起示众，全世界看着，连特拉弗斯也在——他还要把这段故事带出卡灵福德——那光景可怕得不敢想；可他又怎么逃？他正是这样心绪，被每一阵新来的风刮来刮去，捱到了早晨——马乔里班克斯小姐的便函送到了他手上。

===Original===

For the truth was, that, after long consideration, Lucilla had determined that the matter was one which could not be permitted to stand over. She was of too energetic a temperament to let things linger on in an uncertain way when they could be made an end of, and brought to a conclusion; and then, as nobody can predict what sudden and unexpected turn human affairs may take, it was always possible that, if Miss Marjoribanks did not make an end of the business dramatically, and to the satisfaction of everybody concerned, it might be found some fine day to have resolved itself by means of some one of those illegitimate and incomplete expedients which abound in ordinary life. It was with this view that Miss Marjoribanks took the step of writing to Mr. Cavendish. She had written in the sacred retirement of her own maiden chamber, when all the world was still; perhaps at the moment when General Travers was, as he would himself have vulgarly called it, “chaffing” Cavendish about the beautiful and disinterested friendship which united him to the young sovereign of Grange Lane. But naturally such poor raillery was far from the virginal thoughts of Lucilla at that retired and sacred hour; and we may venture to add that the elevating influence of the maiden’s bower in which she composed it, and of that tranquil moment of meditation and solitude, breathed in every line, and gave force to every sentiment of the letter which Mr. Cavendish tore open with an excited hand. Perhaps he was too anxious and curious to give it the solemn perusal which it ought to have received.

**My dear Mr. Cavendish**﻿—It was very unlucky that we should have been interrupted this evening at such an important moment, when I had so much to say to you. But I think the best thing I can do is to write, feeling quite sure that when you know all, *you cannot possibly mistake* my motives. Everybody has retired, and I am quite alone, and the silence2 seems to me full of meaning when I think that the fate of a person for whom I have so great a regard may be hanging upon it. I might be afraid of writing to you so frankly, if I did not feel quite sure that you would appreciate my intention.

===Chinese===

实情是：露西拉经过长考，断定这件事不许再搁。她的性情太干练，受不了听任事情悬着：既然能了断，就该了断；再说，人事的突转谁也料不定，马乔里班克斯小姐若不把这件事戏剧性地、叫当事各方皆大欢喜地做个了断，说不定哪天它会借寻常生活中比比皆是的那种不正不全的权宜之计，自己糊里糊涂了了局——那总有可能。正是为此，马乔里班克斯小姐采取了给卡文迪什先生写信这一步。她是在自己闺房的圣静里写的，其时万籁俱寂；也许正是特拉弗斯将军——用他自己的粗话来说——“打趣”卡文迪什同格兰奇巷年轻女君之间那段美丽无私的友谊的时刻。可是那样可怜的取笑，自然同那个隐秘神圣时辰里露西拉的处女情怀相去天壤；我们不妨放胆补一句：她拟稿的那间闺阁、那一刻静观与独处的时光，那升华的影响沁在字里行间，给它每一句情辞添了力量——卡文迪什先生拆信的那只手，却激动得发抖。他也许太焦灼、太好奇，不曾给这封信以它本该领受的庄重的一读。

**亲爱的卡文迪什先生**——今晚那样要紧的关头，我们偏被打断，我还有那么多话要对你说，实在不巧。可我想，最好还是笔谈；我全然拿得准：等你了解了全部，*你决计不会误会*我的用意。家人都歇下了，只有我独自一个；一想到一位我如此敬重的人的命运也许悬在上面，这寂静2在我听来仿佛充满了意义。倘若不是全然拿得准你会体察我的本意，我这样坦白地给你写信，也许要害怕的。

===Original===

Dear Mr. Cavendish, it is not the Archdeacon who has said anything. *He does not know it is you*; therefore, of course, he could not say anything directly bearing upon you. But then, you know, if he were to meet you by hazard, as he is sure to do some day﻿—and for my part I rather think he is fond of Grove Street﻿—you would be exposed at once, and everything would be lost, for we all know the prejudices that exist in Carlingford. I have another plan of operations to propose to you, which I feel quite sure is for your good, and also naturally for the good of anybody to whom you may intend to unite your fortunes. I feel quite sure that it is far safer to adopt a bold resolution, and to have it over at once. Come to dinner tomorrow. If you may happen to find an enemy, you will find also an unlooked-for friend; and, so far as I am concerned, you *know* that you may calculate on my support. I do not wonder at your being anxious about it; but if you will only have full confidence in me and a little in yourself, believe me it will be all over in a night. If there had ever been anything between you and me, as these stupid people suppose, I might have felt hesitation in writing to you like this; but when I know a thing to be right, I hope I will never be afraid to do it. I have been called upon to do many things that are not common for girls of my age, and perhaps that is why I made up my mind at once to set this all straight for you. Once more I repeat, dear Mr. Cavendish, have confidence in me. Come tomorrow evening as if nothing had happened; and take my word for it that all will go well.﻿—Your friend,

Lucilla Marjoribanks.

P.S.﻿—If you would like to come and talk it over with me tomorrow, I shall be at home till twelve o’clock; but unless it will be a satisfaction to your own mind, it is not necessary for me, for I have all my plans laid.

===Chinese===

亲爱的卡文迪什先生，不是会吏长说了什么。*他并不知道那是你*；所以当然，他不可能说出什么直接落在你身上的话。可是你要知道，倘若他哪一天同你劈面相逢——这一天迟早要来——再说就我看，他倒像是恋着格罗夫街——你就当场败露，一切都完了：卡灵福德的成见，我们谁不知道。我另有整套的作战方略要向你提议；我全然拿得准，这是为你好，自然也是为任何一个你打算共结家业的人好。我全然拿得准：采取一个大胆的决断、一了百了，稳妥得多。明天来吃饭。你许会撞见一个敌人，却也会撞见一位不速的友人；就我而论，你*知道*可以指望我的支持。你为这事焦心，我不奇怪；可你只要全然信我、再稍稍信一点你自己，相信我，一夜之间就全了结。倘若你我之间真有过什么——像这班蠢人所猜想的——我这样给你写信，也许倒要踌躇；可我知道一件事是对的，就望自己永远不怕去做。人家已经要我做许多我这个年纪的姑娘不常做的事了，也许正因如此，我才当下拿定主意，替你把这一切理个清爽。我再说一遍，亲爱的卡文迪什先生：信我。明天晚上若无其事地来；我担保，一切都会顺利。——你的朋友，

露西拉·马乔里班克斯

又启——你若愿意明天先来同我谈一谈，十二点前我都在家；不过除非你自己心上痛快些，这于我并非必要：我的计划全已排定。

===Original===

It would be quite out of the question to attempt any explanation of Mr. Cavendish’s feelings when he read this letter. His utter bewilderment, his terror, his rage, his final helpless sense that it would be utterly hopeless for him, or half a dozen men, to enter the field against this curious complication of unknown friends and open enemies and generous protectors, took away from him the last remnant of courage. He did not know what to do or to think. He swallowed his coffee with a sense of despair, and sent the rest of his breakfast away untasted; thus betraying, without intending it, his emotions to his kitchen. “It stands to reason as there’s a cause for it,” Mr. Cavendish’s domestics concluded in committee of the whole house; and surely, if ever man had good reason for not eating his breakfast, it was he. When he had gone over it all again till his head had grown utterly confused and his thoughts were all topsy-turvy, Mr. Cavendish took a sudden resolution. He went upstairs and changed his dress with a certain solemnity. He made a toilette more careful than if he were going, as he once had gone, to propose. It was like Nelson going into gala uniform for a battle. And then he went out to discover, if possible, what was coming to him. The difference was, that in this battle no honour, but only a possible salvage of reputation and fortunate escape, was to be gained.

===Chinese===

要解释卡文迪什先生读信时的心情，全然无从下笔。他那全然的迷乱、他的恐怖、他的狂怒、他末了那股无助之感——他，或再加半打男人，要同这样一团“未知的朋友、公开的敌人与慷慨的保护人”的乱麻对阵，全然无望——把他最后一点勇气也夺走了。他不知做什么、不知想什么。他绝望地咽下咖啡，把早饭余下的原样打发走；就这样无意之间，把心绪泄漏给了他的厨房。“这里头必定有个缘故，”卡文迪什先生的家仆们在全宅大会上如此裁断；真的，倘若世上有谁有充分理由不吃早饭，那正是他。他把这一切又从头捋了一遍，捋到头昏脑涨、思虑全乱了套，卡文迪什先生猛然拿定了主意。他上楼换衣，带着几分郑重。他修饰装束，比当年去求婚的那次还讲究。这好比纳尔逊上阵前换上礼服。随后他出门去，去尽可能探一探：等着他的是什么。所不同者，这一仗里赢不到荣誉，赢得到的，至多是名誉的抢救与侥幸的脱身。

## XXX / 三十
===Original===

It is possible that some people may think Mr. Cavendish’s emotions too acute for all the danger to which he was exposed; but no doubt every alarm gets intensified when a man broods on it, and thinks of nothing else for weeks at a time. All that he had to do at the present moment was to walk into Carlingford by the most frequented way, and to go up Grange Lane, where every house was open to him, and where nobody was so great a favourite as he. There were as many chances in his favour that he would not in that friendly neighbourhood encounter his one enemy, as there is for every man who goes into action that the bullet which is predestined to strike somebody will not be directed to him; but then Mr. Cavendish had not the excitement of personal conflict, nor the kind of security which is given by sharing a risk with a great many other people. And to see everything smiling and serene around, and yet to know that the most deadly danger may arrive to you at any innocent opening, or round the first street-corner, is a kind of risk which naturally tells upon the nerves more than a more open peril. Mr. Cavendish met Dr. Marjoribanks, and the Doctor was good enough to stop his brougham and keep him in conversation for five minutes with his back to the foe, if foe there was approaching; and then he met Mrs. Chiley, who all but kissed him, and was so glad to see him again, and so pleased that he was in time to make acquaintance with the Archdeacon, and so sure that Lucilla would be quite happy now he had come back. “Perhaps I ought not to say so, but I *know* she has missed you,” said the injudicious old lady; and she took both his hands and held the miserable man in a kind of pillory, from whence he gazed with despairing eyes over her shoulder, feeling sure that now was the fatal moment, and that his enemy *must* be coming. But fortune still favoured him, as it happened. He had the presence of mind to say, “I am going to call on Miss Marjoribanks;” and Mrs. Chiley dropped his hands on the instant as if they burned her, and patted him on the arm and sent him away. “She is sure to be in just now, and I am so glad; and, my dear, you need not mind me, for I am both your friends,” Mrs. Chiley said. But when he was delivered from that danger, something still more formidable awaited the unfortunate man.

===Chinese===

也许有人会觉得，卡文迪什先生的情绪对他所处的危险来说过敏了些；可是，一个人把一场惊吓盘在心里、一几个礼拜不想别的，每一声警报自然都要放大。他此刻要做的，不过是拣人最多的路走进卡灵福德，再走上格兰奇巷——那儿家家都为他开门，人人宠他无双。在那样的友善地段，他不撞见他那唯一的仇人的机会，正如每个上战场的人那注定打中谁的那颗子弹不打中他的机会；可是卡文迪什先生既没有白刃交锋的兴奋，也没有同许多人共担风险的那种保险。四下里样样含笑安详，而你分明知道：致命的危险会在任何一个无幸的门口、任何一个街角撞上你——这样的险，天然比明处的凶险更磨人的神经。卡文迪什先生遇上了马乔里班克斯医生；医生好心地停了双轮车，背对着来敌——倘若真有敌来——同他谈了五分钟；随后他遇见奇利太太，她几乎要亲吻他，为再见他那样高兴，为他赶得及结识会吏总那样欢喜，那样确信：他回来了，露西拉如今要快活了。“也许不该我说，可我*知道*她想过你，”这位欠斟酌的老太太说；她抓住他的双手，把这位苦人儿枷在那里，他越过她的肩头，用绝望的眼睛望着，确信此刻就是那要命的时刻、他的仇人*必*已上路。可是他的运气又一次帮了他。他机灵地说出：“我正要去拜马乔里班克斯小姐；”奇利太太即刻撒开他的双手，仿佛被烫着了，拍拍他的胳膊，打发他走。“这会儿她准在家，我真高兴；还有，亲爱的，你不必避我，你们两个的朋友我都做，”奇利太太说。可他刚脱了这一险，更可怕的东西又等着这位不幸的人。

===Original===

He could not believe his eyes at first, nor conceive it possible that Fate would have such a spite against him; but there was no mistaking the crumpled dress, any more than the straight eyebrows and flashing oblique glances that had already found him out. Of all the horrible chances in the world, it was Barbara﻿—Barbara, who had a right to think he had deserted her on the previous night, and with whom his next interview could not be otherwise than stormy﻿—who thus appeared like a lion in his way. When he saw what awaited him, Mr. Cavendish lost courage. His heart sank down into unfathomable depths. He did not know what he could say to her to shorten the inevitable interview, nor how he could escape, nor how hinder her from discovering that it was Lucilla he was going to see; and he had no longer any doubt in his mind that while he was thus engaged the Archdeacon must inevitably appear. If he had had time to think of ordinary subjects, he would have been sufficiently annoyed at the idea of an interview with Barbara in broad daylight on the sacred soil of Grange Lane, where all the world could or might be spectators; but such a merely prudential sentiment was entirely swallowed up today in much more urgent considerations. He would have been content just now, in the horror of the moment, to plight his troth to Barbara by way of getting rid of her, and leaving his path clear; but he could not stop her or himself from advancing, and dared not give any vent to the panic which was consuming his soul.

“Oh, I am sure I never thought of seeing you here, Mr. Cavendish,” said Barbara, with a toss of her head. She would have done a great deal to secure her wavering lover, but she could not be amiable at a moment when she had him at a disadvantage. “Perhaps you are going to see Miss Marjoribanks,” said the foolish young woman. To tell the truth, she did not suspect him of any such treachery; but her heart was beating louder than usual, and she had the best position of the two, or thought she had, and chose what she supposed the most aggravating thing to say.

===Chinese===

他先是不敢信自己的眼睛，想不通命运何以这样同他为仇；可是那身揉皱的裙子没有认错的余地，正如那两道平直的眉毛、那已经发现了他的一瞥闪闪的斜睨。天底下种种可怕的巧遇里，偏偏是芭芭拉——芭芭拉，她有权认为他昨夜弃了她，同她的下一面除了电闪雷鸣不可能是别的——这样一头狮子拦在他的路上。看清了等他的是什么，卡文迪什先生失了勇气。他的心直沉进无底的深处。他不知对她说什么才能缩短这场躲不掉的会面，不知怎样脱身，不知怎样不叫她发现他去见的是露西拉；而且他已不再怀疑：就在他这样被绊住的当儿，会吏总必会现身。他若有闲心想寻常的事，大白天在格兰奇巷这方圣土上同芭芭拉会面、全城的人都可能围观，这念头本也够他烦的；可这点仅仅出于审慎的情绪，今天全然被急得多的考虑吞了。此刻，在那阵恐怖里，他真肯对芭芭拉山盟海誓，只求打发掉她、腾清路；可他拦不住她、也拦不住自己往前走，又不敢发泄那正在吞噬他灵魂的惊惶。
