“要是我有一百张票，我全都给他，”奇利太太说，“等你听明白了其中的原委，你也会这样的。露西拉，亲爱的，告诉他——我*盼*着你不是要抛弃老朋友吧。”

“不是，”马乔里班克斯小姐说——可她说话时带着一种庄重与迟疑，没有逃过奇利太太的耳朵——“我盼着我永远不会背弃我的老朋友们；可我照样认为，阿什伯顿先生才是配得上卡灵福德的合适人选，”她慢慢地说。她说得不大情愿，因为她知道这会震骇她的听众；可同时她并不在责任面前退缩；此刻已到了这样的时刻——露西拉觉得遮掩已不可能，实话必须说出来。

至于奇利太太，她苦恼得眼泪都涌上了眼睛；连上校也笑了，而且不明白这是怎么回事。奇利上校虽然还远远没有站到卡文迪什先生一边，却也同他的邻居们一样，不能理解马乔里班克斯小姐对公正与正义的那份一心一意的虔诚；何况如今那一位浪漫而悔悟地回来了，把他的荣华丢在她脚前，她何以要把支持转给阿什伯顿——一个不讨女人欢心的人，在上校看来也不是个要娶亲的人，也毫无动人之处——这更是他无力解释的。他只满足于说一声“哼”；可他太太不那么容易罢休。她拉住露西拉的手，倾泻出一大股劝谏与恳求。

===Original===

“I do not understand you, Lucilla,” said Mrs. Chiley. “He whom we know so little about﻿—whom, I am sure, you have no reason to care for. And where could you find anybody nicer than Mr. Cavendish?﻿—and he to have such faith in us, and to come rushing back as soon as he was able. I am sure you have not taken everything into consideration, Lucilla. He might not perhaps do exactly as could have been wished before he went away; but he was young and he was led astray; and I do think you were a little hard upon him, my dear; but I have always said I never knew anybody nicer than Mr. Cavendish. And what possible reason you can have to care about that other man﻿—”

“It was like a special Intimation,” said Lucilla, with solemnity. “I don’t see how I could neglect it, for my part. The day the news came about poor old Mr. Chiltern’s death I was out, you know, and heard it; and just at one spot upon the pavement, opposite Mr. Holden’s, it came into my mind like a flash of lightning that Mr. Ashburton was the man. I don’t care in the least for him, and I had not been thinking of him, or anything. It came into my head all in a moment. If I had been very intimate with poor dear old Mr. Chiltern, or if I believed in spirit-rapping, I should think it was a message from *him*.”

Lucilla spoke with great gravity, but she did not impress her audience, who were people of sceptical minds. Mrs. Chiley, for her part, was almost angry, and could scarcely forgive Lucilla for having made her give grave attention to such a piece of nonsense. “If it *had* been him,” she said, with some wrath, “I don’t see how having been dead for a few hours should make his advice worth having. It never was good for anything when he was alive. And you don’t believe in spirit-rapping, I *hope*. I wonder how you can talk such nonsense,” the old lady said severely. And Colonel Chiley, who had been a little curious too, laughed and coughed over the joke; for the two old people were of the old school, and of a very unbelieving frame of mind.

===Chinese===

“我不明白你，露西拉，”奇利太太说。“那个人我们知道的这么少——你呀，我敢说，没有理由对他上心。你哪里还能找到比卡文迪什先生更好的人呢？——何况他对我们这样信得过，一得脱身就奔回来了。我敢说你没有把一切都考虑进去，露西拉。他走之前也许做事没有完全如人所愿；可他年轻，他被带坏了；我确实觉得你对他有点狠心，亲爱的；可我一向说，我从没见过比卡文迪什先生更好的人。而你能有什么样的理由去关心另外那个人——”

“那像是一次特别的昭示，”露西拉庄重地说。“我看不出我怎么能够忽视它。可怜的老奇尔顿先生死讯传来那天，我正在外面，你知道，听见了这消息；就在人行道上的一个地方，霍尔登先生家的对面，一道闪电似的，‘阿什伯顿先生才是其人’这个念头进了我的脑子。我一点也不喜欢他，我也从没想着他，或想着什么。它是霎时间进到我脑子里的。我若是同可怜亲爱的老奇尔顿先生很亲密，或是我相信通灵敲击，我会当它是*他*捎来的信儿。”

露西拉说得极其庄重，可她没能打动她的听众——那是两位抱着怀疑头脑的人。奇利太太呢，几乎生气了，险些不能原谅露西拉让她把这样一派胡言当正经事听了半天。“就算*真*是他，”她带着几分怒气说，“我也不明白死了几个钟头怎么就能让他的忠告变得值钱了。他活着的时候那忠告就没顶过用。还有，你不信通灵敲击那一套吧，我*盼着*。真奇怪你怎么能说出这样的胡话，”老太太严厉地说。奇利上校本来也有点好奇，这时笑着为这个笑话咳嗽起来；因为两位老人是旧学派的人，一副全然不信的头脑。

===Original===

“I knew you would laugh,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “but I cannot help it. If it had been impressed upon *your* mind like that, you would have been different. And, of course, I like Mr. Cavendish much the best. I am so glad I have no vote,” said Lucilla; “it does not matter to anybody what I think; but if I had anything to do with it, you know I could not stand up for Mr. Cavendish, even though I am fond of him, when I felt sure that Mr. Ashburton is the man for Carlingford﻿—nobody could ask me to do that.”

There followed a pause upon this declaration; for Miss Marjoribanks, though she had no vote, was a person of undoubted influence, and such a conviction on her part was not to be laughed at. Even Colonel Chiley, who was undecided in his own mind, was moved by it a little. “What does the Doctor think?” he asked. “Ashburton doesn’t say a word about his principles that I can see; and the other, you know﻿—”

“Dear Colonel Chiley,” cried Lucilla, “he is not going to be Prime Minister; and I have always heard you say, as long as I can remember, that it was not opinions, you know, but a good *man* that people wanted. I have heard people talking politics for hours, and I always remember you saying that, and thinking it was the only sensible thing that was said; but, of course, I don’t understand politics,” Lucilla added, with humility. As for the Colonel, he took up the poker, perhaps to hide a little pleasant confusion, and again drew near the fire.

“By George! I believe Lucilla is in the right,” he said, with a certain agreeable consciousness. Perhaps he did not quite recollect at what moment of his life he had originated that sentiment, but he thought he could recollect having said it; and it was with the view of carrying off the bashfulness of genius, and not because the coals had any need of it, that he took up the poker﻿—a proceeding which was always regarded with alarm and suspicion by his wife.

“The fire is very nice,” said Mrs. Chiley. “I hate to have the fire poked when it does not want it. Lucilla, if you make him go over to *that* Mr. Ashburton’s side, you will have a great deal to answer for, and I will never forgive you. My dear, you must be dreaming﻿—a man that is as dry as a stick, and not one-hundredth nor one-thousandth part so nice﻿—”

===Chinese===

“我知道你们会笑，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“可我没有法子。这念头若是那样印在*你们*的脑子里，你们就不一样了。而且，我自然是喜欢卡文迪什先生得多。我真高兴我没有选票，”露西拉说；“我想什么，对谁都无关紧要；可倘若这事同我有一丁点关系，你们知道，我就不能站出来替卡文迪什先生说话——尽管我喜欢他——当我确信阿什伯顿先生才是配得上卡灵福德的人的时候。谁也不能要求我那样做。”

这句宣言之后是一阵停顿；因为马乔里班克斯小姐虽然没有选票，却是个影响力无可置疑的人，她这一番确信不是可以一笑置之的。连心里还没拿定主意的奇利上校，也被它触动了一点。“医生怎么看？”他问。“就我看到的，阿什伯顿对他的政见一个字也不提；而那一位呢，你知道——”

“亲爱的奇利上校，”露西拉喊道，“他又不是要当首相；而且从我记事起，就总听你说，人们要的你知道不是政见，是一个好的*人*。我听过人们一连几个钟头谈政治，我总记得你说的那句，心里想那是唯一一句通情理的话；不过，我当然不懂政治，”露西拉谦逊地补了一句。至于上校，他拿起通条——许是为了掩一点愉快的窘意——又凑近了炉火。

“天哪！我看露西拉说得对，”他说，带着几分愉快的自觉。他也许记不太清自己一生中哪个时刻首创了这句名言，可他觉得自己记得说过它；他拿起通条，是为了把天才的羞赧遮掩过去，并不是煤有什么需要——这一举动总是被他的太太怀着惊恐与疑虑注视着。

“炉火好好的，”奇利太太说。“我恨人在火不需要的时候去拨它。露西拉，你要是让他倒到*那个*阿什伯顿先生一边去，你有得交代呢，我永远不会原谅你。亲爱的，你准是在做梦——一个枯燥得像根棍子的男人，好处连人家的百分之一、千分之一都没有——”

===Original===

“I shan’t say another word,” said Lucilla; “I shan’t stay any longer, for I can’t help it, and you would be angry with me. People can’t help what they believe, you know. There is poor little Oswald Brown, who has doubts, and can’t go into the Church, and will ruin all his prospects, and nobody can help it﻿—”

“If I were his mother I should help it!” cried Mrs. Chiley. “I promise you he should not talk of his doubts to me! A bit of a lad; and what is good enough for all the bishops, and everybody in their senses, is not good enough for him! If that is the kind of example you are going to follow, Lucilla﻿—”

“Dear Mrs. Chiley,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “everybody knows what my Church principles are; and perhaps you will come round to think with me; but I am not going to say any more about it now. I am so glad your rheumatism is better this morning; but you must wrap up well, for it is so cold, oh, so cold, out of doors!”

===Chinese===

“我不再多说一个字了，”露西拉说；“我也不再待下去了，因为我没有法子，你们要生我的气的。人信什么，是自己做不了主的，你知道。可怜的小奥斯蒙德·布朗，心里起了疑惑，进不了教会，要把自己的前程全毁了，谁也帮不了他——”

“我要是他母亲，我就帮得了！”奇利太太喊道。“我向你担保，他休想对我讲他的疑惑！一个乳臭小儿；所有主教们、所有神志清醒的人都觉得够好的东西，就他觉得不够好！你要学的要是这一路榜样，露西拉——”

“亲爱的奇利太太，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“谁都知道我的教会原则是什么；说不定你们转过弯来就同我想的一样了；不过现在我不想再多说了。我真高兴你的风湿今早好些了；可你千万要裹严实了，外头冷得很，哦，冷得很呢！”

===Original===

When Lucilla had thus dismissed the subject, she came to her old friend’s side and bent over her in her sealskin cloak, to say goodbye. Mrs. Chiley took her by both hands as she thus stood with her back to the old Colonel, and drew her down close, and looked searchingly into her eyes. “If you have any *particular* reason, Lucilla, you ought to tell me﻿—that would make such a difference,” said the old lady. “I always tell you everything,” said Miss Marjoribanks, with evasive fondness, as she kissed the soft old withered cheek; and naturally, with the Colonel behind, who was standing up before the fire shadowing over them both, and quite unaware of this little whispered episode, it would have been impossible to say more had there been ever so much to say. But it had been a close encounter in its way, and Lucilla was rather glad to get off without any further damage. She did not feel quite successful as she went out; but still she had left a very wholesome commotion behind her; for Colonel Chiley could not but feel that the sentiment which she had quoted from himself was a very just sentiment. “By George! Lucilla was in the right of it,” he said again, after she was gone; and in fact went through a process very similar to that which had modified the sentiments of Dr. Marjoribanks on the previous night. Mr. Cavendish was a young fellow who had rushed off among a set of Frenchmen, because Lucilla Marjoribanks would not have him, or because he could not marry Barbara Lake in addition, or at least somehow because he failed of having his own way. It was all very well for him to come back and make a commotion, and be sentimental about it. But what if, after all, Ashburton, who had the Firs, and lived there, and spent his money like a Christian, was the man for Carlingford? The Colonel’s mind still wavered and veered about; yet it had received an impulse which was by no means unworthy of consideration.

===Chinese===

露西拉就这样撇开了这个题目，走到老朋友身边，穿着海豹皮斗篷俯下身去道别。奇利太太趁她这样背对着老上校站着，双手握住她，把她拉近，细细地看进她眼睛里。“你要是有什么*特别的*缘故，露西拉，你该告诉我——那可就大不一样了，”老太太说。“我什么都告诉你的，”马乔里班克斯小姐带着躲闪的亲爱说，一边吻那柔软的、起了皱的老脸颊；自然，上校就在背后，站在炉火前，把两人都罩在他的影子里，全然不知这段耳语的小插曲——就算有再多的话要说，也不可能再多说了。可这到底算得上一场险些短兵相接的交锋，露西拉没有再受更多的伤便脱了身，倒还高兴。她走出去时并不觉得十分成功；可她身后毕竟留下了一场很有益的骚动；因为奇利上校不能不感到，她引自他本人的那句名言，是一句很公道的话。“天哪！露西拉说得对，”她走后他又说了一遍；事实上，他经历的过程，同昨夜改变了马乔里班克斯医生想法的那个过程极为相似。卡文迪什先生是个年轻人，因为露西拉·马乔里班克斯不肯要他，或是因为他不能把芭芭拉·莱克也娶了，或者至少因为没能随心所欲，就跑到一帮法国人里去了。他回来兴风作浪、伤情感怀，那都随他去。可万一到底还是阿什伯顿——那个拥有冷杉宅、住在那里、像个基督徒似的花钱的人——才配得上卡灵福德呢？上校的心思还在摇摇摆摆地转着；可它已经受了一次推动，那推动绝非不值得掂量。

===Original===

As for Mrs. Chiley, she laid back her head upon her pillows and painfully questioned with herself whether Lucilla could have any *particular* reason for taking Mr. Ashburton’s part so warmly. She thought with justice that Miss Marjoribanks was looking brighter and better, and had more of her old animation than she had shown for a long time﻿—which arose from the simple fact that she had something in hand, though the old lady thought it might have a more touching and delicate motive. If *that* was the case, it would make a great difference. Mrs. Chiley was no longer able to go out in the evening, and had to be dependent on other people’s observation for a knowledge of what happened﻿—and she was wounded by a sense that her young friend had not been appreciated as her worth deserved. If Mr. Ashburton had the sense to see what was for his own advantage, it would be a frightful thing, as Mrs. Chiley said to herself, if Lucilla’s friends should fly in his face. And though it was a hard trial to give up Mr. Cavendish, still if anything of the kind had happened﻿—Thus it will be evident that Lucilla’s visit, though it was not a long one, nor the least in the world an argumentative visit, was not without its fruit.

She went up Grange Lane again cheerful and warm in her sealskin coat. It was a thing that suited her remarkably well, and corresponded with her character, and everybody knows how comfortable they are. The snowflakes fell softly, one at a time, and melted away to nothing upon her sleeves and her shoulders without leaving any trace﻿—and Lucilla, with the chill air blowing in her face, and those feathery messengers in the air, could not but feel that her walk and the general readiness which she felt to face all kinds of objections and difficulties, and to make a sacrifice of her own feelings, had in them a certain magnanimous and heroic element. For after all she had no *particular* reason, as Mrs. Chiley said. Mr. Ashburton was a dry man, and of very little use in a social point of view, and had never paid her any attention to speak of, nor at all put himself forth as a candidate for her favour. If he had done so, she would not have felt that thrill of utter disinterestedness which kept her as warm within as her sealskin did without.

===Chinese===

至于奇利太太，她把头放回靠垫上，苦苦地自问：露西拉这样热切地替阿什伯顿先生出头，会不会有什么*特别的*缘故。她公道地觉得，马乔里班克斯小姐气色比从前明亮、更好了，久违的那股活泼也回来了些——这不过是她手里有了件事要办的简单缘故，可老太太想，它许有一个更动人、更精微的动机。倘若*真是*那样，那就大不一样了。奇利太太晚上已经出不了门，要知道外头发生了什么，只能靠别人的观察——而她心里带着一处创伤，觉得她的年轻朋友不曾受到与她价值相称的赏识。阿什伯顿先生若有那份眼力，看得出什么于他有利，那么——奇利太太对自己说——露西拉的朋友们若同他翻脸，那就是一桩可怕的事了。虽说放弃卡文迪什先生是一场严酷的考验，可倘若真有了什么这一类的事——由此可见，露西拉这一访，虽然不长，也全然不是说理的一访，却并非没有果实。

她又往格兰奇巷上头走去，穿着海豹皮外衣，浑身暖和，兴冲冲的。这衣裳她穿着格外合身，同她的品性也相称，而且人人都知道那种衣裳有多舒服。雪花软软地落，一片一片，落在她袖子上、肩上，化得无影无踪，不留一点痕迹——露西拉，清冽的风吹在脸上，那些羽毛似的信使在空中飘着，不能不感到：她这一趟行走，她面对一切非难与艰难、把一己之情做出牺牲的总体上的甘愿，里头都含有一种豁达大度的、英雄的成分。因为说到底，正如奇利太太所说，她没有什么*特别的*缘故。阿什伯顿先生是个枯燥的人，从社交的观点看没有多少用处，也从没有对她献过什么值得一提的殷勤，更没有半点把自己摆作她青睐的候选人。他若献过，她便觉不出那阵全然无私的战栗了——正是那战栗，让她里头像海豹皮在外头那样暖着她。

===Original===

There was not a soul to be seen in Grange Lane at that moment in the snow, which came on faster and faster, but one of Mr. Wentworth’s (who at that time was new in St. Roque’s) gray sisters, and another lady who was coming down, as quickly as Lucilla was going up, by the long line of garden walls. The gentlemen were either at business or at their club, or keeping themselves snug indoors; and it was only these devoted women who braved the elements outside. The figure in the gray cloak was occupied simply with the poor people, and that is not our present business; but the other two were otherwise inspired. Mr. Cavendish, who had lately arrived, had not been able to make up his mind to face the weather; but his sister was of a different way of thinking. She was not of half the capacity of Lucilla, but still she felt that something ought to be done, and that there was not a moment to be lost. When she saw it was Miss Marjoribanks that was advancing to meet her, a momentary chill came over Mrs. Woodburn. She was thinking so much of her own errand that she could not but jump at the idea that nothing less important could have induced Lucilla to be out of doors on such a day; and her heart beat loud as the two drew near each other. Was it an unexpected and generous auxiliary, or was it a foe accomplished and formidable? For one thing, she was not coming out of Mr. Centum’s, where Mrs. Woodburn herself was going, which at least was a relief. As they came nearer the two ladies instinctively looked to their weapons. They had met already in many a little passage of arms, but nothing like this had ever occurred to them before. If they were to work in union, Mrs. Woodburn felt that they would carry all before them; and if not, then it must be a struggle unto the death.

“Is it really you, Lucilla?” she said; “I could not believe my eyes. What can have brought you out of doors on such a day? You that have everything your own way, and no call to exert yourself﻿—”

“I have been to see Mrs. Chiley,” said Lucilla sweetly; “when the weather is bad she sees nobody, and she is always so pleased to have me. Her rheumatism is not so bad, thank you﻿—though I am sure if this weather should last﻿—”

===Chinese===

那时节，雪越下越急的格兰奇巷里一个人影也不见，只有温特沃斯先生（他那时刚到圣罗克堂）的一位灰衣修女，还有另一位太太，正沿着长长一列花园墙下来——下来得同露西拉上去一样急。先生们或者办事去了，或者在俱乐部里，或者缩在屋里舒服；只有这些献身的女人敢于犯外头的天时。灰斗篷的身影只管着穷人的事，那不是我们眼下的题目；可另外两位的灵感却另有来路。新近抵达的卡文迪什先生没能下定决心来对付这天气；他妹妹却是另一种想法。她不及露西拉一半的才干，可她照样觉得该做点什么，而且一刻也耽误不得。待看清迎面走来的正是马乔里班克斯小姐，一阵寒意掠过伍德本太太心头。她满心想着自己的使命，便不能不立刻认定：露西拉在这样的日子肯到屋外来，所为之事必定非同小可；两人彼此走近时，她的心跳得响。来的是一位意外而大度的同盟呢，还是一位手段老练、令人生畏的敌手？有一点可以放心：她不是从森特姆先生家出来的——伍德本太太自己正要去那里。两人越走越近，便本能地各自检视起兵器来。她们早已在多少回小小的交锋里交过手，可这样的事从前还不曾有过。若是合力去做，伍德本太太觉得她们定能所向披靡；若不然，那便得是一场殊死的争斗。

“真是你吗，露西拉？”她说；“我简直不能相信自己的眼睛。这样的天气，什么把你引到屋外来了？你这人万事随心，用不着劳神——”

“我去看奇利太太了，”露西拉甜甜地说；“天气坏的时候她谁也不见，她总是那样乐意见我。她的风湿不算太坏，谢谢关心——虽说这天气要是老这样，我敢说——”

===Original===

“You would see Mrs. Beverley’s blanket,” said Mrs. Woodburn, who was a little nervous, though perhaps that might only be the cold; “but we know what sort of woman she is, and it must have been the Archdeacon’s nieces, my dear. Do turn back with me a moment, Lucilla; or I shall go with you. I want to speak to you. Of course you have heard of Harry’s coming home?”

“I saw it in the papers,” said Miss Marjoribanks, whose perfect serenity offered a curious contrast to her companion’s agitation. “I am sure I shall be very glad to see him again. I hope he will come to dinner on Thursday as he used to do. It will be quite nice to see him in his old place.”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Woodburn; “but that was not what I was thinking of. You know you used always to say he ought to be in Parliament; and he has always kept thinking of it since he went away﻿—and thinking, I am sure, that it would please you,” said the poor woman, faltering; for Lucilla listened with a smile that was quite unresponsive, and did not change countenance in the least, even at this tender suggestion. “He has come home with that object now, you know, now that poor old Mr. Chiltern is dead; and I hope you are going to help us, Lucilla,” said Mrs. Woodburn. Her voice quite vibrated with agitation as she made this hurried, perhaps injudicious, appeal, thinking within herself at the same moment what would Harry say if he knew that she was thus committing him. As for Lucilla, she received it all with the same tranquillity, as if she expected it, and was quite prepared for everything that her assailant had to say.

“I am sure I wish I had a vote,” said Lucilla; “but I have no vote, and what can a girl do? I am so sorry I don’t understand politics. If we were going in for that sort of thing, I don’t know what there would be left for the gentlemen to do.”

===Chinese===

“你是看见贝弗利太太的毯子了，”伍德本太太说，她有点紧张，虽说那也许不过是冷的缘故；“可我们都知道她是个什么样的女人，亲爱的，那准是会吏总的侄女们织的。陪我回头走一会儿吧，露西拉；不然我就跟你走。我有话要同你说。哈里到家的事，你当然听说了？”

“我在报上看见了，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，她那十足的平静，同同伴的激动形成一种古怪的对照。“再见到他，我肯定是很高兴的。我盼着他照旧来赴星期四的晚宴。在他老位子上见到他，一定很好。”

“是，”伍德本太太说；“可我想的不是这个。你知道你从前总说他该进议会；他走以后也一直想着这件事——而且想着，我敢说，这会叫你高兴，”这可怜的女人说，声音发颤；因为露西拉带着全然不予回应的微笑听着，连这句温柔的话也没有让她神色稍变。“如今可怜的老奇尔顿先生死了，他就抱着这个目的回来了，你知道；我盼着你会帮我们一把，露西拉，”伍德本太太说。她发出这匆忙的、也许失于轻率的呼吁时，声音激动得发颤，心里同时想着：哈里要是知道她这样把他套了进去，会说什么呢。至于露西拉，她以同样的平静接收了这一切，仿佛她早已料到，她那位进攻者要说的话，她句句都有准备。

“我真希望我有一张选票，”露西拉说；“可我没有选票，一个姑娘家能做什么呢？我真遗憾我不懂政治。要是我们女人也掺和进那一类事情里去，我就不知道还剩下什么给先生们做了。”

===Original===

“You have influence, which is a great deal better than a vote,” said Mrs. Woodburn; “and they all say there is nobody like a lady for electioneering﻿—and a young lady above all; and then you know Harry so well, and can always draw him out to the best advantage. I never thought he looked so nice, or showed his talents so much, as when he was with you,” said the eager advocate. She was only wrapped in a shawl herself, and when she looked at Lucilla’s sealskin coat, and saw how rosy and comfortable she looked, and how serene and immovable, poor Mrs. Woodburn was struck with a pang of envy. If Miss Marjoribanks had married ten years ago, it might have been she now who would have had to stand trembling with anxiety and eagerness among the falling snow, knowing sundry reasons why Mr. Cavendish should be disposed to go into Parliament more substantial than that of gratifying a young lady, and feeling how much depended on her ability to secure support for him. This, as it happened, had fallen to his sister’s share instead, and Lucilla stood opposite to her looking at her, attentive and polite, and unresponsive. If Harry had only not been such a fool ten years ago! for Mrs. Woodburn began to think now with Aunt Jemima, that Lucilla did not marry because she was too comfortable, and, without any of the bother, could have everything her own way.

“It is so cold,” said Miss Marjoribanks, “and I do think it is coming on to snow very fast. I don’t think it is good to stand talking. Do come in to lunch, and then we can have a long chat; for I am sure nobody else will venture out today.”

“I wish I could come,” said Mrs. Woodburn, “but I have to go down to Mary Centum’s, and hear all about her last new housemaid, you know. I don’t know what servants are made of for my part. They will go out in their caps and talk to the young men, you know, in a night that is enough to give anyone their death,” the mimic added, with a feeble exercise of her gift which it was sad to see. “But Harry will be sure to come to call the first time he goes out, and you *will* not forget what I have said to you, Lucilla?” and with this Mrs. Woodburn took her young friend’s hand and looked in her face with a pathetic emphasis which it would be impossible to describe.

===Chinese===

“你有影响力，那可比选票好得多，”伍德本太太说；“他们都说搞竞选这一行，谁也比不上一位太太——年轻小姐更是头一份；再说你同哈里这么熟，总能把他最好的一面引出来。我从没见他像同你在一起时那样招人喜欢，那样显露才情，”这位热切的辩士说。她自己只裹着一条披肩，看着露西拉的海豹皮外衣，看她脸色那样红润舒服，那样安详不为所动，可怜的伍德本太太被一阵艳羡刺了一下。倘若马乔里班克斯小姐十年前嫁了人，如今在纷飞的雪里带着焦虑与热望发抖的，也许就是她了——知晓卡文迪什先生想进议会的种种缘由，比讨一位年轻小姐欢心那一条要实在得多——并且感到多少事情都系在她能否为他拉到支持上。这件事，碰巧落到了他妹妹头上；而露西拉站在她对面望着她，专注，客气，而不为所动。要是哈里十年前不那么傻就好了！因为伍德本太太如今开始同吉米玛姨妈想到一处去了：露西拉不嫁，是因为她太舒服了，一点麻烦不担，就能万事随心。

“天真冷，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，“而且我确实觉得雪马上要下大了。站着说话我想是不好的。进来吃午饭吧，那样我们就能好好长谈；因为我肯定今天再没有别人肯出门了。”

“我倒想来，”伍德本太太说，“可我得去玛丽·森特姆那儿，听听她新来的女仆的全部是非，你知道。我就不明白如今的佣人是什么做的。她们偏偏要戴着软帽出去，同年轻男人说话，那样的夜晚，谁挨着都得送命，”这位善模仿的人补了一句，那本领用得有气无力，看着叫人难过。“不过哈里头一回出门，准会来拜访的，我同你说的话，你*千万*不要忘了，露西拉？”说罢，伍德本太太握住她年轻朋友的手，望着她的脸，那份凄切的恳切，笔墨无法形容。

===Original===

“Oh, no, certainly not,” said Miss Marjoribanks, with cheerful certainty; and then they kissed each other in the midst of the falling snow. Mrs. Woodburn’s face was cold, but Lucilla’s cheek was warm and blooming as only a clear conscience and a sealskin cloak could have made it; and then they went their several ways through the wintry solitude. Ah, if Harry had only not been such a fool ten years ago! Mrs. Woodburn was not an enthusiastic young wife, but knew very well that marriage had its drawbacks, and had come to an age at which she could appreciate the comfort of having her own way without any of the bother. She gave a furtive glance after Lucilla, and could not but acknowledge to herself that it would be very foolish of Miss Marjoribanks to marry, and forfeit all her advantages, and take somebody else’s anxieties upon her shoulders, and never have any money except what she asked from her husband. Mrs. Chiley, to be sure, who was more experienced than Mrs. Woodburn, and might have been her grandmother, took a different view of the subject; but this was what the middle-aged married woman felt, who had, as may be said, two men to carry on her shoulders, as she went anxiously down Grange Lane to conciliate Mrs. Centum, wrapping her shawl about her, and feeling the light snow melt beneath her feet, and the cold and discomfort go to her heart. She had her husband to keep in good humour, and her brother to keep up and keep to the mark, and to do what she could to remedy in public the effects of his indolent Continental habits, and carry, if it was possible, the election for him﻿—all with the horrid sense upon her mind that if at any time the dinner should be a little less cared for than usual, or the children more noisy, Woodburn would go on like a savage. Under such circumstances, the poor woman, amid her cares, may be excused if she looked back a little wistfully at Lucilla going home all comfortable and independent and lighthearted, with no cares, nor anybody to go on at her, in her sealskin coat.

===Chinese===

“哦，不，当然不忘，”马乔里班克斯小姐带着爽快的确信说；随后她们在纷飞的大雪中彼此吻别。伍德本太太的脸是冰冷的，露西拉的脸颊却温暖红润——那只有清白的良心加一件海豹皮斗篷才能造得出来；随后她们便各自走进那冬日的空寂里去了。啊，要是哈里十年前不那么傻就好了！伍德本太太不是热情的小媳妇，她深知婚姻自有它的难处，也到了一个能赏识“万事随心而一点麻烦不担”之舒服的年纪。她偷偷回望了一眼露西拉的背影，不能不对自己承认：马乔里班克斯小姐若嫁了人，丢掉这一切好处，把别人的焦虑扛上肩，往后再没有一文钱不伸手向丈夫讨，那才叫傻呢。奇利太太——她比伍德本太太阅历深，做得她的祖母——对这个题目自然另有一番看法；可中年已婚妇人的心情就是这样：她肩上，可以说，扛着两个男人，一面忧心忡忡地沿格兰奇巷下去，去安抚森特姆太太，一面把披肩裹紧，觉着脚下的薄雪化开，寒气和不适一直渗进心里。她要哄着丈夫常开心，又要撑着弟弟、盯住他不放，尽力在众人眼前补救他欧陆式的懒散习性造成的后果，若做得到，替他把这场选举赢下来——心里还压着那可怕的念头：哪一顿晚饭若是照料得比平日稍差一点，或是孩子们吵得凶了些，伍德本就要撒起野来。在这样的境况之下，这可怜的女人在百般操劳之中回望露西拉——穿着海豹皮外衣回家去，又舒服，又独立，又轻快，没有操心的事，也没有谁对她撒野——若带了几分艳羡，也是可以原谅的。

===Original===

This was how Lucilla commenced that effective but decorous advocacy which did Mr. Ashburton so much good in Carlingford. She did not pretend to understand about politics, or to care particularly about Reform or the Income-tax; but she expressed with quiet solemnity her conviction that it was not opinions but a good man that was wanted; that it was not a prime minister they were going to elect, and that Mr. Ashburton was the man for Carlingford. “By George! Lucilla is in the right of it!” Colonel Chiley said; “that was always my opinion;” and the people in Grange Lane soon began to echo the Colonel’s sentiments, which were so sound and so just.

As for Miss Marjoribanks, nobody had any occasion to “go on” about any neglect on her part of her household duties. Dr. Marjoribanks’s dinners were always excellent, and it was now, as ever, a privilege to be admitted to his table; and nothing could be more exemplary than the care Lucilla took of Aunt Jemima, who had always such bad nights. Even on this snowy afternoon she went in from her more important cares, with a complexion freshened by the cold, and coaxed Mrs. John into eating something, and made her as comfortable as possible at the drawing-room fireside.

===Chinese===

露西拉就是这样开始那一场收效极大而又有分寸的鼓吹的——它在卡灵福德替阿什伯顿先生出了大力。她并不假装懂得政治，也不特别关心改革或者所得税；可她带着安静的庄重，说出了她的信念：人们要的不是政见，是一个好人；他们要选的不是一位首相；而阿什伯顿先生才是配得上卡灵福德的人。“天哪！露西拉说得对！”奇利上校说；“我一向就是这个看法；”格兰奇巷的人们不久便开始应和上校的见解——那见解如此健全、如此公道。

至于马乔里班克斯小姐的家务职分，谁也没有机会为她疏忽了什么而“撒野”抱怨。马乔里班克斯医生的晚宴照旧精美，如今同往日一样，上他的餐桌仍是一种体面；而露西拉对老闹难眠之夜的吉米玛姨妈的照料，更是无可挑剔。就在这个落雪的下午，她撇下更要紧的操劳走进去，两颊让冷风吹得新鲜，哄着约翰太太吃了点东西，让她在客厅炉火边尽量舒服。

===Original===

“Now, tell me all about Tom,” Lucilla said, when she had got her work and settled herself comfortably for a quiet afternoon﻿—for the snow had come on heavier than ever, and unless it might be a sister of charity, or such another sister not of charity, as Lucilla had already encountered, nobody was like to stir abroad or to disturb the two ladies in their work and their talk. Lucilla had some very interesting worsted-work in hand; and the drawing-room never looked more cosy, with somebody to talk to inside, and the wintry world and driving snow without. And such an invitation as Miss Marjoribanks had just given lifted Aunt Jemima into a paradise of content. She took Lucilla at her word, and told her, as may be supposed, *all* about Tom, including many things which she was quite acquainted with and knew by heart; and at the same time there was something implied all through, but never obtrusively set forth, which was not displeasing to the auditor. Miss Marjoribanks listened with affectionate satisfaction, and asked a great many questions, and supplied a great many reminiscences, and entered quite into the spirit of the conversation, and the two spent a very pleasant afternoon together﻿—so pleasant that Mrs. John felt quite annoyed at the reflection that it must come to an end like everything else that is good, and that she must get herself once more into her velvet gown and dine with her brother-in-law. If Providence had only given her the girl instead of the Doctor, who would no doubt have got on quite well without any children! but then, to be sure, if Lucilla had been hers to start with, she never could have married Tom.

===Chinese===

“好了，把汤姆的事统统讲给我听吧，”露西拉说。这时她已拿来针线活，舒舒服服安顿下来，预备过一个安静的下午——因为雪下得比先前更大了，除非是哪位慈善修女，或如露西拉已经遇见过的那位并非慈善的修女，谁也不大会出门来搅扰两位太太做活计、说闲话。露西拉手里有一件很有意思的绒线活；里头有个人说话，外头是冬日的大千世界和漫卷的风雪，客厅从来没有像这样温馨过。而马乔里班克斯小姐刚发出的这一邀请，把吉米玛姨妈托进了心满意足的乐园。她拿露西拉的话当真，可想而知，把汤姆的事*从头到尾*讲了个遍，连许多露西拉早已烂熟于心的事情也包括在内；同时话里通篇暗含着一层意思，只是从不露骨地挑明，听的人也并不讨厌。马乔里班克斯小姐带着慈爱的满足听着，问了许多问题，补上了许多旧忆，完全进入了这场谈话的精神，两个人一起度过了一个非常愉快的下午——愉快得约翰太太一想到它同一切美好的事物一样终要结束、想到她还须重新套上天鹅绒长裙去陪小叔子吃饭，心里便十分恼恨。上天若是把那女儿给了她、而不是给那医生——医生没有孩子无疑也过得挺好！——那该多好！只是，当然，露西拉若一开始就是她的，她也就永远嫁不成汤姆了。

===Original===

For this was the extravagant hope which had already begun to blossom in his mother’s breast. To be sure a woman might marry Tom, who was too comfortable at home to think of marrying just anybody who might make her an offer. But it was not easy to tell how Lucilla herself felt on this subject. Her complexion was so bright with her walk, her sensations so agreeable after that warm, cheerful, pleasant afternoon, her position so entirely everything that was to be desired, and her mind so nobly conscious of being useful to her kind and country, that, even without any additional argument, Miss Marjoribanks had her reward, and was happy. Perhaps a touch more exquisite might still come in to round the full proportions of content. But, to tell the truth, Lucilla was so well off that it was not necessary to invent any romantic source of happiness to account for the light of well-being and satisfaction that shone in her eyes.

===Chinese===

因为这正是那已经在他母亲胸中开始开花的不切实际的希望。诚然，一个女人是可以嫁给汤姆的——他在家里太舒服了，不至于想到随便哪个肯向他求婚的就娶。可是露西拉自己对此作何感想，却不容易说。她走了这一趟，脸色那样明亮；那样温暖、愉快、开心的一个下午过后，她的感觉那样惬意；她的处境那样完全是万事俱备；她的心那样高尚地自觉于为同类与国家所用——甚至不必再添什么别的理由，马乔里班克斯小姐已经得了她的报酬，是幸福的。也许还有更精妙的一笔会再来，把圆满的满足补足成它丰盈的轮廓。可是，说句实话，露西拉的境况太好了，她眼里闪耀的那种安康与满足的光，用不着发明什么浪漫的幸福来源来解释。

## XL / 四十
===Original===

The result of Miss Marjoribanks’s wise precaution and reticence was that Sir John Richmond and the Doctor and Colonel Chiley were all on Mr. Ashburton’s committee. They might not agree with his principles; but then when a man does not state any very distinct principles, it is difficult for anyone, however well disposed, to disagree with him; and the fact that he was the man for Carlingford was so indisputable, that nobody attempted to go into the minor matters. “Mr. Ashburton is a gentleman known to us all,” Sir John said, with great effect, in his nomination speech; and it was a sentence which went to the hearts of his audience. The other candidate had been a long time from home, and it was longer still since anybody in Carlingford could be said to have benefited by his residence there. He had had all his things down from town, as Mr. Holden, the upholsterer, pithily remarked﻿—and that made a great difference to start with. As for Mr. Ashburton, though it is true nobody knew what he thought about Reform or the Income-tax, everybody knew that he lived at the Firs, and was supplied in a creditable way by George Street tradesmen. There was no mystery whatever about him. People knew how much he had a year, and how much he paid for everything, and the way in which his accounts were kept, and all about him. Even when he had his wine direct from the growers (for naturally his own county could not supply the actual liquor), it was put in Carlingford bottles, and people knew the kinds he had, and how much, and a hundred agreeable details. And then, “he was a gentleman as was always ready to give his advice,” as some of the people said. All this furnished an immense body of evidence in his favour, and made Sir John’s remark eloquent. And then Carlingford, as a general rule, did not care the least in the world about Reform. There were a few people who had once done so, and it was remarked in Grove Street that Mr. Tozer had once been in a dreadful state of mind about it. But he was quite tranquil on the subject now, and so was the community in general. And what was really wanted, as Lucilla’s genius had seen at a glance, was not this or that opinion, but a good man.

===Chinese===

马乔里班克斯小姐明智的谨慎与缄默，结果是：约翰·里士满爵士、医生、奇利上校，全都在阿什伯顿先生的委员会里。他们未必赞同他的主义；可是一个人既不申明任何很分明的主义，旁人——哪怕再怀着好意——也难于不赞同他；何况他是卡灵福德的天造地设之人，这件事无可争辩，谁也不想去追究那些细枝末节了。“阿什伯顿先生是一位我们人人都识得的绅士，”约翰爵士在他的提名演说里说，极见效力；这一句直说到了听众的心坎里。另一位候选人离家已久；而卡灵福德有谁沾过他住在此地的光，那更是更久以前的事了。他的家当全是从城里运下来的——家具商霍尔登先生说得一针见血——单这一条，起头便大不相同。至于阿什伯顿先生，不错，谁也不知道他对改革法案还是所得税是什么想法；可谁都知道他住在冷杉宅，由乔治街的商贾体体面面地供货。他身上毫无神秘可言。人们知道他一年有多少进项，知道他样样东西花多少钱，知道他的账目是怎么记的，知道他的一切。就连他的酒直接从种葡萄的人手里买来（他本郡自然产不出真正的酒浆），装的也是卡灵福德的瓶子；人们知道他有哪几种、各有多少，还有一百样惬意的细节。再者，用有些人的话讲，“他是位随时乐意给人出主意的绅士”。这一切凑成了一大堆于他有利的证据，也叫约翰爵士那句话显得雄辩。再者，卡灵福德照例对改革法案毫不放在心上。曾有几个人放在心上过；格罗夫街上有人说起，托泽先生从前还为这事心里大大不宁过一阵。可他如今在这题目上十分平静，公众大体也是如此。而真正要的——露西拉的天才一眼看破的——不是这个主义那个主义，是一个好人。

But at the same time it would be vain to deny that Miss Marjoribanks looked forward to a possible visit from Mr. Cavendish with a certain amount of anxiety. She was not frightened, for she knew her own powers; but she was a little excited and stimulated by the idea that he might come in at any minute, bringing back a crowd of recollections with him; and it was a perpetual wonder to her how he would take the inevitable difference, whether he would accept it as natural, or put on the airs of an injured man. Lucilla did not go out the two afternoons after her meeting with Mrs. Woodburn, partly that she might not miss him if he called﻿—for it was better to have it over; but Mr. Cavendish did not come on either of these days. After that, of course, she did not wait for him any longer. But on the third or fourth day, when she was in Miss Brown’s photographing room (the eldest Miss Brown was not married, and was a mother to the younger girls, and always enthusiastic about sitters), Mr. Ashburton called about business, and Thomas came to fetch Miss Marjoribanks. She was sitting with the greatest good-nature for half a dozen pictures, knowing in her secret heart all the time that she would look a perfect fright, and that all Carlingford would see her grinning with imbecile amiability out of the hazy background of Miss Brown’s *cartes*. Lucilla knew this, and had hitherto avoided the process with success; but now she gave in; and as the Major was there, of course they talked of the coming election, which, indeed, at present was almost the only topic of conversation in Grange Lane.

“Of course, you are on Mr. Ashburton’s committee,” said Lucilla; “you must be, or going to be, after what you said the other day at lunch﻿—”

“What did I say?” asked Major Brown, with an air of dismay; for, to tell the truth, his heart inclined a little towards poor Mr. Cavendish, who was an old neighbour, and to whom Major Brown could not but think the Marjoribanks and others had behaved rather cruelly. But then in these electioneering matters one never knows what one may have done to compromise oneself without meaning it; and the Major was a little anxious to find out what he had said.

可同时，无可讳言：马乔里班克斯小姐盼着卡文迪什先生可能的来访，是带着几分焦灼的。她不怕，她知道自己的本事；可一想到他随时可能进门、身后带回一大群旧忆，她就有些兴奋、有些按捺不住；他将怎样看待那无可回避的悬殊——是坦然受之为自然呢，还是摆出一副受了亏负的架势——这是她心头一个解不开的疑团。会过伍德伯恩太太之后的那两个下午，露西拉都没有出门，一半是为了他若来访不至错过——这事还是了结了好；可那两天卡文迪什先生都没有来。那之后，她自然也就不再等了。可到第三天还是第四天，她正在布朗小姐的照相间里（布朗家大小姐没有出嫁，是几个妹妹的母亲，对来照相的人向来热心），阿什伯顿先生为正事来访，托马斯便来请马乔里班克斯小姐回去。她怀着绝大的好性子坐着照半打相片，心底里却一直明白：自己照出来准是个十足的怪物，全卡灵福德都要看见她带着痴傻的和气、咧着嘴笑，从布朗小姐那些名片照朦胧的底子里瞪出来。这个露西拉知道，此前一直躲这桩事躲得很成功；可如今她让步了；少校既在座，他们自然谈起即将到来的选举——那阵子，这几乎是格兰奇巷唯一的话题。

“您当然在阿什伯顿先生的委员会里，”露西拉说；“您一定是在了，要么就要进了——照您那天午饭上说的话——”

“我说了什么来着？”布朗少校问，一脸的惊惶；因为说老实话，他的心有点向着可怜的卡文迪什先生——他是老街坊，布朗少校总不免觉得，马乔里班克斯一家和旁人待他未免太狠。可选举的事，谁也说不准自己无心之下干出了什么把自家搭进去的把柄；少校便有点急着想弄明白自己到底说过什么。

“Please don’t make fun of me,” said Miss Marjoribanks; “as if anybody cared what *I* say about politics. But I know that was what decided poor Mr. Ashburton. Indeed, he told me so; and when he finds you did not mean anything﻿—”

“But, good heavens!﻿—I﻿—I did mean something,” cried the accused, with dismay. He was sitting with Aunt Jemima when Lucilla came in, and talking to her in a steady sort of a way. Nothing could have made Mr. Ashburton socially attractive, but still there are many people to whom this steady sort of talk is more agreeable than brilliancy. When a man is brilliant there is always a doubt in some minds whether he is trustworthy, or sincere, or to be relied upon; but an ordinary commonsense sort of talker is free from such suspicion. Mr. Ashburton was very sorry to hear that Mrs. John Marjoribanks had bad nights, and suggested that it might be nervousness, and hoped that the air of Carlingford would do her good, and was very glad to hear that her son was getting on so well in India; and Aunt Jemima could not help approving of him, and feeling that he was a person of substance and reflection, and not one of those flyaway young men who turn girls’ heads, and never mean anything. Lucilla herself gained something in Mrs. John’s eyes from Mr. Ashburton’s high opinion; but at the same time it was quite clear that he was not thinking of anything sentimental, but was quite occupied about his election, as a man of sense should be. Lucilla came in with a fine bloom on her cheeks, but still with a shade of that sadness which had had so great an effect upon Major Brown. She had taken off her hat before she came in, and dropped into her chair with an air of languor and fatigue which was quite unusual to her. “It makes such a difference in life when one has something on one’s mind,” said Lucilla, and she sighed, as was but natural; for though that did not affect the energy of her proceedings, she knew and remembered at moments of discouragement how seldom one’s most disinterested exertions are appreciated at the end.

“You want your lunch, my dear,” said Mrs. John.

“Perhaps I do,” said Miss Marjoribanks, with a mournful affectionate smile. “I have been sitting to Maria Brown. She has taken six, and I am sure they are every one more hideous than the other; and they will go all over England, you know, for the Browns have hosts of people belonging to them; and everybody will say, ‘So *that* is Miss Marjoribanks.’ I don’t think I am vain to speak of,” said Lucilla, “but that sort of thing goes to one’s heart.”

“These amateurs are terrible people,” said Mr. Ashburton, in his steady way; “and photographs are a regular nuisance. For my part﻿—”

“Don’t say that,” said Miss Marjoribanks. “I know what you are going to say; and you *must* sit to her, please. I have said already she must do one of you; and I will tell you presently about the Major. But wait and talk to Aunt Jemima a little, for I am so tired,” said Lucilla. She was lying back negligently in her seat, with that air of languor which so many young ladies excel in, but which was for her a novel indulgence. Her hand hung over the arm of her chair as if there was no longer any force in it. Her head fell back, her eyes were half closed; it was a moment of abandonment to her sensations, such as a high-principled young woman like Miss Marjoribanks seldom gives way to. But Lucilla went into it conscientiously, as into everything she did, that she might regain her strength for the necessary duties that were before her.

And it was at this moment that Thomas appeared at the door with a suspicion of a grin appearing at the corners of his sober mouth, and announced Mr. Cavendish, who came in before an ordinary woman would have had time to open her eyes. This was the moment he had chosen for his first visit; and yet it was not he who had chosen it, but fate, who seemed to have in this respect a spite against Lucilla. It was not only the embarrassing presence of his rival, but the fact that neither of the two people in the room knew or had ever seen Mr. Cavendish, that put a climax to the horror of the situation. She alone knew him, and had to take upon herself to present and introduce him, and bridge over for him the long interval of absence, and all this with the sense of being in the enemy’s interest, and to a certain extent false to Mr. Cavendish! Lucilla rose at once, but she was not a woman to make pretences. She did not throw off all in a moment her fatigue, and dash into spasmodic action. She held out her hand silently to Mr. Cavendish, with a look which spoke only affectionate satisfaction in a friend’s return. She did not even speak at all for the first moment, but contented herself with a look, which indeed, if he had been younger and less preoccupied, would no doubt have touched his very heart.

“So you have really come back,” she said. “I am so glad! after all that people said about your being married and dead and ever so many stupid things. Oh! don’t look at me, please. It doesn’t matter with a gentleman, but I know as well as if you had told me that you think me dreadfully gone off﻿—”

“*I* entertain such a profane idea!” said Mr. Cavendish; but he was considerably embarrassed, and he was a great deal stouter, and altogether different from what he used to be, and he had not the light hand of his youth for a compliment. And then he sat down on the chair Thomas had given him; and he looked uncomfortable, to say the least of it; and he was getting large in dimensions and a little red in the face, and had by no means the air of thinking that it didn’t matter for a gentleman. As for Miss Marjoribanks, it would be impossible to say what mists of illusion dropped away from her mind at the sight of him. Even while she smiled upon the newcomer, she could not but ask herself, with momentary dismay﻿—Had *she* really gone off as much in the same time?

“I have been looking for you,” Miss Marjoribanks resumed; “I waited in for you Tuesday and Wednesday, and it is so odd you should have come just at this minute. Aunt Jemima, this is Mr. Cavendish, whom you have heard so much about﻿—and don’t go, please, Mr. Ashburton﻿—you two must know each other. You will be hearing of each other constantly; and I suppose you will have to shake hands or something on the hustings﻿—so it will be much the best to begin it here.”

But the two candidates did not shake hands: they bowed to each other in an alarming way, which did not promise much for their future brotherliness, and then they both stood bolt upright and stared at Miss Marjoribanks, who had relapsed, in the pleasantest way in the world, into her easy-chair.

“Now, please sit down and talk a little,” said Lucilla; “I am so proud of having you both together. There never has been anybody in the world that I have missed so much as *you*﻿—you knew that when you went away, but you didn’t mind. Mr. Ashburton is very nice, but he is of no use to speak of in an evening,” said Miss Marjoribanks, turning a reflective glance upon her own candidate with a certain sadness; and then they both laughed as if it was a joke; but it was no joke, as one of them at least must have known.

===Chinese===

“这么说你真回来了，”她说。“我真高兴！外头那些话，说你结了婚、说你死了，还有好些糊涂话。哦！请别看我。男人不打紧，可我就像听你亲口说过一样明白：你准觉得我大大减了色——”

“*我*会有这样亵渎的念头！”卡文迪什先生说；可他窘得厉害，人也发福了许多，同从前全然两样，年轻时夸赞人那份轻巧的手腕，也没有了。随后他在托马斯递上的椅子上坐了；往轻里说，他也坐得不安稳；他块头渐大，脸上微红，全然没有一副“男人不打紧”的神气。至于马乔里班克斯小姐，一见他，心里落下多少幻梦的雾障，那是说不清的。她一面笑脸迎着归客，一面不由自问，霎时间心头一凛——同是这些年，*她*自己莫非也减色了这么多？

“我一直盼着你来，”马乔里班克斯小姐接着说；“礼拜二、礼拜三我都在家等你，偏偏你赶在这个时辰来，多巧。杰迈玛姑妈，这位是卡文迪什先生，您听人讲过他多少回了——阿什伯顿先生，请您也别走——你们两位得认识认识。往后你们要时时刻刻听见彼此；到了演讲台上，我想你们总还得握握手什么的——不如就从此地起头最好。”

可两位候选人并没有握手：他们彼此一躬，躬得叫人心里发毛，于他们日后的手足情分殊无佳兆；随后两人笔挺挺站着，眼睛直勾勾望着马乔里班克斯小姐——她呢，又以世上最从容惬意的姿态，缩回了她的安乐椅里。

“来，请坐，说会儿话，”露西拉说；“你们两位聚在一处，我多得意啊。世上从来没有人，叫我像想念*你*这样想念过的——你走的时候自己知道，可你不在乎。阿什伯顿先生很好，可到了晚上，他简直派不上什么用场。”马乔里班克斯小姐说着，把她自己那位候选人打量了一眼，眼色里带着几分怅惘；两人便都笑了，好像这是句玩笑；可这不是玩笑——两人中至少有一个心里明白。

===Original===

“Lucilla,” said Mrs. John, with consternation, “I never heard anybody talk as you do; I am sure Mr. Ashburton is the very best of society, and as for Mr. Cavendish﻿—”

“Dear Aunt Jemima,” said Lucilla, “would you mind ringing the bell? I have been sitting to Maria Brown, and I am almost fainting. I wish you gentlemen would sit to her; it would please her, and it would not do *you* much harm; and then for your constituents, you know﻿—”

“I hope you don’t wish me to look like one of Maria Brown’s photographs to my constituents,” said Mr. Cavendish; “but then I am happy to say they all know me pretty well.” This was said with a slight touch of gentlemanly spite, if there is such a thing; for, after all, he *was* an old power in Carlingford, though he had been so long away.

“Yes,” said Lucilla reflectively, “but you are a little changed since then; a little perhaps﻿—just a little﻿—stouter, and﻿—”

“Gone off?” said Mr. Cavendish, with a laugh; but he felt horribly disconcerted all the same, and savage with Miss Marjoribanks, and could not think why “that fellow” did not go away. What had *he* to do in Lucilla’s drawing-room? what did he mean by sitting down again and talking in that measured way to the old lady, as if all the ordinary rules of good breeding did not point out to him that he should have gone away and left the field clear?

“Oh, you know it does not matter for a gentleman,” said Lucilla; and then she turned to Mr. Ashburton﻿—“I am sure the Major wants to see you, and he thinks that it was he who put it into your head to stand. He was here that day at lunch, you know, and it was something he said﻿—”

“Quite true,” said Mr. Ashburton in his business way. “I shall go to see him at once. Thank you for telling me of it, Miss Marjoribanks; I shall go as soon as I leave here.”

And then Mr. Cavendish laughed. “This is what I call interesting,” he said. “I hope Mr. Ashburton sees the fun; but it is trying to an old friend to hear of *that* day at lunch, you know. I remember when these sort of allusions used to be pleasant enough; but when one has been banished for a thousand years﻿—”

“Yes,” said Lucilla, “one leaves all that behind, you know﻿—one leaves ever so many things behind. I wish we could always be twenty, for my part. I always said, you know, that I should be gone off in ten years.”

===Chinese===

“露西拉，”约翰太太愕然道，“我从没听见谁像你这样说话；阿什伯顿先生可是头一流的体面人，至于卡文迪什先生——”

“亲爱的杰迈玛姑妈，”露西拉说，“麻烦您拉一下铃好么？我给玛丽亚·布朗当模特来着，几乎要晕了。我倒盼着你们两位先生去让她照一照；她一定欢喜，于*你们*也没有多大损处；再说，为了你们的选民，你们知道的——”

“但愿你不是要我在选民眼里活像玛丽亚·布朗的一张相片，”卡文迪什先生说；“不过，幸而他们全都相当识得我。”这话里带一丝绅士式的怨毒——世上若真有这种东西；因为毕竟，他*曾*是卡灵福德的一路旧势力，虽然阔别了这么久。

“是啊，”露西拉沉吟道，“只是你比那时略略变了些；也许略微——就略微——发福了，还有——”

“减了色？”卡文迪什先生说，一笑；可他心里还是窘得要命，对马乔里班克斯小姐憋着一腔火，想不通“那家伙”怎么还不走。*他*在露西拉的客厅里有什么事？他重新坐下、拿腔拿调地同老太太攀谈，算是什么意思——仿佛寻常教养的一切规矩不曾明明指点他：他早该走人，把场地让干净？

“哦，你是知道的，男人不打紧，”露西拉说；随后她转向阿什伯顿先生——“少校一定想见您，他还当是他把出马的主意放进您脑子里的呢。那天午饭他正在座，您知道的，他说了句什么话——”

“确是如此，”阿什伯顿先生用他办正事的口吻说。“我这就去看他。多谢您告诉我，马乔里班克斯小姐；我一离开此地就去。”

卡文迪什先生于是笑了。“这才叫有味呢，”他说。“但愿阿什伯顿先生也领略这份妙处；只是听人提起*那个*午饭的日子，老朋友心里不好受啊。我记得从前，这一类的暗语原是怪受用的；可一个人放逐了一千年之后——”

“是啊，”露西拉说，“人总要把那些丢在身后——要丢好多好多东西在身后呢。要依我，但愿我们永远二十岁。我老早说过，你知道，不出十年我准得减色。”

===Original===

“Was it the only fib you ever told that you repeat it so?” said Mr. Cavendish; and it was with this pretty speech that he took her downstairs to the well-remembered luncheon. “But you *have* gone off in some things when you have to do with a prig like that,” he said in her ear, as they went down together, “and cast off old friends. It was a thing a fellow did not expect of *you*.”

“I never cast off old friends,” said Miss Marjoribanks. “We shall look for you on Thursday, you know, all the same. Must you go, Mr. Ashburton, when lunch is on the table? But then, to be sure, you will be in time at the Browns’,” said Lucilla sweetly, and she gave the one rival her hand while she held the arm of the other, at the door of the dining-room, in which Mr. Ashburton had gallantly deposited Aunt Jemima before saying goodbye. They were both looking a little black, though the gloom was moderate in Mr. Ashburton’s case; but as for Lucilla, she stood between them a picture of angelic sweetness and goodness, giving a certain measure of her sympathy to both﻿—Woman the Reconciler, by the side of those other characters of Inspirer and Consoler, of which the world has heard. The two inferior creatures scowled with politeness at each other, but Miss Marjoribanks smiled upon them both. Such was the way in which she overcame the difficulties of the meeting. Mr. Ashburton went away a little annoyed, but still understanding his instructions, and ready to act upon them in that businesslike way he had, and Mr. Cavendish remained, faintly reassured in the midst of his soreness and mortification, by at least having the field to himself and seeing the last (for the present) of his antagonist﻿—which was a kind of victory in its way.

“I thought I knew you better than to think you ever would have anything to do with *that* sort of thing,” said Mr. Cavendish. “There are people, you know, whom I could have imagined﻿—but a prig like that.” He became indeed quite violent, as Aunt Jemima said afterwards, and met with that lady’s decided disapproval, as may be supposed.

“Mr. Ashburton is very well-bred and agreeable,” Mrs. John said, with emphasis. “I wish all the young men I see nowadays were as nice.”

“是你一辈子只撒过这一句谎，才这样挂在嘴边么？”卡文迪什先生说；他便是拿这句漂亮话，携她下楼，去赴那顿记忆犹新的午饭。“可是同那样的一个道学家伙打起交道来，你在有些事上*当真*减了色了，”两人一路下楼，他附在她耳边说，“还甩了老朋友。这种事，谁料得到出在*你*身上。”

“我从来不甩老朋友，”马乔里班克斯小姐说。“礼拜四我们照样等你，你可别忘了。阿什伯顿先生，饭菜都上桌了，您非走不可么？不过说起来，您赶到布朗家倒还来得及。”露西拉甜甜地说；在饭厅门口，她把一只手递给这一位对头，胳膊却挽着那一位——阿什伯顿先生道别之前，正殷勤地把杰迈玛姑妈安顿进了饭厅。两人脸色都有些阴沉，不过阿什伯顿先生那边的阴云淡些；至于露西拉，她立在他们两人之间，一幅天使般甜善的画，把她的同情分给两造各一份——女人，这调解者，与那世人早已听闻的另两个角色、鼓舞者与慰藉者，并肩而立。两个较次等的生灵客客气气地相视而怒目，马乔里班克斯小姐却对两人都微笑。她就是这样渡过了会面的重重难关。阿什伯顿先生走了，心里略有些恼，可他的训令是听明白了，准备以他那副干练的做派照办；卡文迪什先生留了下来，酸楚与羞恼之中，总算得了些微的宽慰——场地至少归了他独自，也目送了他的对头（暂时地）最后一线背影——这在其本身，也算得一种胜利。

“我还自以为了解你，不至于想到你会同*那*种事沾边，”卡文迪什先生说。“有些人，你知道，我倒想得出来——可那样一个道学家伙。”他当真激烈起来了——杰迈玛姑妈事后这么说——并且如可想见，招来了那位太太斩截的不以为然。

“阿什伯顿先生很有教养、很可亲，”约翰太太加重语气说。“但愿如今我见到的年轻人都像他这样好。

===Original===

“Young men!” said Mr. Cavendish. “Is that what people call young nowadays? And he must be insane, you know, or he would never dream of representing a town without saying a single word about his principles. I dare say he thinks it is original,” said the unhappy man. He thought he was pointing out his rival’s weakness to Lucilla, and he went on with energy﻿—“I know you better than to think you can like that milk-and-water sort of thing.”

“Oh, I don’t pretend to know anything about politics,” said Lucilla. “I hear you gentlemen talk, but I never pretend to understand. If we were not to leave you *that* all to yourselves, I don’t know what you could find to do,” Miss Marjoribanks added compassionately; and as she spoke she looked so like the Lucilla of old, who had schemed and plotted for Mr. Cavendish, that he could not believe in her desertion in his heart.

“That is a delusion like the going off,” he said. “I can’t believe you have gone over to the enemy. When I remember how I have been roving about all those ten years, and how different it might have been, and whose fault it all was﻿—”

This Mr. Cavendish said in a low voice, but it did not the less horrify Aunt Jemima, who felt prepared for any atrocity after it. She would have withdrawn, in justice to her own sense of propriety; but then she thought it was not impossible that he might propose to Lucilla on the spot, or take her hand or something, and for propriety’s sake she stayed.

===Chinese===

“年轻人！”卡文迪什先生说。“如今人们管这个叫年轻么？还有，他准是疯了，不然绝不会梦想着代表一座城，对自己的主义却只字不提。我敢说他还自以为别出心裁呢。”这个不幸的人说。他自以为正给露西拉指点对头的软处，遂愈加起劲地讲下去——“我了解你，知道你不会喜欢那种掺了水的玩意儿。”

“哦，政治的事我从不装懂，”露西拉说。“我听你们先生们谈论，可我从来不装明白。这个若也不留给*你们*自己，我真不知道你们还有什么可干的了。”马乔里班克斯小姐又怜悯地添了一句；她说这话时，那神气同旧日的露西拉——那个为卡文迪什先生出谋划策、运筹布置的露西拉——像到了十足，害得他从心底里没法相信她真的倒戈了。

“那是妄想，同那减色论一样，”他说。“我不能信你投了敌。想想我这十年怎样漂泊四方，想想事情本可以多么不同，再想想这一切是谁的过错——”

这话卡文迪什先生是压低了声音说的，可杰迈玛姑妈照样听得魂飞魄散，从此之后，什么伤风败俗的事她都觉得防得了。论体统，她本该退出去；可转念一想，他说不定当场就要向露西拉求婚，或者握她的手，或者做出点什么来，为了体统起见，她留下了。

===Original===

“Yes,” said Lucilla﻿—and her heart did for one little moment give a faint thump against her breast. She could not help thinking what a difference it might have made to him, poor fellow, had he been under her lawful and righteous sway these ten years. But as she looked at him it became more and more apparent to Miss Marjoribanks that Mr. Cavendish *had* gone off, whatever she herself might have done. The outlines of his fine figure had changed considerably, and his face was a little red, and he had the look of a man whose circumstances, spiritual and temporal, would not quite bear a rigid examination. As she looked at him her pity became tinged by a certain shade of resentment to think that after all it was his own fault. She could not, notwithstanding her natural frankness of expression, say to him, “You foolish soul, why didn’t you marry me somehow, and make a man of yourself?” Lucilla carried honesty very far, but she could not go as far as that. “Yes,” she said, turning her eyes upon him with a sort of abstract sympathy, and then she added softly, “Have you ever seen Her again?” with a lowering of her voice.

This interesting question, which utterly bewildered Aunt Jemima, drove Mr. Cavendish wild with rage. Mrs. John said afterwards that she felt a shiver go through her as he took up the carving-knife, though it was only to cut some cold beef. He grew white all at once, and pressed his lips tightly together, and fixed his eyes on the wall straight before him. “I did not think, after what I once said to you, Miss Marjoribanks, that you would continue to insult my judgment in that way,” he said, with a chill which fell upon the whole table, and took the life out of everything, and dimmed the very fire in the chimney. And after that the conversation was of a sufficiently ordinary description until they went back again into the drawing-room, by which time Mr. Cavendish seemed to have concluded that it was best to pocket the affront.

“I am going to begin my canvass tomorrow,” he said. “I have not seen anybody yet. I have nobody but my sister to take *me* in hand, you know. There was once a time when it might have been different”﻿—and he gave Lucilla a look which she thought on the whole it was best to meet.

===Chinese===

“是啊，”露西拉说——她的心也确乎有一小下，在胸口轻轻撞了一下。她不由得想：这可怜的人，这十年若是在她合法而正义的治下，又会是多么不同。可她越看他，马乔里班克斯小姐越看得明白：卡文迪什先生*确乎*减了色——不论她自己减没减。他当年堂堂身量的轮廓变了许多，脸有些红，一副精神与家计都经不起细查的神气。她望着他，怜惜里渐渐掺进一丝怨怼——想来想去，这终究是他自己的错。她生性直言无隐，可就连她也说不出那句：“你这糊涂人，当初怎么不管怎样不把我娶了，把自己成全成个像样的人？”露西拉的诚实走得极远，可再远也走不到那一步。“是啊，”她说，把眼睛转向他，带着一种超然的怜悯；随后她放轻了声音，柔柔地添了一句：“后来，你见过*她*没有？”

这一句有味的话，问得杰迈玛姑妈如坠五里雾中，却把卡文迪什先生气得发狂。约翰太太事后说，他拿起切肉刀的时候，她只觉一股寒颤穿身而过——尽管那不过是切几片冷牛肉。他霎时白了脸，双唇紧闭，两眼直直盯住面前的墙壁。“马乔里班克斯小姐，我从前同你说过那番话之后，不想你还要这样一而再地糟践我的识见。”他说，一股寒气罩住了整张餐桌，抽走了万物的生气，连烟囱里的炉火都黯了。此后谈话便平平无奇，直到众人回到客厅；到那时，卡文迪什先生似乎已经拿定主意：这口屈辱，还是咽下的好。

“明天我就开始拉票，”他说。“人还一个没见呢。你晓得的，拉扯*我*这桩事，除了我妹妹再没有别人。从前也曾有过一个时候，事情本可以不同”——他向露西拉递去一瞥，她思量再三，觉得还是迎住这一瞥为上。

===Original===

“Yes,” said Miss Marjoribanks, with cruel distinctness, “there was a time when you were the most popular man in Grange Lane﻿—everybody was fond of you. I remember it as if it had been yesterday,” said Lucilla, with a sigh.

“You don’t give a man much encouragement, by Jove!” said the unlucky candidate. “You remember it like yesterday? It may be vanity, but I flatter myself I shall still be found the most popular man in Grange Lane.”

Miss Marjoribanks sighed again, but she did not say anything. On the contrary she turned to Aunt Jemima, who kept in the background an alarmed and alert spectator, to consult her about a shade of wool; and just then Mr. Cavendish, looking out of the window, saw Major Brown conducting his rival through his garden, and shaking hands with him cordially at the door. This was more than the patience of the other candidate could bear. A sudden resolution, hot and angry, as are the resolutions of men who feel themselves to have a failing cause, came into his mind. He had been badgered and baited to such an extent (as he thought) that he had not time to consider if it was wise or not. He, too, had sat to Maria Brown, and commanded once the warmest admiration of the household. He thought he would put it to the test, and see if after all his popularity was only a thing to be remembered like yesterday;﻿—and it was with this intention that he bade a hurried goodbye to Lucilla, and, rushing out, threw himself at once upon the troubled waves of society, which had once been as smooth as glass to the most popular man in Grange Lane.

===Chinese===

“是啊，”马乔里班克斯小姐说，清楚得近乎残忍，“从前是有过一个时候，你是格兰奇巷最得人心的人——人人都喜欢你。我记着呢，就像昨天一样。”露西拉说着，叹了一口气。

“天哪，你可真不给人打气啊！”这位倒霉的候选人说。“你记着像昨天一样？也许是自负吧，可我自己还窃以为，格兰奇巷最得人心的男人，数来数去还得数我呢。”

马乔里班克斯小姐又叹了口气，可什么也没说。她反而转向杰迈玛姑妈——她一直在边上提心吊胆、时刻戒备地旁观着——去同她商量一种毛线的颜色；恰在此时，卡文迪什先生望出窗外，看见布朗少校正领着他的对头穿过自家的花园，在门口同他热热乎乎地握手。这可叫另一位候选人的耐性再受不住了。一个火热的、忿忿的决断——自觉大势日颓的人所常有的那种决断——霎时涌上心头。他（自己觉得）被纠缠折辱到了这个地步，哪里还顾得上掂量明智不明智。他也是给玛丽亚·布朗照过相的，也曾一度赢得过那一家子最热辣的倾慕。他要试它一试，看看他的人心到底是不是只堪“记着像昨天一样”的旧物；——便是抱着这个主意，他匆匆向露西拉道了别，一冲而出，当即纵身跃上社交界那动荡的波涛——那波涛，从前于格兰奇巷最得人心的男人，曾平滑如镜。

## XLI / 四十一
===Original===

Mr. Cavendish thought he had been an object of admiration to Maria Brown, as we have said. He thought of it with a little middle-aged complacency, and a confidence that this vague sentiment would stand the test he was about to apply to it, which did honour to the freshness of his heart. With this idea it was Miss Brown he asked for as he knocked at the Major’s door; and he found them both in the drawing-room, Maria with gloves on to hide the honourable stains of her photography, which made her comparatively useless when she was out of her “studio”﻿—and her father walking about in a state of excitement, which was, indeed, what Mr. Cavendish expected. The two exchanged a guilty look when they saw who their visitor was. They looked as people might well look who had been caught in the fact and did not know how to get over it. They came forward, both of them, with a cowardly cordiality and eagerness to welcome him﻿—“How very good of you to come to see us so soon!” Miss Brown said, and fluttered and looked at her father, and could not tell what more to say. And then a dead pause fell upon them﻿—such a pause as not unfrequently falls upon people who have got through their mutual greetings almost with an excess of cordiality. They stopped short all at once, and looked at each other, and smiled, and made a fatal conscious effort to talk of something. “It is so good of you to come so soon,” Miss Brown repeated; “perhaps you have been to see Lucilla,” and then she stopped again, slightly tremulous, and turned an appealing gaze to her papa.

“I have come to see *you*,” said Mr. Cavendish, plucking up all his courage. “I have been a long time gone, you know, but I have not forgotten Carlingford; and you must forgive me for saying that I was very glad to hear I might still come to see﻿—Miss Brown. As for Lydia?” said the candidate, looking about him with a smile.

“Ah, Lydia,” said her sister, with a sigh﻿—“her eldest is eight, Mr. Cavendish. We don’t see her as often as we should like﻿—marriage makes such a difference. Of course it is quite natural she should be all for her own family now.”

===Chinese===

如我们所说，卡文迪什先生自以为曾是玛丽亚（Maria）·布朗倾慕的对象。他想起这事，带着一点中年人的自得，又自信那点朦胧的情意经得起他即将施下的考验——这自信足为他心地之新鲜添彩。怀着这个念头，他敲响少校家的门时，指名要见的是布朗小姐；他在客厅里见到她们父女俩——玛丽亚手上戴着手套，遮住她摄影工作那光荣的污渍，那污渍使她一出“工作室”便几乎派不上用场——她的父亲正激动地走来走去，这果然不出卡文迪什先生的所料。两人一见来客是谁，交换了一个心虚的眼色。他们那副样子，正像当场被人拿住、又不知如何遮掩过去的人。两人一齐迎上前来，带着怯懦的热忱与急切欢迎他——“你这么快就来看我们，真是太好了！”布朗小姐说，又慌乱地看看父亲，再说不出别的话来。随后一阵死寂落在他们身上——这样的冷场，倒也不时落在刚刚互道寒暄、几乎热忱过头的人们身上。他们猛地顿住，面面相觑，笑了笑，又费力而心虚地想找话说。“你这么快就来，真是太好了，”布朗小姐重复道；“也许你去看了露西拉，”说完又顿住，微微发颤，向她爸爸投去求援的一望。

“我是来看*你*的，”卡文迪什先生鼓起全部勇气说。“我走了很久，你知道，可我没有忘掉卡灵福德；你们得原谅我说，听说我仍可以来看——布朗小姐，我很高兴。莉迪亚呢？”这位候选人笑着环顾四周。

“啊，莉迪亚，”她姐姐叹了口气说——“她的大孩子八岁了，卡文迪什先生。我们不像想的那样常见到她——婚姻把人变得这样不同。当然，她如今一心扑在自己家里，那是再自然不过的。”

“Quite natural,” said Mr. Cavendish, and then he turned to the Major. “I don’t think there are quite so many public changes as I expected to see. The old Rector always holds out, and the old Colonel; and you have not done much that I can see about the new paving. You know what I have come home about, Major; and I am sure I can count upon you to support me,” the candidate said, with a great deal more confidence than he felt in his voice.

Major Brown cleared his throat; his heart was moved by the familiar voice, and he could not conceal his embarrassment. “I hope nothing will ever occur,” he said, “to make any difference in the friendly feelings﻿—I am sure I shall be very glad to welcome you back permanently to Carlingford. You may always rest assured of that,” and he held out his hand. But he grew red as he thought of his treachery, and Maria, who was quaking over it, did not even try to say a word to help him﻿—and as for Mr. Cavendish, he took up his position on the arm of the sofa, as he used to do. But he had a slim youthful figure when he used to do it, and now the attitude was one which revealed a certain dawning rotundity, very different, as Maria afterwards said, from one’s idea of Mr. Cavendish. He was not aware of it himself, but as these two people looked, their simultaneous thought was how much he had changed.

“Thank you, you are very kind,” said Mr. Cavendish. “I have been a little lazy, I am afraid, since I came here; but I expect my agent down tonight, and then, I hope, you’ll come over to my place and have a talk with Woodburn and Centum and the rest about it. I am a poor tactician, for my part. You shall contrive what is best to be done, and I’ll carry it out. I suppose I may expect almost to walk over,” he said. It was the confidence of despair that moved him. The more he saw that his cause was lost, the more he would make it out that he was sure to win﻿—which is not an unusual state of mind.

“I﻿—I don’t know, I am sure,” said poor Major Brown. “To tell the truth, I﻿—though I can safely say my sympathies are always with you, Cavendish﻿—I﻿—have been so unfortunate as to commit myself, you know. It was quite involuntary, I am sure, for I never thought my casual expression of opinion likely to have any weight﻿—”

“Papa never will perceive the weight that is attached to his opinion,” said Miss Brown.

“再自然不过，”卡文迪什先生说，随即转向少校。“我看公共的变化不像我料想的那么多。老教区长照旧撑着，老上校也照旧；新铺的石子路嘛，我看你们也没大动。你知道我是为什么回来的，少校；我确信可以指望你支持我，”这位候选人说，口气里的信心远多于他心里有的。

布朗少校清了清嗓子；这熟悉的声音打动了他，他掩不住自己的窘迫。“我希望无论发生什么，都不要伤了这份友好的情谊——”他说，“你从此长住卡灵福德，我一定非常高兴欢迎你回来。这一点你永远可以放心，”他说着伸出手来。可他想到自己的背信，脸涨红了；玛丽亚为此正瑟瑟发抖，连一句帮他解围的话也没试着说——至于卡文迪什先生，他往沙发扶手上一坐，同当年一个样子。只是当年他这么坐时，身条瘦削年轻；如今这个姿势却显出几分初起的发福，同人们心目中的卡文迪什先生大不相同——玛丽亚后来说。他自己并不觉得，可这两个人看在眼里，同时想到的都是：他变得多么厉害。

“谢谢你，你太好了，”卡文迪什先生说。“我回来以后怕是有点懒了；不过我盼着我的代理人今晚到，那时我想请你们到我家来，同伍德本、森特姆他们大家商量商量。我自己是个蹩脚的军师。该怎么做最好，你们去筹划，我来执行。我想我差不多可以不战而胜吧，”他说。动他的是绝望者的自信。他越看出这局已输，越要装出必赢的样子——这也不是少见的心理。

“我——我说不好，真的，”可怜的布朗少校说。“说老实话，我——虽说我的同情心无疑总在你这一边，卡文迪什——我——不幸已经许了人家，你知道。那全不是有意的，真的，我从没想到我随口发表的一点意见会有什么分量——”

“爸爸就是永远看不出大家把他的意见看得多重，”布朗小姐说。

“I was not thinking of it in the least, Maria,” said the modest Major; “but the fact is, it seems to have been *that* that decided Ashburton to stand; and after drawing a man in to such a thing, the least one can do is to back him out in it. Nobody had an idea then, you know, that you were coming back, my dear fellow. I assure you, if I had known﻿—”

“But even if you had known, you know you never meant it, papa,” said Maria. And Mr. Cavendish sat on the arm of the sofa, and put his hands deep into his pockets, and dropped his upper lip, and knit his eyebrows a little, and listened to the anxious people excusing themselves. He did not make any answer one way or another. He was terribly mortified and disappointed, and it went against his pride to make further remonstrances. When they had done, he got down off his seat and took his right hand out of his pocket and offered it to Miss Brown, who, putting her own into it, poor soul! with the remembrance of her ancient allegiance, was like to cry.

“Well,” he said, “if that is the case, I suppose I need not bother you any longer. You’ll give me your good wishes all the same. I used to hear of Ashburton sometimes, but I never had the least idea he was so popular. And to tell the truth, I don’t think he’s any great things to brag of﻿—though I suppose it’s not to be expected *I* should appreciate his qualities,” Mr. Cavendish added, with a laugh. As for Miss Brown, it was all she could do to keep from crying as he went away. She said she could see, by the way he left the drawing-room, that he was a stricken deer; and yet, notwithstanding this sympathetic feeling, she could not but acknowledge, when Miss Marjoribanks mentioned it, that, to have been such a handsome man, he was inconceivably gone off.

“好吧，”他说，“既然如此，我就不再打扰你们了。好意你们总还是肯给我的吧。阿什伯顿我从前也偶尔听人说起，可我万万没想到他这么得人心。说句实话，我看他也没什么了不得的可夸——不过我想，*我*是不见得会赏识他的长处的，”卡文迪什先生笑着补了一句。至于布朗小姐，他走的时候她强忍着才没哭出来。她说，凭他走出客厅的那副样子，她就看得出他是一头受伤的鹿；可尽管怀着这份怜悯之情，等到马乔里班克斯小姐提起时，她也不能不承认：他从前那样漂亮的一个男人，竟然老得叫人不敢相认。

Mr. Cavendish went up Grange Lane with his hands in his pockets, and tried to think that he did not care; but he did care all the same, and was very bitter in his mind over the failure of friends and the vanity of expectations. The last time he had walked past those garden walls he had thought himself sure of the support of Carlingford, and the personal esteem of all the people in all the houses he was passing. It was after the Archdeacon had broken down in his case against the man whom he called an adventurer, and when Mr. Cavendish felt all the sweetness of being a member of an oligarchy, and entitled to the sympathy and support of his order. Now he went along the same path with his hat over his ears and his hands in his pockets, and rage and pain in his heart. Whose fault was it that his friends had deserted him and Carlingford knew him no more? He might as well have asked whose fault it was that he was getting stout and red in the face, and had not the same grace of figure nor ease of mind as he used to have? He had come very near to settling down and becoming a man of domestic respectability in this quiet place, and he had just escaped in time, and had laughed over it since, and imagined himself, with much glee, an old fogy looking after a lot of children. But the fact is that men do become old fogies even when they have no children to look after, and lose their figure and their elasticity just as soon and perhaps a little sooner in the midst of what is called life than in any milder scene of enjoyment. And it would have been very handy just now to have been sure of his election without paying much for it. He had been living fast, and spending a great deal of money, and this, after all, was the only real ambition he had ever had; and he had thought within himself that if he won he would change his mode of life, and turn over a new leaf, and become all at once a different man.

===Chinese===

卡文迪什先生双手插兜走上格兰奇巷，竭力想叫自己不在乎；可他到底在乎，心里为朋友的负心和期望的虚妄苦涩得很。上一回他走过这些花园墙时，他还自以为稳拿卡灵福德的支持，稳拿眼前这一家家住户每个人的敬重。那是在会吏总告倒他称为冒险家的那个人、败下阵来之后；那时卡文迪什先生正尝尽作为一个寡头集团成员的全部甜头——有权利享他那个阶层的同情与支援。如今他走的是同一条路，帽子压到耳朵上，两手插在口袋里，一腔愤懑与疼痛。朋友们背弃了他，卡灵福德不再认识他——这是谁的错？他不妨再问：他发了福、红了脸，没了当年的身段与心境，这又是谁的错？他差一点就在这安静地方安顿下来，做个有家室的体面人了，而他及时逃脱了，事后想起还要笑，还要得意地想象自己变成一个看管一大群孩子的老古板。可实情是，男人即便没有孩子要看管，也照样会变成老古板；身段和弹性丢起来一样快——在这所谓的人世中心，说不定还比任何温和些的享乐场中丢得更快一点。而眼下，若能不大破费就稳稳当选，那可太顺手了。他一直活得快，花钱花得凶；说到底，这才是他平生唯一真正的抱负；他心里盘算过：若是赢了，他就换一种活法，翻开新的一页，霎时间变成另一个人。

===Original===

When a man has made such a resolution, and feels not only that a mere success but a moral reformation depends upon his victory, he may be permitted to consider that he has a right to win; and it may be divined what his state of mind was when he had made the discovery that even his old friends did not see his election to be of any such importance as he did, and could think of a miserable little bit of self-importance or gratified vanity more than of his interests﻿—even the women who had once been so kind to him! He had just got so far in his thoughts when he met Mr. Centum, who stared for a moment, and then burst into one of his great laughs as he greeted him. “Good Lord! Cavendish, is this you? I never expected to see you like that!” the banker said, in his coarse way. “You’re stouter than I am, old fellow; and such an Adonis as you used to be!” Mr. Cavendish had to bear all this without giving way to his feelings, or even showing them any more than he could help it. Nobody would spare him that imbecile suggestion as to how things used to be. To be growing stouter than Centum without Centum’s excuse of being a well-to-do householder and father of a family, and respectable man from whom stoutness was expected, was very bitter to him: but he had to gulp it down, and recollect that Centum was as yet the only influential supporter, except his brother-in-law, whom he had in Carlingford.

“What have you been doing with yourself since you came that nobody has seen you?” said Mr. Centum. “If you are to do any good here, you know, we shall have to look alive.”

“I have been ill,” said the unfortunate candidate, with a little natural loss of temper. “You would not have a man to trudge about at this time of year in all weathers when he is ill.”

“I would not be ill again, if I were you, till it’s all over,” said Mr. Centum. “We shall have to fight every inch of our ground; and I tell you that fellow Ashburton knows what he’s about﻿—he goes at everything in a steady sort of way. He’s not brilliant, you know, but he’s sure﻿—”

“Brilliant!” said Mr. Cavendish, “I should think not. It is Lucilla Marjoribanks who is putting him up to it. You know she had an old grudge at me.”

===Chinese===

一个人下了这样的决心，又觉得不但一场成功、连一场道德的洗心革面都系于他的胜利，那便可以容许他自认为有赢的权利了；所以当他发觉，连他的老朋友们也不把他的当选看得像他那样要紧，反倒把一点可怜的小小的自尊、一点虚荣的满足看得比他的利益还重——连从前待他那么好的太太们也这样！——他是什么心境，可想而知。他刚想到这里，就遇见了森特姆先生；森特姆先生怔了一怔，随即迸出一声他的大笑来招呼他。“我的天！卡文迪什，这是你吗？我可从没料到你会成了这副模样！”这位银行家用他那粗鲁的方式说。“你比我还发福了，老伙计；想当年你是何等的一个美男子！”卡文迪什先生只得忍下这一切，不发作感情，能不露就不露。谁也不肯饶过他，偏要提那些当年如何如何的蠢话。他发福发得赛过了森特姆，却没有森特姆的托辞——一个殷实的户主、一家之父、众人眼里理当发福的体面人——这于他是很苦的一杯；可他只得咽下去，还要记着：在卡灵福德，森特姆是他眼下除内弟之外唯一有分量的支持者。

“你回来以后干什么去了，谁也没见着你的人影？”森特姆先生说。“你要想在这儿成事，你知道，我们就得抓紧了。”

“我病了，”这位倒霉的候选人说，不免带出一点火气。“总不能叫一个人病着还一年到头顶风冒雪地四处奔走。”

“我要是你，在一切了结之前就不再病了，”森特姆先生说。“我们得寸土必争；我告诉你，阿什伯顿那家伙心里有数——他做什么都是稳扎稳打的一路。他不耀眼，你知道，可他靠得住——”

“耀眼！”卡文迪什先生说，“我想也是。是露西拉·马乔里班克斯在背后撮弄他。你知道她跟我有宿怨。”

It was a sort of thing Mr. Cavendish was not used to, and he felt it accordingly. To be sure he knew that he was ten years older, and that there were several things which he could not do with the same facility as in his youth. But he had saved up Carlingford in his imagination as a spot in which he would always be young, and where nobody should find out the difference; and instead of that, it was precisely in Carlingford that he was fated to hear how changed he was, with a frankness which only old friends would have been justified in using. “不过我看你没法子再像从前那样来这一套了，卡文迪什。你如今发得这么福，就该娶个太太，安顿下来，做个社交界稳重的成员。”连他自己的支持者也用这样一番话打发他，说罢又一声大笑，忙着办事去了。这一套是卡文迪什先生不惯受的，所以他格外觉得难受。不错，他知道自己老了十岁，好几件事再不能像年轻时那样轻而易举。可他在想象里一直把卡灵福德储存成一个他永远年轻的地方，一个谁也看不出差别的地方；谁料偏偏在卡灵福德，他命定要听人说他变得多么厉害，而且是用只有老朋友才配用的那种直率。至于露西拉·马乔里班克斯，她毋宁说比从前更好看了，压根儿没有见老。卡文迪什先生不曾想到，这也许是因为露西拉如今还不像他十年前那么老——十年前那一段，如今是被他算作自己的青年时代的。他反倒更愿意取一个道德的看法，认定是马乔里班克斯小姐那份女人的不能过度的天性，挡住了岁月与欢场，没能在她身上生出应有效力。而他呢，可怜的人，*倒是*过度了。他过日子不曾像留在卡灵福德本可以做到的那样检点；如今他在付出代价。他走到格罗夫街顶头时，心里那番有益的觉悟正是这般。就在那里，一阵柔软的旧忆拂过他的心头。四顾无一人同情，他不由得回想起旧日那位魔女——她惯常为他唱歌，听他说话，对他发火。多半他会终于沿着那条熟路踱下去，为莱克先生的选票游说一番——那在卡灵福德于他毫无益处——可正在那时，马乔里班克斯医生的马车停住了。医生那天早晨脸色很怪，虽说谁也没有特别留意——也许因为他在马车里想事情时总把脸色抹平，那车厢是他有心事时的避难所。可他突然停车，要同卡文迪什
